en: In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a mere ocean. Therein, Prajāpati alone came into being upon a lotus leaf. Within his mind, desire arose: "May I create this. Therefore, what a person first conceives with the mind, that he expresses with speech and performs through action. Concerning this, it has been said: "In the beginning, desire arose within the mind; it was the first seed of mind."

"Being found the kinsman in non-being, the seers discovered him by means of meditation and inspired thought. Thus, whatever desire he had, it approached him. He performed austerity; having performed austerity, he beheld this Nārasiṃha king of mantras in the Anuṣṭubh meter. By means of it, indeed, he created all this, whatever exists here. Therefore, they say that all this is Anuṣṭubh, whatever exists here. From the Anuṣṭubh, indeed, these beings are born; once born, they live by the Anuṣṭubh; [into] the Anuṣṭubh...

They depart and they enter into it; for this [chant] there is an *anuṣṭubh* as the first and an *anuṣṭubh* as the last. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech; by means of speech they depart, and by means of speech they rise up. This *anuṣṭubh* is the supreme among the meters. Thus it is said. || 1 ||

One should know that the earth, together with its oceans, mountains, and seven continents, is the first foot of that Sāman; one should know that the intermediate space, frequented by hosts of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases, is the second foot of that Sāman; one should know that heaven, frequented by all the gods—the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—is the third foot of that Sāman; and one should know that the stainless nature of Brahman, situated in the supreme ether, is the fourth foot of that Sāman. He who knows this attains immortality.

The four Vedas—Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan—along with their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) and branches (śākhās), constitute its four feet. What is the meditation? What is the deity? What are the auxiliary sciences? What are their deities? What is the metre? Who is the seer? || 2 ||

The connection is: "The waters were. The word *vai* indicates what is well-known. This water, perceived through direct perception and other means, was indeed that very Prajāpati. By the masculine pronoun *saḥ*, which refers back to what has preceded, he points to the subject under discussion, in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "He who first ordains the Brāhmaṇa, and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him"—that Prajāpati, being alone, came into being (*samabhavat*) upon the lotus leaf.

In the mind—that is, within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—of that Prajāpati, desire (*kāma*), which is the will, arose; the meaning is that it arose with respect to creation, in the form "I shall create this. Therefore, whatever a person approaches with the mind—that is, desires with the internal organ—that he expresses through speech. He shows that the performance of action is preceded by the speaking of speech, as is well known in the world, saying: "He performs that action through work. To strengthen the very point already stated, he cites a *ṛc* verse as witness: "And so this has been declared."

The meaning of the *ṛc* is indeed firmly established; however, a looseness of meaning in the *sāman* and *yajus* is also possible, according to the Vedic revelation: "Whatever is performed in the sacrifice by *sāman* or *yajus* is loose, but that which is done by *ṛc* is firm. With regard to that very same meaning, this *ṛc* about to be recited is proclaimed: "The desire of the mind arose before that; the seed, the water, was first at the beginning, at the time of creation, from which cause it came to be."

Alternatively, this is a specification of time: "when" (*yadā*) means at that very time when water first existed, the desire of the mind (*manasaḥ kāmaḥ*) came into being (*samavartata*) with respect to the object, namely, the subject of creation; this is the meaning. The seers (*kavayaḥ*), seeking through their wisdom (*vipaścitaḥ*), discovered within the heart (*hradi*) the connection (*bandhum*), that is, the bond or manifestation, of the existent (*sataḥ*) Brahman. This is because the word "non-existent" (*asat*) is used for Brahman in the sense of being undifferentiated by name and form, as in such passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*).

Having established [the Self] within the heart (*hṛd*) and having beheld the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) with wisdom (*manīṣā*), that is, with an intellect seeking the Supreme, they discovered the Kinsman of the Brahman—the Supreme Brahman who is like a kinsman, the explicator, distinguished by attributes such as the ocean of milk, the creator of the future creation, and the one to be worshipped through the root-mantra and the *sāman*—within the heart. This is the hidden intention of the second half of the verse. The word "iti" indicates the completion of the *ṛc*.

That which is desired approaches this seeker of desire; whatever he desires comes to pass. He is Prajāpati. He performed austerity (*atapyata*), for according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), "Austerity is the one-pointedness of the mind and the senses; that is the highest austerity. Thus, he brought about the one-pointed concentration of his mind and his senses.

He is Prajāpati; having performed austerity—as previously explained—that Prajāpati [discovered] this King of Mantras (mantrarāja), which is the subject under discussion and referred to by the pronoun "this" (*etam*), indicated here with a hidden intention by the phrase "the bond of Being" (*sato bandhum*) according to the maxim: "Because light is designated as the feet. It is the king of the mantras belonging to this context, the primary one, or the king of the *Sāmans*. Regarding the word "mantra," [it is said]: "O Ahebudhnya, protect my mantra—[that mantra] which the seers who know the three Vedas (*trayīvid*) know."

Because [the term] is applied to the *sāman* as well in passages such as "the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*s," [the word] "Nārasiṃha" refers to the *sāman* and so forth related to Nṛsiṃha, derived from the secondary suffix (*taddhita*). To exclude the possibility that it might refer to the *Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī* and other such verses, the word "Ānuṣṭubha" specifies a particular *ṛk* characterized by the *anuṣṭubh* meter, according to the principle: "This day consists of the *gāyatra*. The intended meaning is that he "beheld," that is, saw.

The meaning is as follows: in the second, third, fourth, and fifth Upaniṣads, three words beginning with "Mantrarāja" are employed; by virtue of their being Tatpuruṣa compounds, Bahuvrīhi compounds, and Taddhita derivatives, they express the meaning of each preceding Upaniṣad and, being used at the outset, encompass the entire Brāhmī-vidyā. Therefore, the sense is that he beheld the entire Brāhmī-vidyā which is about to be described.

By that which was indeed previously mentioned—*vai* meaning "well-known"—he created all this, that which is established by perception and other means of knowledge; he created whatever exists here clearly. Therefore, they call all this *ānuṣṭubha*, including whatever is designated by the terms "King of Mantras" (*mantrarāja*) and "Narasimha. Here, by the use of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in the word *ānuṣṭubha*, it demonstrates the capacity of those very thirty-two syllables and of that *sāman*.
Furthermore, in this narrative, it is said that Prajāpati, desiring to know the cause for the sake of creating the three worlds through austerity, [proceeded].

Because his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) was utterly pure, he beheld an *anuṣṭubh* verse that is endowed with the three powers (*śakti*), whose nature is Brahman, and which is the cause of all creation, preceded by the creation of the elements; thus [the text] says. By stating, "From the *anuṣṭubh* indeed these beings are born, by the *anuṣṭubh* those born live, into the *anuṣṭubh* they enter and merge," it demonstrates that this [verse] is characterized by the definition of Brahman according to the sūtra: "From which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this [world]."

To reinforce the very point already stated, he cites a *ṛc* as witness: "This *ṛc* about to be mentioned is the witness (*sākṣiṇī*) of that [Brahman] whose nature is the *brāhmaṇa*. The *anuṣṭubh* is the first; it is the first and primordial of all creation. The *anuṣṭubh* is the last and most excellent. He shows that speech indeed is the *anuṣṭubh*, for the entire expansion of speech is dissolved within the *anuṣṭubh*. Since the creation of forms is preceded by the creation of names, and since the *anuṣṭubh* is of the nature of speech, the *anuṣṭubh* alone is the root cause.

By speech alone do beings proceed; by the *anuṣṭubh* alone they go to dissolution. By speech alone—that is, by the *anuṣṭubh* alone—they rise up, that is, they emerge. This [speech] is indeed the supreme among the meters, such as the *gāyatrī* and others, or among the meters, that is, the Vedas. And the supremacy of the *anuṣṭubh* is due to its being the substratum of the Sāman.

And the preeminence of the Sāman is established by the Śruti: "The gods, indeed, did not find support in the Ṛk nor in the Yajus; they found support in the Sāman alone," and by the Smṛti: "Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda. The word "iti" in the phrase "yat anuṣṭub iti" indicates the conclusion of the Ṛk.

Thus, having first understood the words "mantrarāja," "nārasiṃha," and "anuṣṭubh"—which summarize the entire worship of Narasiṃha at the conclusion of the narrative—and having thereby summarized the complete worship performed by Prajāpati for the sake of creation using those very words, since the performance [of the rite] would now otherwise occur without distinction, [the author proceeds]: because the Sāman manifests the syllables of the Ṛk, and because that which is manifested is preceded by its manifestor, and because the Sāman is the most excellent of all the Vedas—[it is said: "The gods, indeed, were not in the Ṛk... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1).

Based on the Vedic revelation, "They took refuge in the Yajus, they took refuge in the Sāman," and the Smṛti statement, "Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda," and because this [Lord] is the king of the Sāmas, when the meditation upon Him is to be undertaken, he speaks [the following] after first indicating the sequence:

Prajāpati said: "He who knows that eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra [mantra] which is consecrated by glory (*śrī*), and who knows it as a limb (*aṅga*) of the Sāman—he is indeed consecrated by glory. All the Vedas have the *praṇava* (Om) as their beginning; he who knows that *praṇava* as a limb of the Sāman conquers the three worlds. The twenty-four-syllabled Mahālakṣmī is a *yajus*; he who knows it as a limb of the Sāman becomes possessed of long life, fame, renown, knowledge, and sovereignty. Therefore, one should know this Sāman with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality."

One goes to the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, and the Yajurlakṣmī; they do not desire [to teach] these to a woman or a Śūdra. He who knows the twenty-eight-syllable Sāman goes to immortality. If a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, Yajus, and Praṇava, he goes downward after death. Therefore, one should never speak of them; if the teacher speaks of them, he too, upon death, goes downward. 3.

Since it might otherwise have been understood as a mere form of worship performed in any way whatsoever, the mention of the ocean at the very beginning with the words "together with the ocean" (sasāgarām) indicates that the worship is preceded by the ocean. For this very reason, some explain that "sāgara" is not an adjective qualifying the earth.

And then, first having meditated upon the ocean, the Sea of Milk, and having performed the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) of the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* while seated in its shadow—or rather, while he [the practitioner] is seated there—one should understand that worship as "with the ocean," meaning that worship which exists together with the ocean, following the phrase "in that very [place], along with the mountains," and so forth; this is the ellipsis. It is not correct [to claim] that there is a separation from the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), as in the passage beginning, "The Brahman is the head, the foundation is the tail."

The word "ocean" (sāgara) does not, for its part, denote a specific form of meditation; rather, it indicates [the sequence] by way of the principle of "beginning with that" (*tad-ādi-nyāya*) within a series of objects arranged in a fixed order. This remains the same even when there is syntactic unity through its being an attribute of something else. Therefore, because the word "ocean" is employed at the very beginning, the meditation characterized by a fixed sequence must be understood as starting with the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīroda-arṇava*). And thus is the meaning.

The meaning is that one should know the earth—characterized by the aforementioned attributes—to be the first quarter of that *anuṣṭubh* verse which has been deposited, and of that *sāman* which has been deposited, within the heart-lotus of the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) as he lies or sits upon the ocean of milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*). This is because it exists within his heart.

In the same way, regarding the three subsequent quarters [of the verse], one should understand that the forms of the Yakṣa, Gandharva, Vasu, Rudra, and Brahmā correspond to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) by virtue of their worldly association; and that these constitute the second, third, and fourth quarters of that *Sāman*—of that *Anuṣṭubh* which has been deposited and of the *Sāman* which has been deposited—as being situated within the head, crest, and armor of that Man-Lion (*nṛkesarin*). Thus the connection is to be made.

Thus, because of the mention of "going" in the statement, "He who knows the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) goes to immortality," that immortality is a product (*kārya*) and not absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), according to the principle: "Bādari [holds] that this [immortality] is a product, because going is logically possible for it. Alternatively, since it is heard at the end [of the passage]: "At the end of the body, the God explains the supreme Brahman, the attributeless Brahman, the Savior, as the oneness of the individual self and the inner Brahman by means of the *tāraka* syllables alone," immortality here refers to absolute liberation.

In this manner, its immortality, which is heard of in both ways above, is to be explained. It has been explained that the Great Wheel consists of four feet—the four Vedas, namely the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan, along with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas) and branches (śākhās). In its hub, we shall describe the fifth limb, known as the Weapon (astra), which belongs to the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) who either reclines or sits upon the Ocean of Milk.

But surely, having not yet completed the meditation on the Sāman with its limbs and sub-limbs, what is this sudden commencement of an inquiry into the object of meditation in the middle? It is like the prattle of a ghost—what is the meditation, what is the deity, what are the limbs, what are the deities of those limbs, what is the metre, and who is the seer? Why this inquiry into the meditation, the deity, the limbs, the deities of the limbs, the metre, and the seer? To this it is replied: In this narrative, it is said that after Prajāpati had completed one meditation by way of the Sāman for the gods who had ceased [their questioning], he became silent, desiring to awaken the understanding of his listeners.

To investigate—whether they are asking about a specific sub-division regarding the very subject previously mentioned, or whether there is some other collection of matters useful for that purpose, or not—with this intention, the inquiry occurs in the middle rather than at the beginning. In that regard, there are six questions. In the first question, "one should know," there is the inquiry as to whether, following the previously stated injunction and up until the completion of the Upaniṣads, it is mere knowledge or meditation.

Since the injunction "one should know" (*jānīyāt*) does not mention the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*), and because no [other] answer is given there, the maxim "what is not forbidden is consented to" (*apratiṣiddhamanumataṃ bhavati*) applies; thus, "one should know" here means "one should meditate. The root *dhyai* is used in the sense of the practice of knowledge. [The questions are: "What is its deity? What is its meter? Who is its seer? (*kiṃ daivataṃ kiṃ chandaḥ ka ṛṣiḥ*)?

Regarding the *praṇava*, because the *nārasiṃha-anuṣṭubh* is heard as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and because Prajāpati Brāhmaṇa himself is the narrator, the subsequent [section] concerns the deity, meter, and seer; for according to the traditional rule of Āśvalāyana: "He whose words [they are] is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and that which is spoken by him is the deity. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the *praṇava*.

Since it might otherwise have been understood as a form of worship performed in any random manner, the mention of the ocean at the very outset in the phrase "together with the ocean" (*sasāgarām*) indicates that the worship is preceded by the ocean. For this very reason, some commentators do not explain "ocean" (*sāgara*) as an adjective qualifying the earth.

And then, first having meditated upon the ocean, the Milky Sea (kṣīrodārṇava), and being seated within its shadow, or having performed the five-limbed assignment (pañcāṅganyāsa) of the Ṛg and Sāman verses upon it, one should understand that very [meditation] as "together with the ocean"—that is, the meditation whose occurrence is accompanied by the ocean, according to the phrase "with the mountains," and so forth; this is the ellipsis. Just as in the passage beginning "the Brāhmaṇa is the tail, the support," there appears to be a separation from the Ānandamaya [Self], so too here [it would seem]. That, however, is incorrect.

The word "ocean" (sāgara) does not, for its part, denote a specific form of meditation; rather, it indicates [the sequence] by the principle of "beginning with that" (*tad-ādinyāya*) within a series of objects arranged in a fixed order. This remains the same even when there is syntactic unity through its being an attribute of something else. Therefore, because the word "ocean" is employed at the very beginning, the meditation with a fixed sequence must be understood as starting with the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*). And thus is the meaning.

The meaning is that one should know the earth—characterized by the aforementioned attributes—as the first quarter of that *anuṣṭubh* verse which has been deposited, and of that *sāman* which has been deposited, located within the heart of the Man-Lion (*nṛkesarin*) as he lies upon or sits in the ocean of milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*). This refers to the heart as the specific limb, existing within the interior of the heart.

In this same manner, regarding the three subsequent quarters as well, one should understand that the forms of the Yakṣa, Gandharva, Vasu, Rudra, and Brahmā—due to their association with the worlds—are the second, third, and fourth quarters of that *sāman* belonging to the *anuṣṭubh* verse that has been deposited, and they exist within the head, crest, and armor of that Man-Lion (*nṛkesarin*). This is how the connection should be understood.

Thus, he who knows the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) attains immortality (*amṛtatva*). Since "attaining" (*gacchati*) is mentioned as an action, this immortality is something to be produced (*kārya*), not absolute liberation (*kaivalya*); for according to the principle, "Bādari [holds that] this [immortality] is something to be produced, because the going [to Brahman] is logically possible. Alternatively, at the end of the body, the Lord teaches the supreme Brahman—the attributeless Brahman, the Savior—by means of the syllables of the Savior-mantra, explaining the oneness of the inner Self and Brahman; since this is heard at the conclusion [of the teaching], immortality here is absolute liberation.

Thus, the immortality of this [deity] mentioned above in both ways is to be explained. It has been explained that the Mahācakra consists of four feet, namely the four Vedas—Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan—along with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas) and branches (śākhās). Now we shall describe its fifth limb, called the *astra*, which pertains to the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) who reclines or sits upon the Ocean of Milk at its hub (*nābhi*).

But surely, having not yet completed the meditations on the limbs (*sāṅgopāsanā*), what is this sudden introduction of the objects of meditation in the middle? It is like the prattle of a ghost—what is the meditation, what is the deity, what are the limbs, what are the deities of the limbs, what is the meter, and who is the seer? Why this inquiry into the meditation, the deity, the limbs, the deities of the limbs, the meter, and the seer? To this it is replied: In this narrative, it is said that after Prajāpati had completed a single meditation by way of the Sāman for the gods who were weary, he became silent, desiring to awaken the understanding of his listeners.

To investigate—whether they are asking about a specific sub-variety within the very subject previously mentioned, or whether there is some other collection of matters useful for that purpose, or not—with this intention, he does not begin [the formal teaching] in the middle; rather, he introduces it at the outset. In that regard, there are six questions. In the first question, the inquiry is whether, according to the previously stated rule "one should know," there is merely knowledge or meditation [that follows] later in the Upanishads until their conclusion. This is the question.

Since the injunction "one should know" (*jānīyāt*) does not mention the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*), and because no answer is given on that point, the maxim "what is not prohibited is consented to" (*apratiṣiddhamanumataṃ bhavati*) applies; thus, in the phrase "one should know," the meaning is "one should meditate. The root *dhyai* (to meditate) occurs here in the sense of the practice of knowledge. [One should ask: "What is its deity? What is its meter? Who is its seer? (*kiṃ daivataṃ kiṃ chandaḥ ka ṛṣiḥ*)?

Regarding the *praṇava*, because the *nārasiṃha-anuṣṭubh* is heard as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and because Prajāpati Brāhmaṇa himself is the narrator, the subsequent [verse] has him as its deity, meter, and seer (*ṛṣi*). This is according to the traditional rule of Āśvalāyana: "He whose words [constitute the mantra] is the seer; that which is spoken by him is the deity. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the *praṇava*.

Prajāpati said: "Agni is indeed the Vedas; he is all this, all beings, the vital breaths, the senses, cattle, food, immortality, the sovereign (samrāṭ), the self-ruler (svarāṭ), and the radiant ruler (virāṭ). One should know that to be the first foot of the Sāman. The Sun, who consists of the forms of Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan, the golden person within the sun—this one should know to be the second foot of the Sāman. He who prevails over the plants, the Lord of Stars, Soma—this one should know to be the third foot of the Sāman. He is Brāhma, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra."

That is Agni; that is the imperishable, supreme, self-ruling Svarāj. One should know the fourth foot of the Sāman; he who knows it attains immortality. One should know the Sāman as "Ugra" (the fierce), the first part of the first [foot]; "Jvala" (the blazing), the first part of the second; "Nṛsiṃha" (the Man-Lion), the first part of the third; and "Mṛtyu" (Death), the first part of the fourth. He who knows this attains immortality. Therefore, one should not recite this Sāman anywhere at all. If one wishes to give it, one may give it to a son or to a disciple who is obedient. Thus ends the fourth section.

Prajāpati said: "He who indeed knows that eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra [mantra], which is consecrated by glory (*śrī*), as a limb of the Sāman—he is indeed consecrated by glory. All the Vedas have the *praṇava* as their beginning; he who knows that *praṇava* as a limb of the Sāman conquers the three worlds. The Great Lakṣmī consists of twenty-four syllables; it is a *yajus*. He who knows that as a limb of the Sāman becomes possessed of long life, fame, renown, knowledge, and excellence. Therefore, one should know this Sāman with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality."

One goes to [the state of] Sāvitrī, Praṇava, Yajurlakṣmī; they do not desire [to teach] these to a woman or a Śūdra. He who knows the twenty-eight-syllable Sāman attains immortality. If a woman or a Śūdra should know Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, Yajus, and Praṇava, he goes downward after death. Therefore, one should never teach them; if he teaches them, that teacher, because of that very act, goes downward after death. || 3 ||

In this context, it is said that the four sets of six *praṇavas* are independent [of one another], because the knowledge of the principal (*aṅgin*) presupposes the knowledge of the auxiliary (*aṅga*), and by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), they are auxiliaries of the *sāman*. That Prajāpati, having observed the understanding and the desire for instruction of the listeners, was delighted; since particles have multiple meanings, he spoke the subsequent words: "He who indeed... By means of repetition (*vīpsā*), he demonstrates his state of being filled with joy.

The eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra [verse] is "consecrated by Śrī," meaning it is consecrated by the seed-syllable (bīja) of Śrī placed above it. By stating that one "knows this limb of the Sāman as consecrated," since consecration begins with the head, he prescribes its status as a limb by means of the phrase "one knows the limb of the Sāman" when that [seed-syllable] has been consecrated in the position of the head-limb.

"He is indeed consecrated with glory"—this is a statement of result heard everywhere regarding the limbs [of the ritual]. "In the case of substances, preparatory acts, and rituals, because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a result must be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)," according to which it is an *arthavāda*; or else, by the principle of "He strews the grass so as not to be overtopped; he thus makes him not overtopped with progeny and cattle," it constitutes a section on results arising from subsidiary qualities (*guṇaphalādhikāra*).

All the Vedas begin with the *praṇava*; thus, "that *praṇava*" refers to all the Vedas and the eight Upavedas. By placing the *praṇava* in that position—that is, in the place of the heart-limb (*hṛdayāṅga*)—it shows that the syllables of the Sāman are more significant than the *praṇava*, which is the source of all the Vedas. The statement, "He who knows that limb of the Sāman conquers the three worlds," has already been explained.

The *mahālakṣmī* [verse] consists of twenty-four syllables and belongs to the *Yajus*. Therefore, in that place of the twenty-four syllables, above the third foot of the *Sāman*, one should know the limb of the *Sāman*; the meaning is that it stands in the position of the *śikhā-aṅga*. It is longevity, glory, praise of knowledge, fame, and praise by the people; it has been stated that one becomes possessed of the excellence of knowledge. Since the fruit of the limb of the *Sāman* is thus, therefore one should know this *Sāman* with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality—the meaning has already been explained.

The displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the *Sāvitrī* and other mantras—which would otherwise have been assigned to the locations of the heart and other limbs—is intended to prescribe them as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) at the very beginning; this demonstrates that the unity of the meditation is the intended meaning through the correspondence between the opening and the conclusion. By enjoining the prohibition, "One should not [teach] the *Sāvitrī*, the *Praṇava*, or the *Yajurlakṣmī* to a woman or a Śūdra" (*strīśūdrāya*), where "woman and Śūdra" (*strīśūdra*) refers to a woman and a Śūdra together, the text shows that even women and Śūdras possess the qualification for the primary meditation.

"One should know the Sāman as having thirty-two syllables"—thus he enjoins the connection of the thirty-two syllables with the Sāman. "He who knows," and so forth, has its meaning already explained. By showing the transgression—that if a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, or the Praṇava, he goes to the nether regions (naraka) after death—he strengthens the prohibition itself. Therefore, the statement "he never teaches" shows the teacher's prohibition that he must not teach at any time whatsoever.
And if the Teacher explains it thus, by that very statement he confirms the prohibition itself, showing the transgression incurred by one who dies and goes to the lower realms.

In this context, it is said that while there are four *praṇavas*, three of them are independent because the knowledge of the principal (*aṅgin*) presupposes the knowledge of its members (*aṅga*); by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the remaining one is the member belonging to the *sāman*. Prajāpati, having observed the understanding and the desire for instruction of his listeners, was delighted—and since particles have multiple meanings—he spoke the subsequent words, "sa yo ha vā... He uses repetition (*vīpsā*) to demonstrate the intensity of his joy.

The eight-syllabled *pada* of the *Sāvitra* [verse] is "consecrated by Śrī," meaning it is consecrated by the *Śrī*-seed syllable (*śrī-bīja*) at its upper part. By stating that one "knows the limb of that Sāman as being consecrated," since consecration begins with the head, he prescribes its status as a limb by means of the phrase "one knows the limb of the Sāman" when that [limb] has been consecrated in the position of the head-limb.

"He is indeed consecrated with glory"—such is the hearing of results mentioned everywhere regarding the limbs [of the sacrifice]. This is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), according to the principle: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and ritual actions, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a result must be an *arthavāda*. Alternatively, it may be a section concerning the fruit of a subsidiary quality (*guṇaphalādhikāra*), according to the rule: "He strews the grass so as not to be seen through; verily by means of progeny and cattle he makes him not to be seen through."

All the Vedas begin with the *praṇava*; thus, "that *praṇava*" refers to all the Vedas and the eight Upavedas. By placing the *praṇava* in that position—in the place of the heart and the limbs—it shows that the syllables of the Sāman are more significant than the *praṇava*, which is the source of all the Vedas. The statement, "He who knows that limb of the Sāman conquers the three worlds," has already been explained.

The *mahālakṣmī* [verse] consists of twenty-four syllables and belongs to the Yajurveda. In that place of twenty-four syllables, above the third foot of the Sāman, one should know the limb of the Sāman; this means it stands in the position of the *śikhā-aṅga*. It is longevity, fame, praise of knowledge, renown, and praise by the people; it has been stated that one becomes possessed of the excellence of knowledge. Since such is the fruit of the limb of the Sāman, therefore one should know this Sāman with its limbs (*sāṅga*); he who knows it attains immortality—this is the meaning already stated.

The displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the *Sāvitrī* and other mantras—which would otherwise have been assigned to the locations of the heart and other limbs—is for the purpose of enjoining them as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) at the very beginning; this demonstrates that the unity of the meditation (*vidyaikya*) is the intended meaning, as shown by the opening and concluding statements. By stating the prohibition, "They do not desire to [teach] the *Sāvitrī*, the *Praṇava*, or the *Yajurlakṣmī* to a woman or a Śūdra" (*strīśūdrāya*), [the text] shows that women and Śūdras also possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the primary meditation.

"One should know the Sāman as having thirty-two syllables"—thus he enjoins the connection of the thirty-two syllables with the Sāman. "He who knows," and so forth, has its meaning already explained. By showing the transgression—"if a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, or the Praṇava, he, upon death, goes down to hell"—he confirms the prohibition itself. Therefore, by stating "one should never teach it," he demonstrates the teacher's prohibition that one must not teach it at any time whatsoever.
And if the teacher explains it, by that very explanation he confirms the prohibition itself through the observation of the transgression that "one who is dead goes downwards."

One should know the *Sāman* as the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) reclining upon the ocean of milk, the supreme state meditated upon by yogis; he who knows it attains immortality. One should know the *Sāman* as the Hero (*vīram*) at the end of the first half-verse, *taṃsaḥ* at the end of the second half-verse, *haṃbhī* at the end of the third half-verse, and *mṛtyum* at the end of the fourth half-verse; he who knows it attains immortality. Therefore, whoever knows this *Sāman* through the mouth of any teacher whatsoever is liberated from *saṃsāra* with that very body.

Through this very recitation, one who desires liberation is liberated; with that same body, one beholds the Deity. Therefore, this alone is the primary gateway in the Kali age, and not others. Consequently, one should know this Sāman together with its limbs; he who knows it becomes a seeker of liberation. 5.

Prajāpati said: "Agni is indeed the Vedas; he has spread out all these beings, the vital breaths, the senses, cattle, food, immortality, the Samrāṭ, the Svarāṭ, and the Virāṭ—one should know this to be the first foot of the Sāman. The Sun, who consists of the form of Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan, the golden person within the sun—one should know this to be the second foot of the Sāman. He who rules over the plants, the Moon, the lord of the stars—one should know this to be the third foot of the Sāman. He is Brahman, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra."

That is Agni; that is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-Ruling Lord. One should know this as the fourth foot of the Sāman; he who knows it attains immortality. One should know the Sāman whose first syllable of the first [foot] is *ugram*, the first syllable of the second is *jvalam*, the first syllable of the third is *nṛsiṃ*, and the first syllable of the fourth is *mṛtyum*; he who knows it attains immortality. Therefore, one does not recite this Sāman anywhere at all. If, however, one desires to give it, one shall give it to a son who is obedient, or to another disciple. || 4 ||

Having thus explained the constituent parts (*sāmāṅga*) and having stated that the qualification for their worship excludes women and *śūdras*, [the author] proceeds to state the deities (*daivata*) of the final sections (*praṇa*). To declare that the very deity of the *Sāman* is the deity of each respective limb situated in its place, that Prajāpati, being delighted, spoke the subsequent [text] regarding the final sections: from "Agni indeed is the Vedas, this all... up to "...he who knows this attains immortality," which is to be connected with the passage beginning "together with the oceans. This is what is meant.

Whether the Lord is reclining upon the ocean of milk or seated, one should know that the earth—possessing the aforementioned qualities—is situated within the heart as the deity of the Sāman with its limbs (aṅga) arranged quarter by quarter. Thus: "Agni is indeed the Vedas; he pervades all this; the elements, the vital breaths, the senses, cattle, food, nectar, the sovereign (samrāṭ), the self-ruler (svarāṭ), and the universal ruler (virāṭ)—these are the deities of the first quarter of the Sāman, of its limb which is the *praṇava*, and of the *hṛdaya* mantra. In this way, the supreme *hṛdaya* has been explained.

Likewise, the intermediate space (antarikṣa), distinguished by the qualities of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and so forth, is the head; and because it resides within the head, the golden person (puruṣa) who is the Sun, consisting of all the Vedas, is the deity of the second foot of that Sāman as well as of its head-mantra and its subsidiary Sāvitra mantra. Thus, the supreme head has been explained.

And thus, the supreme *pārameśvara* limb of the *śikhā* has been explained: he who, as the moon—the lord of stars—prevails over the medicinal herbs by abiding within the crest (*śikhā*) of the celestial realm frequented by the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, is the deity of that *sāman*, the third foot of the *śikhā-mantra*, and the *lakṣmī-yajus*.

And thus, because it exists within the *Brahmaloka-kavaca*, it has been explained as the *Pārameśvara-kavaca*—the presiding deity of the mantra beginning with "He is Brahman" (*sa brahmā*), of the fourth foot of that *Sāman*, of the *Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī* which is its limb, and of the *kavaca-mantra*. Likewise, the *Pārameśvara-astra* has been explained by means of the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*) associated with the *Sāman* through the abundance of the syllable *Oṃ*.

Because the worlds are included within the limbs, because of the association with the deities of the limbs of the *sāman*, and because of the injunctive statement, "These worlds are interwoven; therefore, let the limbs be interwoven," this is the sequence of meditation. Having thus completed the supreme meditation by means of the deposited *sāman*, he now extracts the deposited *sāman*: "The fierce (*ugram*). Now, one might object: this is not an extraction of a *sāman*, but rather an extraction of a mantra; however, the word *sāman* is used here in its etymological sense (*yaugika-vṛtti*) by virtue of that capacity.

It is argued that *sāman* is that which exists together (*saha vartate*), meaning the root mantra; but that is not so, because the word *sāman* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "song" (*gīti*), according to the maxim that "conventional usage overrides etymological derivation. Therefore, it is simply the extraction of the *sāman*. Objection: But the Veda has made the word *sāman* etymological (*yaugika*), for the Śruti begins, "Thou art indeed *sā*, and I am *ama*," and concludes, "The two became *sā* and *ama*; that became *sāman*; that is the *sāman*-ness of the *sāman*."

Granted that the term may be etymological (*yaugika*), nevertheless, when both [the general and specific] are extracted, the extraction of the *sāman* itself is indeed established. Thus, since the extraction of the *sāman* is settled through its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and Vedic application, and the connection with the *sāman* has been established in a general form by the rule "one should know the thirty-two-syllabled *sāman*," the author speaks—beginning with "The fierce is the first's first"—in order to prescribe the connection with the *sāman* specifically for the syllables of the root-mantra. For here, among the Sāma-chanters, the determination of the pitch (*mukhasvara*) in the hand must be observed.

For the musical tone (*svara*) is sevenfold, distinguished by the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*. In that regard, the vocalization of the chant (*gīti*) follows the tones situated in the hand. Therein, when the highest joint of the thumb of the hand is raised in the manner known as *krauṣṭaka*, one should perform the chant over the prescribed syllables, having made it entirely acute (*udātta*) and consisting of three, four, or five morae (*mātrā*). That [first tone] they call the independent primary tone (*nirapekṣasvara*).

Then, when the thumb is bent at its upper joint, it is *anudātta* with respect to the preceding *udātta* and *udātta* with respect to the subsequent one; likewise, when the thumb touches the middle joint of the index finger, when it touches the fingers adjacent to that [middle finger], when it touches the middle joint of the ring finger, and when it touches the base joint of the little finger—having thus chanted the prescribed syllables as consisting of *udātta* and *anudātta* tones relative to each preceding and succeeding [joint]—and finally, when the thumb touches the base joint of the little finger...

One should utter the chant with all syllables unaccented; they call that the final tone. In this manner, the seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja* are produced in their proper order by means of the mouth and hands. This is the determination of the notes common to all *sāmans* among the Sāmavedic singers.

Furthermore, [the text] prescribes: "One should know the *sāman* consisting of the first vowel-sound within the two syllables uttered through the connection with the *sāman*-words as being 'fierce' (*ugram*), the first [syllable], and entirely acute (*sarvodātta*). Otherwise, since the fact that one should know the first two syllables of the first quarter-verse would already be known from the extraction of the words stated in the second *upaniṣad*, the maxim "an instruction is purposeful when it concerns what is not [otherwise] established" would be contradicted; the word *sāman* would be redundant; and if both were prescribed, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Once the specific connection with the *sāman* and its particular musical notes (*svara*) have been prescribed, how could a *sāman* whose specific notes have not yet been determined be enjoined? Therefore, it is precisely the connection with the *sāman*—consisting of the specific notes denoted by the word "first" (*ādya*)—that is enjoined for the first two syllables of the first quarter-verse mentioned in the root mantra. This same principle should be applied to the three subsequent sentences as well. One should know that "Jvala" is the first *sāman* (chant) of the second quarter-verse; "Nṛsiṃ" is the first [of the third], the meaning of which has already been explained.

The passage beginning with "death is the first of the fourth" and ending with "he goes" has its meaning already explained. Since this *sāman* is the most supreme secret, therefore one does not explain—meaning one does not speak of—this *sāman* to just anyone among men; this is a prohibition against the teacher. However, if he desires to give it to a son who is intent on service—that is, one devoted to service and desirous of hearing by approaching the teacher—he shall give it, meaning he should bestow it. And [he may give it] to another disciple who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics.
The word "iti" indicates the completion of the qualification of both the giver and the receiver of the *sāman*.

Having thus established the relationship between the giver and the recipient in connection with the *sāman*, he now speaks in order to prescribe the meditation characterized by the specific relationship of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayi-lakṣaṇa-sambandha*) upon the one who is to be meditated upon—the Man-Lion reclining on the ocean of milk—who, like a yogin, is either seated or lying down, and which [meditation] yields its complete fruit: ... [the text continues] ...he says: "He who knows this, having become a *brahman* through the *brahman*, goes to the world of *brahman* and becomes immortal there. Here, "this" refers to the aforementioned meditation. "Becoming a *brahman*" means becoming one whose nature is that of the *brahman*. "The world of *brahman*" is the world presided over by the *brahman*. "Immortal" means one who has transcended death. The sense is that he attains immortality in that world. This is because the nature of *brahman* cannot be attained without such meditation. Having thus explained the constituent parts of the Sāman and having stated that the qualification for its worship belongs to all except women and Śūdras, Prajāpati—delighted—spoke the subsequent portion concerning the deities of the final *praṇava* limbs, namely that the deity of the Sāman itself is the deity of each limb as it falls into its respective place. This section, beginning with "Agni indeed is the Vedas, this All... and ending with "...he goes to immortality," is to be connected with the passage beginning "together with the oceans. This is what is meant.

Whether the Lord is reclining upon the Ocean of Milk or seated, one should know that the earth—possessing the aforementioned qualities—is situated within the heart as the deity of the Sāman with its limbs (aṅga) arranged foot by foot; likewise, Agni, the Vedas, all this [universe], the elements, the vital breaths, the senses, cattle, food, nectar, the Samrāṭ, the Svarāṭ, and the Virāṭ are the deities of the first foot of the Sāman, of its limb which is the Praṇava, and of the Hṛdaya-mantra. Thus, the supreme Hṛdaya has been explained.

Likewise, the intermediate space (antarikṣa), distinguished by the qualities of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and others, is the head; the golden Sun, consisting of all the Vedas, is the Puruṣa. Thus, the supreme head has been explained as the deity of the second foot of that Sāman—the mantra of the head—and also of its limb, the Sāvitra mantra.

And thus, having explained that the Supreme Lord is the deity of the third foot of the *Sāman*, of the *Śikhā-mantra*, and of the *Lakṣmī-yajus*—the latter being served by the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas in the celestial realm and existing within the crest as the Moon, the lord of stars who brings forth all herbs—the limb of the *Śikhā* has been expounded according to the *Pārameśvara*.

And thus, because it exists within the armor (*kavaca*) of the Brahma-world, as indicated by the wording of the mantra beginning with "He is Brahman" (*sa brahmā*), and because it is the presiding deity (*daivata*) of the fourth foot of that *Sāman*, of the *Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī* which is its limb, and of the armor-mantra, the *Pārameśvara-kavaca* has been explained. Likewise, the *Pārameśvara-astra* has been explained by means of the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*) consisting predominantly of the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*), through the gateway of the *Sāman*.

Because the worlds are included within the limbs, because of the association with the deities of the limbs of the *sāman*, and because of the injunctive statement, "These worlds are interwoven; therefore, let the limbs be interwoven," this is the sequence of meditation. Having thus completed the supreme meditation by means of the *sāman* as it was deposited, he now extracts the *sāman* that was deposited—beginning with "Ugram. Now, one might object: "This is not an extraction of a *sāman*, but rather an extraction of a mantra;
the word *sāman* is used here through its etymological function (*yaugika-vṛtti*) on account of its capacity [to convey the same meaning]."

"It exists together" (*saha vartate*), thus [it is] *sāman*, the root mantra. That is not so; for the word *sāman* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of "chanting," according to the rule: "Conventional meaning overrides etymological derivation. Therefore, it is simply the extraction of the *sāman*. But is it not the case that the Veda has made the word *sāman* etymological? For the Śruti, beginning with "Thou wast indeed named *Sā*, and I was named *Ama*," continues: "They became *Sā* and *Ama*; that became *Sāman*; that is the *sāmatva* of the *sāman*."

Granted that it may be etymological (*yaugika*), nevertheless, when both [the general and the specific] are extracted, the extraction of the *sāman* itself is indeed established. Thus, since the extraction of the *sāman* is settled through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and Vedic application, and the connection with the *sāman* has been established in a general form by the rule "one should know the thirty-two-syllabled *sāman*," the author speaks—beginning with "The fierce is the first's first"—in order to prescribe the connection of the syllables of the root-mantra with the *sāman* in a specific form. For here, among the Sāma-chanters, the determination of the pitch (*svara*) for the hand and the mouth must be observed.

For the musical tone (*svara*) is sevenfold, distinguished by the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*. In that regard, the vocalization of the chant (*gīti*) is performed through the mouth in accordance with the tones held by the hand. Therein, when the highest joint of the thumb of the hand is raised in the manner known as *krauṣṭaka*, and having made it acutely accented (*udātta*) for three, four, or five morae (*mātrā*), one should sing the chant over the prescribed syllables. That [first tone] they call the "independent primary tone" (*nirapekṣa-svara*).

Then, when the thumb is bent at its upper joint, it is *anudātta* with respect to the preceding *udātta* and *udātta* with respect to the following; likewise, when the thumb touches the middle joint of the index finger, when it touches the fingers adjacent to that, when it touches the middle joint of the ring finger, and when it touches the base joint of the little finger—having uttered the melody consisting of *udātta* and *anudātta* syllables as prescribed in relation to each preceding and succeeding [joint]—and then the thumb touches the base joint of the little finger.

One should utter the chant with all syllables unaccented; they call that the final tone. In this manner, the seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja* are produced in their proper order by means of the mouth and hands. This is the determination of the notes common to all *sāmans* among the Sāmavedic singers.

Furthermore, [the text] prescribes: "One should know the *sāman* consisting of the first vowel-sound in the two syllables spoken [as] the fierce (*ugra*), the first of the first [verse], entirely acute (*sarvodātta*), due to its connection with the *sāman*-words. Otherwise, since the fact that one should know the first two syllables of the first quarter-verse is already known from the extraction of the words stated in the second *upaniṣad*, the maxim "an instruction is purposeful when [its object] is not [otherwise] established" would be contradicted; the word "*sāman*" would be redundant; and if both were prescribed, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Once a specific connection with a *sāman* characterized by particular musical notes has been prescribed, how could a *sāman* whose specific notes have not yet been determined be enjoined? Therefore, it is precisely the connection with the *sāman*—consisting of the specific notes denoted by the word "first"—that is enjoined for the two syllables of the first quarter-verse mentioned in the root mantra. This same principle should be applied to the three subsequent sentences as well: one should know that *jvalam* is the *sāman* (the chant) for the first [syllable] of the second quarter-verse; *nṛsiṃ* is the first of the third, the meaning of which has already been explained.

The passage beginning with "Death is the first of the fourth" and ending with "he goes" has its meaning already explained. Since this Sāman is the most supreme secret, therefore one should not speak of this Sāman to just anyone; this is a prohibition against the teacher. However, if he desires to give it—to a son who is devoted to service, who is intent on attending upon the teacher, and who possesses the desire to hear by approaching the teacher—he shall give it, that is, he may impart it. And to another disciple who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the qualifications for both the giver and the receiver of the Sāman.

Thus, having first established the relationship between the giver and the recipient in connection with the *sāman*, he now speaks in order to prescribe the meditation on the specific relationship characterized as the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayi*)—pertaining to the Man-Lion who reclines upon the ocean of milk—whether seated or lying down like a yogin, which meditation yields its full fruit: ... [The text continues with the verses] ... In this way, having first established the relationship between the giver and the recipient in connection with the *sāman*, he now speaks in order to prescribe the meditation on the specific relationship characterized as the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayi*)—pertaining to the Man-Lion who reclines upon the ocean of milk—whether seated or lying down like a yogin, which meditation yields its full fruit.

Oṃ! One should know that Sāman which is Truth, Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa whose form is the Man-lion (Narasimha), who is dark-brown and tawny, whose seed is cast upwards, the Three-eyed One, the Beneficent, the Blue-and-Red, the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Creatures, the Wielder of the Pināka bow, whose splendor is like lightning, the Sovereign of all sciences, the Lord of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Vedas, who is expressed by the Yajurveda—he who knows this attains immortality.

One should know that the first half of the *mahāprathamānta* is the *ṛc*, the first half of the second [half] is the *ṣaṇa*, the first half of the third [half] is the *namas*, and the first half of the fourth [half] is the *sāman*. He who knows this attains immortality. Therefore, one should know this supreme Brahman, which consists of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss; he who knows it thus becomes immortal in this very world. Therefore, one should know this *Sāman* with its limbs (*sāṅga*); he who knows it attains immortality. 6.

One should know the *Sāman* as the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) reclining upon the ocean of milk, the supreme state meditated upon by yogis; he who knows it attains immortality. One should know the *Sāman* as the Hero (*vīram*) at the end of the first half-verse, *taṃsaṃ* at the end of the second half-verse, *haṃbhī* at the end of the third half-verse, and *mṛtyum* at the end of the fourth half-verse; he who knows it attains immortality. Therefore, whoever knows this *Sāman* through the mouth of any teacher whatsoever is liberated from *saṃsāra* with that very body.

One who desires liberation is liberated; through this very recitation, one beholds the deity even with this physical body. Therefore, in the Kali age, this alone is the primary gateway, and not others. Consequently, one should know this Sāman together with its ancillaries; he who knows it becomes a seeker of liberation. || 5 ||

He who lies upon the ocean of milk is both a man (*nṛ*) and a lion (*kesarī*); thus he is the Man-Lion (*nṛkesarī*). The form *nṛkesarin* is a Vedic (archaic) usage. He sits like a yogin, encircled by the head of the coils of Śeṣa; that is, by reflecting on the secret teachings of other Kalpas, and by reflecting on the various recensions of the Vedas and other Śrutis, he sits in this very place, surrounded by the head of the body of Śeṣa. This Upaniṣad belongs to two branches: the Bhṛgu branch and the Āṅgirasa branch. It is the supreme station, the ultimate refuge.

The phrase "one should know" (*jānīyāt*) is to be supplied everywhere. The section beginning with "the Sāman" and ending with "goes" has its meaning already explained. The sense is that whatever Sāman one may know, one should know it as being deposited along with its ancillaries upon the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) characterized by the aforementioned qualities.

Now, for the purpose of establishing the specific relationship between the vowels and the syllables of the second extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *sāman*, he says: "One should know the *vīra* [syllable] as the last of the first half, belonging to the final vowel, according to the principle that 'when two syllables are mentioned in the first phrase, [the word] refers to the last one because there is no reason to skip the first'. Therefore, in this very place, in another recension (*śākhā*), there is a different reading: "The *vīra* [syllable] is the last of the first half of the first [phrase]."

Here too, regarding the previously mentioned injunction and its resolution of objections: *ta* is a chant consisting of the anudātta (unaccented) tone; *raṃ* is a chant consisting of the middle pitch; this same principle should be applied to the subsequent extraction-utterances as well. *Taṃsaṃ* is the final syllable of the second half-verse, as has already been explained. *Tam* is a chant consisting of the anudātta tone; *haṃsabhī* is the final syllable of the third half-verse. There is an alternative reading: "the final syllable of the first half of the third [verse]. *Ham* is a chant consisting of the anudātta tone.

*Bhī* is a chant (*gīti*) consisting of a middle tone; *mṛ* is a chant consisting of an anudātta (low) tone; *tyuṃ*, by the principle of remainder (*pāriśeṣya*), is a chant consisting of a middle tone; "the last syllable of the second half of the fourth [section]" has its meaning already explained. *Mṛtyuṃ* is an alternative reading for "the last syllable of the first half of the fourth. The passage beginning with "Sāma" and ending with "goes" has its meaning already explained. Because, through the complete knowledge of even a single part of the Sāman...

Regarding the attainment of the complete fruit, he says "how much more so" (*kimuta*) in reference to the thorough knowledge of the entire *sāman*: "Therefore, this entire *sāman* has been extracted from the prescribed syllables by whomever"—the ellipsis being "whosoever knows [it] even by means of any collection of sentences for extracting the *sāman*. The phrase "whosoever knows it from the mouth of the teacher" (*ācāryamukhena*) indicates an option (*vikalpa*) between the teacher's mouth as a means and other means. Alternatively, the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) denotes the Veda, because of its usage in such passages as "therefore, the word of the teacher is authoritative" (*tasmād ācāryavacaḥ pramāṇam*).

The meaning is: by means of a collection of words for extracting the *sāman* from the mouth of the teacher, which is itself the mouth of the Veda. By that very thorough knowledge of the *sāman*, he himself is liberated from *saṃsāra*, or he liberates another by making him know the *sāman*. Through the thorough knowledge of the *sāman*, even one possessed of passion becomes a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) by means of its recitation (*japa*); since no specific number is prescribed, it occurs through the recitation of the *sāman* just once.

By means of that very Sāman with its ancillaries—which is explained by the collection of words beginning with "the supreme, excellent body, reclining upon the ocean of milk"—one effects the vision of the deity; the deity becomes manifest. Therefore, this very Sāman with its ancillaries is the primary gateway for the vision of the deity and for its manifestation. The meaning is that in the Kali age, due to the abundance of sin, the vision of the deity does not occur swiftly for others who are devoid of the Sāman and know only the root mantra.

Since this Sāman with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) is the primary gateway for the vision of the deity and for the manifestation of the deity’s form, therefore one should know this Sāman with its constituent parts. Even though one has ascended to human bliss, through this thorough knowledge one becomes a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), abandoning human bliss and desiring liberation. Alternatively, the grammatical connection is: "one who desires liberation should know this. The statement "it happens for him" (*tasya bhavati*) is the indication of the result. This is a form of the verbal root *bhū* (to exist). The meaning is that by means of the meditation on Brahman with form, one attains the state of pure existence (*sanmātratā*).

He who lies upon the ocean of milk is both a man (*nṛ*) and a lion (*kesarī*), thus he is the Man-Lion (*nṛkesarī*). The form *nṛkesarin* is Vedic. He sits like a yogin, encircled by the head of the coils of Śeṣa; that is to say, by reflecting on other secret Kalpas, he sits in this very place surrounded by the head of the coils of Śeṣa, according to the reflection on other recensions and other scriptural texts. This Upaniṣad belongs to two branches: the Bhṛgu branch and the Āṅgirasa branch. It is the supreme station, the ultimate refuge.

The phrase "one should know" (*jānīyāt*) is to be supplied everywhere. The passage beginning with "the Sāman" and ending with "goes" has its meaning already explained. The sense is that whatever Sāman one should know, one should know it as being deposited along with its limbs upon the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) characterized by the aforementioned qualities.

Now, he speaks for the purpose of establishing the connection between the specific vowels of the syllables in the second extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *sāman*: "One should know the *sāman* to be the last [syllable] of the first half of the first [word], which consists of the final vowel, according to the principle that 'there is no reason to skip the first [syllable] when two syllables are mentioned in the first word'. For this very reason, in another recension (*śākhā*) at this same place, there is a different reading: "The last [syllable] of the first half of the first [word] is *vīram*."

In this case as well, regarding the previously mentioned injunction and its resolution: *ta* is a chant (*gīti*) consisting of the anudātta accent; *raṃ* is a chant consisting of the middle tone (*madhyamasvara*). The same should be applied to the subsequent extraction-utterances (*uddhāvākya*) as well. *Taṃsaṃ* is the final syllable of the second half [of the verse], as has already been explained. *Tam* is a chant consisting of the anudātta accent; *haṃsabhī* is the final syllable of the third half. There is an alternative reading: "the final syllable of the first half of the third [verse]. *Ham* is a chant consisting of the anudātta accent.

*Bhī* is a chant consisting of a middle tone (*svarita*); *mṛ* is a chant consisting of an unraised tone (*anudātta*); *tyuṃ*, by process of elimination, is a chant consisting of a middle tone. The phrase "the last [syllable] of the second half of the fourth" has its meaning already explained. *Mṛtyuṃ* is an alternative reading for "the last [syllable] of the first half of the fourth. The passage beginning with "Sāma" and ending with "gacchati" has its meaning already explained. Because [one attains this] through the thorough knowledge of even a single part of the Sāman...

Regarding the attainment of the complete fruit, he asks: "What need is there to mention [the case] when the entire *sāman* is fully known? He says: "Therefore, this entire *sāman* extracted from the prescribed syllables—this is to be construed with the phrase 'whoever knows it,' even by means of any particular collection of sentences for extracting the *sāman*. The statement "whoever knows it through the mouth of the teacher" implies an option between the mouth of the teacher and other means. Alternatively, the word *ācārya* denotes the Veda, as seen in such usages as "therefore the word of the *ācārya* is authoritative."

The meaning is: by means of a collection of words for extracting the *sāman* from the mouth of the teacher, that is, from the mouth of the Veda. By that very thorough knowledge of the *sāman*, he himself is liberated from *saṃsāra*, or he liberates another by making him know the *sāman*. Through the thorough knowledge of the *sāman*, even one possessed of passion becomes a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) by means of recitation (*japa*); since no specific number is prescribed, it is by reciting the *sāman* just once.

By means of that very *sāman* with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), which is explained by the collection of words beginning with "the supreme, excellent body, reclining upon the ocean of milk," one effects the vision of the deity; the deity becomes directly perceived. Therefore, this *sāman* with its constituent parts alone is the primary gateway for the vision of the deity and for its manifestation. The meaning is that in the Kali age, due to the abundance of sin, for others who are devoid of the *sāman* and know only the root mantra, the vision of the deity does not occur instantaneously.

Since this Sāman with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) is the primary gateway for the vision of the deity and for the manifestation of the deity’s form, therefore one should know this Sāman with its constituent parts. Even one who has ascended to human bliss becomes a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) through this thorough knowledge, abandoning human bliss and desiring liberation. Alternatively, the grammatical connection is: "The seeker of liberation should know this. "It happens to him" (*tasya bhavati*) is the indication of the result. This is a form of the verbal root *bhū* (to exist). The meaning is that, by means of the meditation on Brahman with form, one attains the state of pure existence (*sanmātratā*).

By this indeed the creators of the universe (Viśvasṛjs) created this entire universe; because they created the universe, they are called the Viśvasṛjs. After them, everything is born. They attain union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. Therefore, one should know this Sāman together with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality.

One should know the *sāman* as the final syllable of "Viṣṇu" for the first [foot], the final syllable of "Bhadram" for the second, the final syllable of "Myaham" for the third, and the final syllable of "Sāma" for the fourth; he who knows this attains immortality. He who knows that which is in the self—this *brāhmaṇa* and the *anuṣṭubh*—he who knows it attains immortality.

Whether it be for a woman or a man, whoever desires to remain right here [in this world], he bestows all sovereignty; wherever one dies, at the end of the body, the Lord utters the supreme *brāhma* *tāraka*, by which that person, having become immortal, attains immortality. Therefore, one should mutter this which is situated within the *Sāman*; therefore, this is a limb (*aṅga*) of the *Sāman*; therefore, this is a limb of the *Sāman* belonging to Prajāpati. "He who knows thus"—thus it is in the *Mahopaniṣad*. He who knows this *Mahopaniṣad* becomes Mahāviṣṇu, even if he has not performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*); he becomes Mahāviṣṇu, he becomes Mahāviṣṇu. 7.
Thus ends the first Upaniṣad.

Oṃ! *Ṛta* and *satya*, the supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa whose form is that of the Man-lion (*nṛkesarin*), dark-brown and tawny, with upward-flowing vital seed (*ūrdhvaretas*), the three-eyed one (*virūpākṣa*), the benefactor (*śaṃkara*), blue-and-red (*nīlalohita*), the Lord of Umā (*umāpati*), the Lord of Creatures (*paśupati*), the wielder of the Pināka bow (*pinākin*), he whose splendor is like lightning—He is Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, the Chief of all beings, the Sovereign of Brahman, the Overlord of Brahman. One should know Him as the Sāman who is expressed by the Yajurveda; he who knows this attains immortality.

One should know that the first half of the *mahāprathamānta* is the *ṛc*, the first half of the second [half] is the *ṣaṇa*, the first half of the third [half] is the *namas*, and the first half of the fourth [half] is the *sāman*; he who knows this attains immortality. Therefore, one should know this supreme Brahman, which consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandamaya*); knowing it thus, one becomes immortal here. Therefore, one should know this *sāman* with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality. || 6 ||

Thus, first indicating that very limb which is capable of manifesting the form of the deity to be meditated upon, he says: "Om. He will clarify this in the fourth Upaniṣad with the passage beginning, "This syllable Om," and so forth. The anthropomorphic form of the Man-Lion has already been explained.

He is not a playful body produced by his own *māyā*; rather, since beings such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others who are purely animal in form, or beings such as Vāmana and others who are purely human in form, are seen to possess bodies that are merely playful in nature, and since this [Lord] is distinct from them, it might be suspected that he does not have a playful body produced by his own *māyā*. To remove this doubt, the author cites a mantra: "The Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, whose form is that of the Man-Lion (*Nṛkesarin*), is the eternal Truth."

"Puruṣa," "keśarī," "siṃha," and "nṛkeśarī" [are the terms used]. Therein, having referred back to "puruṣa" as the subject (*anūdya*), it is enjoined that one should know the Supreme Brahman as Truth (*satyam*). This is what is meant: one should know that the form of Puruṣa, which is the playful embodiment (*līlāvigraha*) of the Supreme Brahman—the Truth—manifested through its own *māyā*, is indeed "ṛta," meaning the ultimate reality.

Alternatively, *ṛtam* means the supreme Truth, the Brahman, which is of the nature of Brahman and has the form of Puruṣa; it is explained by the syllable *om*. Since *ṛta* is a name for wealth (*dhana*), the meaning is that one should know it as consisting of *ṛta*, that is, consisting of gold. For this very reason, it is explained by Kaivalya that "the kinsman of Being" (*sato bandhum*)—where *bandhu* is a name for wealth—is the golden manifestation of Brahman, which they discovered within the non-existent heart of Brahman. It is called "black-and-tawny" (*kṛṣṇapiṅgalam*), meaning he whose two eyes are black and tawny.

The term *ūrdhvaretas* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) form. It refers to one whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretaska*), who is established in yoga (*yogārūḍha*), and who is seated. He is Virūpākṣa, meaning "the one with an eye on the forehead. To preclude the notion that he possesses a fierce nature due to having an eye on the forehead, he is called Śaṅkara, the "Bringer of Happiness," with hands granting boons and fearlessness. Because of his association with Śaṅkara, he is described as *nīlalohita*: blue-throated (*nīlakaṇṭha*) in the remaining part [of his body] and red (*lohita*). It is stated thus because the two colors, blue and red, are borne by him on his forehead and eyes according to their respective fitness. However, in another Kalpa, he is white in color.

Thus, the conceptualization of forms as golden, red, and white is established through the power of desire. "Umāpati" means Umā—Gaurī—and her husband. Regarding "Śrī," Lakṣmī, these seven Śaktis will be described later. "Paśupati" is the lord of *paśus*, meaning living beings; or alternatively, the lord of the *paśus*, namely the Vedas such as the Gāyatrī and others, according to the Vedic scripture: "The meters are indeed the *paśus*. "Pinākin" means one who holds the Pināka bow in his hand. The particle *hi* has the sense of emphasis. "Amitadyuti" means one of immeasurable splendor.

The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign; the Bestower of boons, the Lord of all beings. The Lord of *brāhman*: *brāhman* is austerity (*tapas*) consisting of the discernment that withdraws the mind from sense objects—the aforementioned meditation—and He is its presiding protector. He is the Lord of *brāhman*, the sustainer of *brāhman*. Furthermore, *brāhman* is a name for food; it refers here to milk, and thus He is the sustainer of milk. Alternatively, He is the presiding deity of *brāhman*, the Atharvaveda.

In this way, that which is denoted by the *Yajurveda*—meaning that which is to be expressed by the *yajus* or the *veda* as previously described—is "denoted by the *Yajurveda*" (*yajurvedavācya*). To connect this with the previously mentioned qualities listed first, he designates it with the second case ending (*dvitīyānta*) in the singular sense of its uniqueness, saying "that" (*tam*). The passage from "Sāma... up to "...goes" has already been explained. Thus, one should understand the previously described form as belonging to the Man-Lion (*nṛkesarin*) alone.

In this regard, some maintain that the previously mentioned form is to be meditated upon as distinct from the syllables of the mantra; that is incorrect, for in that case, the unity of the Nṛsiṃha-brāhmaṇa-vidyā—established through the opening and concluding passages—would be contradicted. Furthermore, at the time of explaining the word "Nṛsiṃha," the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "Nṛsiṃha" and "the Supreme Being" (Paraśvara)—expressed as "He was indeed Nṛsiṃha, the Supreme Being"—would be contradicted. Therefore, it is established that in this vidyā, the object of meditation is Nṛsiṃha himself, characterized by forms such as having three eyes.

Now he states the third extraction together with its melody (*sāmoddhāra*): *ma*—by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the melody resides in the middle tone (*madhyasvara*); *hā*—the melody consists entirely of the acute accent (*udātta*); "of the first half [of the second foot], the first"—this is to be supplied as follows: one should know that the *sāman* associated with the first tone of the latter half of the two syllables mentioned in the first quarter-verse is joined with that first tone. *rva*—by process of elimination, the melody resides in the middle tone; *to*—the melody consists entirely of the acute accent; "of the second half [of the third foot], the first"—the meaning has already been explained. *ṣa*.

By process of elimination, the *gīti* (melodic recitation) occurs with a middle accent; *ṇam*, the *gīti* consists entirely of the acute (*udātta*) accent; "the first half of the third ending"—this has already been explained. By process of elimination, the *gīti* does not occur with a middle accent; *mā*, the *gīti* consists entirely of the acute accent; "the first half of the fourth ending"—this has already been explained. The passage beginning with "Sāma" and ending with "goes" has already been explained.

Now, one might ask: why is it not prescribed here that between the two syllables, the first vowel is connected with the "half of the final syllable"—that is, the long vowel (*mātrā*) and so forth? That is not so, because a *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. [In the *karmadhāraya*,] "the end and its half" (*antārdham*) means the second syllable relative to the first; it is both the "end" (*anta*) and the "half" (*ardham*).

Otherwise, the compound *antākṣaramātrārdham* would be a genitive *tatpuruṣa*, meaning "half of the measure of the final syllable," according to the principle [of the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*] found in the injunction: "With this [verse], one should cause the *niṣāda-sthapati* to sacrifice. But is this not extremely trivial, since even in the case of a *mātrā*, a *karmadhāraya* is possible by depending on its substratum? True. However, in the passage "the *sāman* consists of thirty-two syllables" (*dvātriṃśadakṣaraṃ sāma*), it is heard that the connection with the *sāman*, which is of the nature of musical notes (*svara*), belongs to the thirty-two syllables themselves, and not to the *mātrās*.

Therefore, it is established that by the word "half of the end" (*antārdha*), the connection of the first vowel with the second syllable itself is prescribed. Since even a single part of the *Sāman* is capable of securing the entire fruit, how much more so the knowledge of the complete *Sāman*? Consequently, this Supreme Brahman, consisting of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—which manifests the root mantra denoting such a Nṛsiṃha—one should know it to be the Supreme Brahman; this is the sense of the sentence.

One relationship is this: that which is expressed by the root mantra manifested through the Sāmans is the Supreme Brahman in the form of Nṛsiṃha, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). Alternatively, there is another relationship: that Brahman consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. A doubt may arise that although the nature of Brahman was previously established through the words of the mantra, it might still be considered unfirm; to dispel that doubt, this is stated: "One should know Brahman as consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss."

Knowing—that is, understanding—this one who has the form of Nṛsiṃha in the manner described, one becomes preeminent in this very world; for the word *amṛta* is seen to mean milk in such passages as "Bring the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) to the *amṛta* (milk). Alternatively, when the assignment of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) has been performed in this way, one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) in this very world; that is to say, one becomes blissful.

Since the *Sāman* with its limbs (*sāṅga*) is the manifestor of the root mantra that sets forth the entire Nṛsiṃha-Brāhmaṇa-vidyā, therefore [the passage] beginning with "This" and ending with "goes" has the meaning already stated.
In order to demonstrate that this *sāman* possesses the quality of being the "dispeller of obstacles" (*vi-varuṇa-aṣṭṛtva*) in the manner previously described, he says:

"Thus, first of all, pointing out that very limb which is capable of manifesting the form of the deity to be meditated upon, he says: 'Om'. This will be clarified in the fourth Upaniṣad with the passage beginning, "This syllable 'Om'... The form of the Man-lion (*nṛkesarin*) has already been explained.

He does not possess a body for divine play (*līlā-vigraha*) through his own *māyā*; rather, since beings such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others who are born solely from the ripening of karma and exist merely as animals, or beings such as Vāmana and others who exist merely as non-animals, are seen only as forms of divine play, and since this [Lord] is distinct from them, it might be suspected that He does not possess a body for divine play through His own *māyā*. To dispel this doubt by means of the words of a mantra, he states the mantra: "The Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, the Truth, the Reality, whose form is that of the Man-Lion (*nṛkesarin*)."

"Puruṣa," "Kesarin," "Siṃha," and "Nṛkesarī. Therein, having referred to "Puruṣa" as the subject (*anūdya*), it is enjoined that one should know the supreme *brāhman* as truth (*satyam*). This is what is meant: one should know the play-form (*līlā-vigraha*) of the supreme *brāhman*, which is Truth, in the form of a Puruṣa manifested through its own *māyā*, as *ṛtam*—that is to say, as the ultimate reality.

Alternatively, *ṛtam* means truth, the supreme Brahman, whose nature is Brahman and who has the form of a person (*puruṣākāra*). It is explained by the syllable *om*; the meaning is that one should know it to be "consisting of *ṛta*"—that is, consisting of gold. For this very reason, it is explained by Kaivalya that "the kinsman of Being" (*sato bandhum*)—where "kinsman" (*bandhu*) is a name for wealth—is the golden manifestation of Brahman, which they discovered within the non-existent heart of Brahman. He is called "black-and-tawny" (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*), meaning he whose two eyes are black and tawny.

The term *ūrdhvaretas* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) form. It refers to one whose semen is drawn upward, who is established in yoga, and who is seated. He is Virūpākṣa, "the one with the eye on the forehead. To preclude the notion of ferocity (*raudratā*) that might arise from the mention of an eye on the forehead, he is called Śaṅkara, "the bringer of happiness," with hands granting boons and fearlessness. Because of his association with Śaṅkara, he is called Nīlalohita: blue-necked (*nīlakaṇṭha*), being blue in the remaining parts of his body and red (*lohita*).
