It is said that the two colors, blue and red, are worn by him on his forehead and eyes according to their respective fitness. However, in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), his color is described as white.

Thus, the conceptualization of forms as golden, red, and white is established by the power of desire. "Umāpati" refers to Umā—Gaurī—and her Lord. "Śrī" refers to Lakṣmī; these seven Śaktis will be described later. "Paśupati" is the Lord of *paśus*, meaning living beings; or else, the Lord of *paśus* as the Vedas, such as the Gāyatrī and others, according to the Vedic revelation: "The meters are indeed the *paśus*. "Pinākin" means one who holds the Pināka bow in his hand. The particle "hi" is used for emphasis. "Amitadyuti" means one of immeasurable splendor.

The Lord of all sciences, the Master; the Bestower of boons, the Master of all beings. The Lord of *brāhman*: *brāhman* is austerity consisting of the discernment [of the Self] by withdrawing the mind from sense objects, as previously described; He is its Lord, the one who presides over and protects it. Or, *brāhman* is a name for food—namely milk—and thus He is the presider over that milk. Alternatively, He is the presider over the *Brāhman*, that is, the Atharvaveda.

Thus, "expressed by the Yajurveda" means expressed by the *yajus* or the Veda previously mentioned; he refers to it with the accusative case ending (*tam*) in order to connect it with the previously mentioned qualities listed first, intending to treat them as a single unified whole. The passage beginning with "Sāma" and ending with "goes" has already been explained. In this way, one should understand the aforementioned form as belonging to Nṛkesarī alone.

In this regard, some maintain that the previously mentioned form is to be meditated upon as distinct from the syllables of the mantra; that is incorrect, for in that case, the unity of the Nṛsiṃha-Brāhmaṇa meditation—established by the opening and concluding passages—would be contradicted. Furthermore, at the time of explaining the word "Nṛsiṃha," the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "Nṛsiṃha" and "the Supreme Being" (*paraṃ varaḥ*) in the statement "He was indeed Nṛsiṃha, the Supreme Being" would be contradicted. Therefore, it is established that in this meditation, it is Nṛsiṃha himself, characterized by forms such as the three-eyed one, who is the object of worship.

Now he states the third extraction along with its melody (*sāmoddhāra*): *ma*—by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the chant (*gīti*) resides in the middle tone; *hā*—the chant consists entirely of the acute accent (*udātta*); "of the first half, the first"—this is to be understood as follows: one should know that the *Sāman* belonging to the second half of the two syllables mentioned in the first quarter-verse is joined with the first tone. *rva*—by process of elimination, the chant resides in the middle tone; *to*—the chant consists entirely of the acute accent; "of the second half, the first"—the meaning has already been explained. *ṣa*.

By process of elimination, the *gīti* (melodic recitation) belonging to the middle tone [is indicated]; *ṇam* is a *gīti* consisting entirely of the acute accent (*udātta*); "the first of the half ending in the third [letter]" has its meaning already explained. By process of elimination, the *gīti* belonging to the middle tone [is indicated]; *mā* is a *gīti* consisting entirely of the acute accent; "the first of the half ending in the fourth [letter]" has its meaning already explained. The passage beginning with "Sāma" and ending with "goes" has its meaning already explained.

Now, one might ask: why is it not prescribed here that between the two syllables, the first vowel is connected with the "half of the final syllable"—that is, the long and other prosodic measures (*mātrā*) belonging to the latter half of the syllable? That is not so, because a *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. [In this case,] *antārdham* means "the end and its half"; that is, the second syllable relative to the first is the "end," and it is both the end and its half.

Otherwise, the compound *antākṣaramātrārdham* would be a genitive *tatpuruṣa*, meaning "half of the measure of the final syllable," according to the principle [of the *nyāya*] in the passage: "With this [offering], one should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice. But is this not utterly trivial? For even in the case of a *mātrā*, a *karmadhāraya* is possible by depending on a substratum. True. However, in the passage "the *sāman* consists of thirty-two syllables" (*dvātriṃśadakṣaraṃ sāma*), the connection with the *sāman*, which is of the nature of vowels, is heard as belonging to the thirty-two syllables themselves, not to the *mātrās*.

Therefore, it is established that by the word "half of the end" (*antārdha*), the connection of the first vowel with the second syllable itself is prescribed. Since even a single part of the *Sāman* is capable of securing the entire fruit, how much more so the knowledge of the complete *Sāman*? Therefore, this supreme Brahman, consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, should be known as the supreme Brahman because it manifests the root mantra that represents such a Nṛsiṃha; this is the sense of the ellipsis.

One relationship is this: that which is expressed by the root mantra revealed through the Sāman is the Supreme Brahman in the form of Nṛsiṃha, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). Alternatively, there is another [relationship]: that Brahman consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. One might have the doubt that although the nature of Brahman was previously established based on the wording of the mantra, it might still remain unfirm; therefore, to dispel that doubt, this is stated: "One should know Brahman as consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss."

Knowing—that is, understanding—this one who has the form of Nṛsiṃha in the manner described, one becomes preeminent in this very world; for the word "amṛta" (nectar) is seen to refer to milk in such passages as "Bring the five nectars," and so forth. Alternatively, when this five-limbed ritual placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) has been performed, one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) in this very world; that is to say, one becomes blissful.

Since the *Sāman* with its limbs (*sāṅga*) manifests the root mantra that expounds the entire Nṛsiṃha-Brāhmaṇa-vidyā, therefore [the passage] beginning with "This" and ending with "goes" has the meaning already stated.
In order to demonstrate that this *sāman* possesses the quality of "unfettering" (*vivaraṇa*) in the manner described, he says:

"Unfetter it with this. Indeed, by means of this they unfettered this world. Because they unfettered it, it is called "the unfetterer" (*vivaraṇa*). Through this unfetterer, one is born after [the gods]; they attain union (*sāyujya*) and co-residence (*salokatā*) with the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, one should know this *sāman* together with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality.

One should know the *sāman* as Viṣṇu, the final [syllable] of the first [foot], Bhadra, the final of the second, Myaha, the final of the third, and Sāma, the final of the fourth; he who knows this attains immortality. He who knows that which exists here—whatever there is within the Self—should know the *anuṣṭubh* of the Brāhmaṇa; he who knows this attains immortality.

Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever desires to remain right here [in this world], he grants all that is desirable; wherever one dies, at the end of the body, the Lord teaches the supreme *brāhma* *tāraka* [mantra], by which one becomes immortal and attains immortality. Therefore, one mutters this which is situated within the *Sāman*; therefore, this is a limb (*aṅga*) of the *Sāman*, for Prajāpati [taught] this as a limb of the *Sāman*. "He who knows thus"—thus it is said in the *Mahopaniṣad*. He who knows this *Mahopaniṣad* becomes Mahāviṣṇu, even though he has previously performed [other] rites; he becomes Mahāviṣṇu, he becomes Mahāviṣṇu. || 7 ||
Thus ends the first Upaniṣad.

"By this *sāman*, which manifests the root mantra that sets forth the *Nṛsiṃha-brāhmaṇa-vidyā*, they indeed—well known—emitted all this. Because they emitted all this, therefore he explains the word *vivasṛk* as "they emitted. "One is born after him"—this indicates the distinction in results based on the difference between meditating on identity and meditating on difference, stating: "They attain union with the Brāhmaṇa and residence in the same world."

Since such is the fruit for those who meditate upon the Sāman together with its limbs—namely, that they attain union (*sāyujya*) and residence in the same world (*salokatā*) with Brāhmā—the passage beginning with "Therefore, this... and ending with "...goes" has already been explained. The intention behind the repeated practice of the thought, "Therefore, this is the Sāman with its limbs," is this: only through the Sāman with its limbs is there the manifestation of the mantras that convey the entire Brāhma-vidyā; thus, it is precisely that Brāhma-vidyā which arises [from the Sāman] that is fruitful, and no other.

Therefore it has been said: "Hence, this alone is the primary door in the Kali age. This means that in this time which abounds in sin, this [method] alone possesses primacy, while others are secondary. However, in other times, the primacy of this or another is optional; thus, everything is faultless. Now, he states the extraction of the fourth *sāman*: "Viṣṇu is the chant consisting of all unraised (anudātta) notes."

Regarding "the last of the first": one should know that even for the two syllables mentioned in the first quarter, [the Sāman] is joined with the final vowel; this connects back to what was stated previously. Regarding "the face of the second": the connection is that the Sāman is joined with the final vowel even for the two syllables mentioned in the second quarter, where "face" refers to a chant (*gīti*) consisting entirely of unaccented (*anudātta*) tones.

Now, why are the words "first" and "second" in all the extractions (*uddhāra*) explained with reference to the quarters (*pāda*), and not with reference to the number of syllables mentioned? For instance, regarding the phrase "the last of the first," one should know the final vowel among the two mentioned syllables as belonging to the first; likewise, regarding "the last of the second," one should know the final vowel among the two mentioned syllables as belonging to the second.

If this is so, why is it not explained that even in the first extraction (*uddhāra*), one should know the initial vowel of the first syllable [to be] the second syllable? It is said in reply: for everywhere, the terms "first," "second," "third," and "fourth" are heard only by means of the mention of two syllables.

For it is not logical to apply the terms "third" and "fourth" to the mention of two syllables, because there is an absence of a third and fourth syllable; thus, it is determined that these terms must be explained with reference to the *pādas* (quarters). By association with them, it is established that the terms "first" and "second," though mentioned in reference to two syllables, are not to be explained with reference to the syllables themselves, but rather exclusively with reference to the *pādas*. This being so, the meaning already stated—that the chant (*gīti*) consisting entirely of grave accents (*anudātta*) belongs to the end of the third [quarter]—is confirmed.

"Mine" (*myaham*): the chant consisting entirely of anudātta accents is the end of the fourth [section]; this has already been explained. Now, why is there no extraction of the *sāman* in its entirety? For if the *sāman* were extracted in its entirety, it would be easier—just like the extraction of the words taught in the second Upaniṣad.

It is said: It is true that it would be easy; however, although Prajāpati, the seer of the Sāman, was capable of seeing all the gods, he did not perceive this Sāman like the root mantra. Rather, for the sake of perceiving it, having his internal organ slightly purified by the performance of a portion of this meditation (*upāsanā*), he perceived the first extraction (*uddhāra*); and again, having meditated upon the object of worship, such as the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*).

He did not see the second extraction; thus, because his internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) was purified to a greater degree through the performance of superior worship, he saw the third and the fourth—indicating that even for Prajāpati there was great effort in seeing them, let alone for others. This shows the absence of continuous extraction of the Sāman and demonstrates its rarity and difficulty of perception.

That Prajāpati who is [the source] has declared—that is, he has announced or taught—this as well: namely, this meditation which was previously mentioned, "in the self" (*ātmani*), meaning "in the Brāhmaṇa-self" (*brāhṛṇyātmani*). Having fully realized his own nature as the Brāhmaṇa-self, whoever knows the *Ānuṣṭubha* meditation related to the *Anuṣṭubh*, by means of the Sāman, and whoever knows it, he attains immortality; thus the meaning has been stated.

The meaning is that Prajāpati taught this aforementioned meditation either to a woman or a man, or to a woman or a man [as the case may be]. Alternatively, this meditation belongs to Hiraṇyagarbha in the Brāhmaṇa; or rather, one should know that the Ānuṣṭubha Sāman is deposited in the supreme Brahman, which is the Brāhmaṇī. In this latter view, the word "yat" (which) mentioned previously refers to the object of meditation, and not to Prajāpati.

The word *vā* (or) in the expression *strīpuṃsor vā strīpuṃso vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), as seen in such passages as *vāyurvā tvā manurvā tvā*. This is what is meant: having performed the placement of the *vara* upon the object of worship (*upāsya*), the practitioner (*upāsaka*) must also perform the placement of the *vara* upon himself. To that practitioner who desires to abide in excellence in this world, [the deity] grants all boons (*vara*).

At the end of the body, however, the Lord explains the supreme Brahman, the Savior (*tāraka*), specifically with reference to the seeker of desire (*kāmin*), because of the inclusion of the qualification "at the end of the body" and because of his prior qualification as one possessing desire. For the one free from desire (*niṣkāma*), even before the end of the body, the Lord explains the supreme Brahman—the Savior situated within the *praṇava*, which is a limb of the Sāman and explained by means of the *praṇava*. By means of that *praṇava* thus explained, having become immortal, that hearer attains immortality, which is liberation (*kaivalya*).

Since the Supreme Brahman is to be explained as residing in the *tāraka*, therefore one mutters this *tāraka* situated within the *sāman*—that is, existing in the middle of the *sāman*. This shows that the muttering of the *praṇava*, which is a limb of the *sāman*-meditation, should be performed according to one's capacity. He says this very thing: "Therefore, this *tāraka* is a limb of the *sāman*; Prajāpati [is its] seer (*ṛṣi*)."

Alternatively, this *Tāraka* [mantra] is [essential] by virtue of its declaration of the supreme and excellent essential nature (*svarūpa*); the *Sāman* is [essential] by virtue of its manifestation of the root-mantras that establish the knowledge concerning the supreme and excellent object; and Prajāpati is [essential] by virtue of his exposition of both—this triad is necessarily a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the meditation. To show that this very triad is indispensable for this meditation, there is a double repetition: "Therefore, this *Sāman* is a constituent part, Prajāpati"; "Therefore, this *Sāman* is a constituent part, Prajāpati."

Since it is thus a *sāman*, its extraction (*uddhāra*) is clearly demonstrated in uninterrupted succession. Therein, among the eight syllables of the first quarter of the root mantra, one should first exhale the first two syllables through the mouth with both hands raised so that the thumbs touch the upper joints; then, touching the lower joint of the little finger, one should likewise exhale the third syllable through the mouth; and then the fourth and fifth syllables, each one by one.

One should sing first with the mouth in the same manner by touching the upper joint of the thumb separately, then the index finger, then the finger adjacent to it, then the ring finger, then the little finger, and then the middle joint of the middle finger; then one should sing with the mouth in the same manner by raising the upper joint of the thumb as the sixth.

By touching the root joint of the little finger with the seventh and eighth syllables while pronouncing the prescribed vowels—one being attentive—one should likewise chant [the Sāman] with the first two syllables, the third syllable, the final fourth syllable, the fifth syllable, the middle sixth syllable, and the seventh and eighth syllables. In the same manner, one should hold the [syllables] long with the third and sixth fingers. Thus, the Sāman is to be chanted upon the eight syllables of the second, third, and fourth quarters.

The sixth syllable of the second foot, the fourth syllable of the third foot, and the sixth syllable of the fourth foot are long; this is the pure *sāman*. If it is with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), one should chant the *praṇava* at the end of the first foot, the *Sāvitrī* at the end of the second foot, the *Yajurlakṣmī* at the end of the third foot, and the *Nṛsiṃhagāyatrī* at the end of the fourth foot. If [the chanter] is a woman or a *śūdra*, they should chant the pure *sāman*, omitting these three. This is the extraction of the *sāman* in its continuous form.

Because it is extremely difficult to obtain and highly secret, even though it has been written, it is not displayed after being transcribed; rather, it is clarified through speech alone. He who knows and meditates in the manner thus described—the word "iti" (thus) serves to give a name to this meditation. In the Upaniṣads, this is the convention: that meditations centered on the *praṇava* and abounding in the *praṇava* are given the name "Mahopaniṣad" in various places.

Regarding the term *mahopaniṣad*: since the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *upa-ni* takes the suffix *kvip* and carries the senses of "going," "bringing to rest," and "dissolving," it is called the *Mahopaniṣad* because it causes one to go to (*gamayati*) or makes known (*jñāpayati*) the Great Brahman; or alternatively, it is the *Mahopaniṣad* because it brings to rest (*avasādayati*), afflicts (*kleśayati*), or destroys (*nāśayati*) the great cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). This is according to the Vedic scripture: "One should unite the Self with the syllable *Om*; this indeed is the *Mahopaniṣad*."

He who knows—that is, worships—this Great Upaniṣad as it has been set forth in the manner described, that worshipper, having performed the preliminary practice (kṛtapuracaraṇa)—meaning he by whom the aforementioned worship has been performed—becomes Mahāviṣṇu. [The root] *viṣlṛ* means "to pervade. The repetition [of the final word] indicates the completion of the first Upaniṣad.

"By means of this *sāman*—which manifests the root mantra that sets forth the *Nṛsiṃha-brāhmaṇa-vidyā*—they indeed, as is well known, emitted all this. Because they emitted all this, therefore he explains the word *vivasṛk*: "They emitted (*vi-vasṛjan*). "One is born after them," meaning one is born following them. "They attain union (*sāyujya*) and residence in the same world (*salokatā*) with the Brāhmaṇa"—this is the specification of the fruits according to the distinction between the meditations on identity and difference for those who practice worship.

"Since such is the fruit for those who meditate upon the Sāman together with its limbs—namely, that they attain union (*sāyujya*) and residence in the same world (*salokatā*) with Brahman—therefore [the text says] 'this' and so forth, ending with 'goes,' the meaning of which has already been explained. The intention behind this repeated practice of "therefore this is the Sāman with its limbs" is as follows: only through the Sāman with its limbs is there the manifestation of the mantras that convey the entire Brāhma-vidyā; thus, it is only the Brāhma-vidyā produced in this way that is fruitful, and no other.

Therefore it has been said: "Therefore, this alone is the primary door in the Kali age. This means that in this time which abounds in sin, this [method] alone possesses primacy, while others are secondary. However, in other times, the primacy of this or another is optional; thus, everything is faultless. Now, he states the extraction of the fourth *sāman*: "Viṣṇu" is the chant consisting of entirely unaccented (*anudātta*) syllables.

Regarding the phrase "the last of the first": it is understood from the preceding context that one should know that even for the two syllables mentioned in the first quarter-verse (*pāda*), [the *sāman*] is joined with the final vowel. Regarding "the last of the second": the connection is that for the two syllables mentioned in the second quarter-verse as well, the *sāman* is joined with the final vowel; thus, the "mouth" is a chant (*gīti*) consisting entirely of unaccented (*anudātta*) tones.

Now, why are the words "first" and "second" in all the extractions (*uddhāra*) explained with reference to the quarters (*pāda*), and not with reference to the number of the syllables mentioned? For instance, in the case of "the last of the first," one should know the final vowel among the two syllables mentioned; likewise, in the case of "the last of the second," one should know the final vowel among the two syllables mentioned.

If this is so, why is it not explained that even in the first extraction (*uddhāra*), one should know the initial vowel of the first syllable [to be] the second syllable? It is said in reply: for everywhere, the terms "first," "second," "third," and "fourth" are heard only with reference to the mention of two syllables.

For it is not logical to apply the terms "third" and "fourth" to the mention of two syllables, because there are no third and fourth syllables [in that context]; thus, one concludes that they must be explained with reference to the *pādas* (quarters). By association with those, it is established that the terms "first" and "second," though mentioned in reference to two syllables, are not to be explained with reference to the syllables themselves, but rather exclusively with reference to the *pādas*. As for the phrase "the end of the third," this refers to the fact that the chant (*gīti*) consists entirely of *anudātta* accents.

The meaning has already been stated: "myaham" is a chant consisting entirely of grave accents (*anudātta*), and it is the final [syllable] of the fourth [part]. Now, why is there no extraction of the *sāman* in its continuous form? For if the *sāman* were extracted continuously, it would be more convenient—just like the extraction of the words taught in the second *upaniṣad*.

It is replied: True, it would be easy; however, although Prajāpati was capable of seeing all the gods, he did not see this Sāman like the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Rather, for the sake of seeing it, having purified his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) slightly through the performance of a single part of this meditation (*upāsanā*), he saw the first extraction (*uddhāra*); and again, having meditated upon the object of worship such as the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*).

He did not see the second extraction; thus, through the performance of increasingly superior worship, his internal organ became increasingly purified, and he saw the third and the fourth—indicating that even for Prajāpati there was great effort in seeing them, let alone for others. This shows the absence of continuous extraction of the Sāman, and demonstrates its rarity and difficulty of perception.

That Prajāpati who is [the source] informed—that is, he announced or taught—this as well: namely, this meditation previously mentioned, "in the Brāhmaṇa" and "in the Self," meaning that having fully realized his own nature as the Brāhmaṇa-Self, whoever knows the meditation connected with the *Anuṣṭubh* by means of the Sāman, he attains immortality; thus the meaning has been stated.

The meaning is that Prajāpati taught the aforementioned meditation either to a woman or a man, or to a woman or a man. Alternatively, this meditation belongs to Hiraṇyagarbha in the Brāhmaṇa; or rather, one knows that the Ānuṣṭubha Sāman is deposited in the supreme Brahman, which is the Brāhmaṇī (the female aspect of Brahman). In this latter view, the word "yat" (which) mentioned previously refers to the object of meditation, and not to Prajāpati.

The word *vā* (or) in the phrase *strīpuṃsor vā strīpuṃso vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), as seen in such examples as *vāyur vā tvā manur vā tvā*. This is what is meant: having performed the placement of the *vara* upon the object of worship (*upāsya*), the practitioner (*upāsaka*) must also perform the placement of the *vara* upon himself. To that practitioner who desires to abide in excellence in this world, [the deity] grants all that is desirable.

At the end of the body, however, the Lord explains the supreme Brahman, the Savior (Tāraka), specifically with reference to the seeker of desire (*kāmin*), because of the inclusion of the qualification "at the end of the body" and because of his prior qualification as a seeker of desire. For the one free from desire (*niṣkāma*), even before the end of the body, the Lord explains the supreme Brahman—the Savior situated within the *praṇava* and forming a limb of the Sāman—which is explained by means of the *praṇava*. By being explained through that *praṇava*, the hearer becomes immortal and attains immortality, which is liberation (*kaivalya*).

Since the Supreme Brahman is to be explained as residing in the *tāraka*, therefore one mutters this *tāraka* which is situated within the *sāman*, that is, existing in the middle of the *sāman*; this shows that the muttering of the *praṇava* is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the meditation (*upāsanā*) on the *sāman*, to be performed according to one's capacity. He says this very thing: "Therefore, this *tāraka* is an ancillary of the *sāman*, [revealed] by Prajāpati as its seer (*ṛṣi*)."

Alternatively, this *tāraka* [mantra] is [the essence] by virtue of its proclamation of the supreme and excellent essential nature (*svarūpa*); the *sāman* is [the essence] by virtue of its manifestation of the root-mantras that establish the knowledge concerning the supreme and excellent object; and Prajāpati is [the essence] by virtue of the exposition of both—this triad is necessarily a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the meditation. To show that this very triad is indispensable for this meditation, there is a repetition: "Therefore, this *sāman*-limb is Prajāpati; therefore, this *sāman*-limb is Prajāpati."

Since the *sāman* is thus [defined], its extraction (*uddhāra*) is now clearly demonstrated in its continuous sequence. Therein, among the eight syllables of the first quarter of the root mantra, one should first exhale the first two syllables through the mouth by raising the thumb of the hand with both hands; then, touching the base joint of the little finger, one should likewise exhale the third syllable through the mouth; and then each of the fourth and fifth syllables individually.

One should likewise sing first with the mouth while touching the upper joint of the thumb separately with each finger—the index, middle, ring, and little fingers—and touching the middle joints of those same fingers respectively; then one should likewise sing first with the mouth while raising the upper joint of the thumb.

With the seventh and eighth syllables, one should sing with the prescribed vowels while touching the root joint of the little finger, remaining vigilant; likewise, one should chant with the mouth using the first two syllables, the third syllable, the final fourth syllable, the fifth syllable, the middle sixth syllable, and the final seventh and eighth syllables. In the same manner, one should hold [the breath] long with the third and sixth fingers. Thus, the *sāman* should be sung upon the eight syllables of the second, third, and fourth quarters.

The sixth syllable of the second foot, the fourth syllable of the third foot, and the sixth syllable of the fourth foot are long; this is the pure *sāman*. If it is with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), one should insert the *praṇava* at the end of the first foot, the *Sāvitrī* at the end of the second foot, the *Yajurlakṣmī* at the end of the third foot, and the *Nṛsiṃhagāyatrī* at the end of the fourth foot while chanting. If [the chanter] is a woman or a *śūdra*, they should chant the pure *sāman*, omitting these three [ancillaries]. This is the extraction of the *sāman* in its continuous form.

Because it is extremely difficult to obtain and highly secret, even though it has been written, it is not displayed after being transcribed; rather, it is clarified through speech alone. He who knows and meditates upon it in the manner thus described—the word "iti" serves to provide a name for this meditation. In the Upaniṣads, this is the convention: that meditations centered on the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) and abounding in the *praṇava* are given the name "Mahopaniṣad" in various places.

Regarding the term *mahopaniṣad*: since the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *upa-ni* takes the suffix *kvip* and carries the meanings of "going," "causing to settle," and "dissolving," it is called the *Mahopaniṣad* because it causes one to go to—that is, makes known—the Great Brahman (*mahadbrahma*). Alternatively, it is called the *Mahopaniṣad* because it settles, afflicts, or destroys the great cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). This is according to the Vedic scripture: "One should unite the Self with the syllable *Om*; this indeed is the *Mahopaniṣad*."

He who knows—that is, meditates upon—this Great Upaniṣad as it has been set forth in the manner described, that meditator, having performed the preliminary practice (kṛtapuracaraṇa)—meaning he by whom the aforementioned meditation has been accomplished—becomes Mahāviṣṇu. [The root] *viṣlṛ* means "to pervade. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] indicates the completion of the first Upaniṣad.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering mendicant teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
The commentary on the first Upaniṣad of the Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīyopaniṣad is complete.

The gods, indeed, were afraid of death, of evil, and of transmigratory existence. They approached Prajāpati, and he bestowed upon them this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter. By means of it, they indeed conquered death, they crossed over evil, and they crossed over transmigratory existence. Therefore, whoever fears death, evil, and transmigratory existence should receive this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter; he conquers death, he crosses over evil, and he crosses over transmigratory existence. Of him—

Indeed, that which is the first *mātrā* of the *praṇava* is the earth, the syllable *a*; it consists of the *ṛc*s, the *Ṛgveda*, the *brahmans*, the Vasus, the *gāyatrī* meter, and the *gārhapatya* fire; it constitutes the first foot of the *sāman*. The second [mātrā] is the intermediate space, the syllable *u*; it consists of the *yajus* formulas, the *Yajurveda*, Viṣṇu, the Rudras, the *triṣṭubh* meter, and the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire; it constitutes the second foot of the *sāman*. The third is heaven, the syllable *m*; it consists of the *sāmans*, the *Sāmaveda*, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the *jagatī* meter, and the *āhavanīya* fire; it constitutes the third foot of the *sāman*.

At the very end of this, there is a three-quarter mātrā; that is the world of Soma, the syllable Om. It is the Atharvaveda with its Atharvan mantras, the Saṃvartaka fire, the Maruts, the Virāj, and the one seer. That radiant fourth foot belongs to the Sāman. || 1 ||

The gods, who had not yet performed their preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), were indeed afraid of death. Those gods, being practitioners (*upāsakāḥ*), were afraid of death—that is, of Vaivasvata as the cause of death—and of that death which is preceded by evil (*pāpman*); and of that evil which is preceded by transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and of transmigratory existence itself, arising from the fear of ignorance (*ajñāna*)—both in its collective and its individual forms. Thus, "they were afraid" is to be connected with each [of these]. For there are two kinds of practitioner-gods: those desirous of liberation (*mumukṣu*) and those not desirous of liberation (*amumukṣu*).

In this context, for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the triad is a collective qualification. For those not seeking liberation (*amumukṣu*) who have not performed the preparatory rites (*puracaraṇa*), the two [other] qualifications are taken separately: some desire only victory over death, some only victory over evil, while others desire victory over all three. These two classes of gods approached Prajāpati; the verb *dhāvati* preceded by *upa* denotes worship. Having approached him, they honored Prajāpati with hymns of praise, service, and sacrificial fees.

To those gods, Prajāpati, being pleased, gave—that is, bestowed—all this which begins with "this king of mantras" and ends with "the Anuṣṭubh," whose meaning has already been explained. By that bestowal, indeed, Prajāpati conquered death; the gods also conquered death. Regarding the use of both plural and singular forms—since the application of the primary sense would apply to both, one should construe the number according to what is appropriate. Likewise, by the word "by that" (*tena*), the acceptance [of the gift] is referred to as being implied by the sense.

This is what is meant: by that giving, Prajāpati conquered death; by that acceptance, the gods conquered death. Some have explained it thus—taking *samṛtyum* as a compound, they say that ignorance which exists together with death (*mṛtyu*) is so described—but that is not correct, because such [ignorance] was not previously introduced as the subject. If it is argued that it is introduced here because it is implied by the sense of the matter, let it be so; there is no contradiction whatsoever.

However, if the fruit for the giver were not proclaimed, how would the giver be motivated? If it is argued that he is motivated by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, we say no; for what can be said of one who is dispassionate? Therefore, the superior interpretation is that this meditation bears fruit in both cases. The same should be explained for the subsequent passages as well—namely, "he crossed over evil" and "he crossed over transmigratory existence."

Since this [practice] is fruitful in both cases, therefore, that aforementioned worshiper who should fear death, evils, and saṃsāra—whether collectively, individually, or from both—should approach a guru and receive this King of Mantras, and so forth, ending with "he crosses over saṃsāra"; this has a clear meaning. "He should accept" means he should take it as his own. By this, he shows that approaching a guru is necessary for the mere reception of the root mantra alone.

Regarding the portion concerning the meditations on the *sāman* and so forth, there is an option: one may learn them either by approaching a teacher or from their exposition [in the texts], because of the Śruti passage: "Therefore, this *sāman* [should be learned] through the mouth of any teacher whatsoever. For this very reason, if one is incapable, one should hear these secret ritual manuals (*kalpa-grantha*) regarding this subject from the mouth of a teacher; if capable, one should examine them oneself, having received from the mouth of a teacher the root mantra along with its seed-syllable (*bīja*), its power (*śakti*), its limbs (*aṅga*), and its ritual renunciation (*nyāsa*).

Thus, for the aforementioned lay practitioner (upāsaka) who seeks liberation, the previously mentioned triad constitutes the qualification; for the other [the householder], the pair constitutes the qualification. In both cases, however, this triad—namely, the praise established by the *stutyupaniṣad*, the worship (*upāsana*) of those manifestations (*vyūha*), and the manifestation of the root mantra through the *sāman*—is common to both, as it constitutes the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).

Having thus described the qualified aspirant, and since the commencement of his worship must be preceded by the worship of the *praṇava*, [we consider] the array of the *Nṛsiṃha* consisting of the *mātrās* of the *praṇava*. Although this array is established as being included within the *puraścaraṇa* worship—on account of the wording of the mantra: "Oṃ saṃ oṃ! To that very Lord, the divine Nṛsiṃha, who is the four *mātrās* and the half-*mātrā*, salutations indeed unto him"—nevertheless, because of the presence here too of the word *mātrā*, the word *ardha*, and the word *catur* (four), there is a recognition of that very same array (*vyūha*). In that very array...

He describes a specific form of meditation by way of its connection with the four *mātrās*: "Of that aforementioned King of Mantras, whose syllables are manifested through the *Sāman* and which exists in an encapsulated (*saṃpuṭita*) state—*ha*, certainly—it has a connection with the *Sāman* because it exists as being encapsulated by the syllables of the root mantra manifested as the *Sāman*; for there is the Śruti: 'Therefore, there is an *oṃkāra* on both sides of every syllable. The passage beginning with "The first *mātrā* of the *praṇava*" and ending with "becomes the fourth foot of the *Sāman*" is of clear meaning. [The *praṇava*] consists of the *akāra*, *ukāra*, *makāra*, and the half-*mātrā*, respectively.

The *praṇava* consists of earth, atmosphere, heaven, the world of Soma, the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāman*, and *Atharva-veda* mantras, the *Brāhmaṇas*, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Oṃkāra, the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Virāj, Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, Āhavanīya, and Saṃvartaka fires; it abides within that *Nṛsiṃha-vyūha* according to the principle of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) and is thus to be meditated upon. Now, one might ask: why are there not many playful incarnations (*līlā-vigrahas*)? We say: no. Because of the singular number in the phrases "to him" (*tasmai*) and "to that" (*tasyai*), it is understood that this playful incarnation is indeed one.

Having thus described the worship of the array of *mātrās* within the *praṇava* included in the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), [the author] now intends to describe the worship of the *brāhma* [Sāman] by means of the root mantra manifested as a Sāman. Anticipating the objection—given the increase in the number of syllables due to the encapsulation of the root mantra by the *praṇava*—as to how the Sāman consists of thirty-two syllables, and intending to describe the five-limbed ritual placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) according to its quarters, he states the total number of syllables of the root mantra preceded by the syllable count of each quarter: [The verse: "Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, Oṃ, O

The first foot consists of eight syllables; there are three feet consisting of eight syllables each, thus they amount to thirty-two syllables. Indeed, the *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables. By means of the *anuṣṭubh*, all this was created; by means of the *anuṣṭubh*, all this is withdrawn. For it has five limbs: four feet are its four limbs, and the entire group of nine [syllables] constitutes the fifth limb. *Oṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ* to the head, *svāhā*.

"Oṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; Oṃ kavacāya huṃ; Oṃ astrāya phaṭ. Thus, the first [syllable] is joined with the first [mantra], the second with the second, the third with the third, the fourth with the fourth, and the fifth with the fifth. These worlds are indeed interwoven; therefore, the limbs [of the mantra] become interwoven. "Oṃ"—this syllable is all this. Therefore, the syllable *oṃ* occurs on both sides of every syllable. Thus do those who recite the Brāhmaṇas teach the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables.

The passage beginning with "The first foot consists of eight syllables" and ending with "all [this] becomes the fifth, together with the *praṇava*," has a clear meaning. Since the five limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) beginning with "oṃ hṛdaya" have already been explained by means of the Sāman-limb-mantras themselves, there is no need for a separate explanation; thus, the section from "hṛdaya" up to "by the fifth" has a clear meaning.

"These worlds are interwoven; therefore, the limbs are interwoven"—this prescribes the interweaving of the limbs (such as the heart and so forth), which are to be meditated upon with the thought that they are the worlds, within the Nṛsiṃha-Brāhmaṇa-manifestation (vyūha) expressed by the root-mantras of the Sāman, whether He is reclining on the ocean of milk or seated. Thus, in the statement "therefore the limbs are interwoven," the meaning is that the limbs to be meditated upon are interwoven, that is, mutually mixed, according to their suitability.

And from this, the following meaning is established: the limb called *hṛdaya* (heart) of the Supreme Lord, which resides within the region below the head-limb of the Supreme Lord, is to be worshipped starting from the region of the heart. For this very reason, during the occasion of explaining the *hṛdaya*-limb of the root mantra by means of the explanation of the *praṇava* as a limb of the Sāman, the *hṛdaya* of the Supreme Lord was explained; otherwise, that explanation would have been out of place.

Therefore, it is established that the exposition of that [the third eye] is introduced precisely by the injunction regarding its interconnection with the [other] limbs. Since the worship of the three eyes is in fact the worship of the heart-limb alone because they are contained within it, for this very reason the worship of the three eyes as a separate limb has not been mentioned. Likewise, in what follows, the limb called the tuft (*śikhā*), which belongs to the Supreme Lord, is to be worshipped as interwoven with the head-limb and the crown (*mūrdhan*), having been explained through the *Sāmāṅgalakṣmī* Yajus mantra.

The second limb, the head, is joined as previously described at the center of the *brahmabila*; it is explained by the *Sāvitrī* mantra, which is a limb of the Sāman, and is to be meditated upon. The armor (*kavaca*) of the Supreme Lord, which pervades the region of the back from above the navel to below the neck at one part of the aforementioned *brahmabila*, is explained by the *Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī*, which is a limb of the Sāman, and is to be meditated upon.

Thus, the fifth limb, called *astra*, which exists in the relationship of upper and lower and resides in the center of its navel, is to be meditated upon as interwoven (*vyatiṣakta*) by virtue of pervading the limbs of the fourfold manifestation (*vyūha*) of the Supreme Lord who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk; in this way, according to its suitability, the word "interwoven" finds its place among the limbs. This presentation of the assignment of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) does not include a sixth limb, because—as was previously stated—that [sixth limb] is contained within the heart.

In order to prescribe the inclusion of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) in the fifth limb, he says: "Because this entire [universe] is the syllable *om*. Since this collection of objects—which consists of both the designator (*abhidhāna*) and the designated (*abhidheya*)—is not distinct from its designator, and since the distinctions among designators are not distinct from the *oṃkāra*, therefore all this is indeed the *oṃkāra*.

Therefore, there is an *oṃkāra* on both sides of every syllable; one should enclose each individual syllable of the root mantra with the *praṇava*. Thus, those who profess the Brahman (*brāhmavādinaḥ*)—those who maintain that the Brahman alone is to be worshipped—instruct and declare this placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the root mantra within the limb known as the *astra*. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the qualifying term "instruct" (*upadiśanti*), he demonstrates that the entire collection of limbs of the root mantra is to be understood through direct instruction.

Having performed this *pañcāṅganyāsa*—characterized by the aforementioned attributes—upon the Supreme Lord who possesses those aforementioned attributes, one should likewise perform it upon one's own self; for in this section, that entire collection of matters is heard for the most part as being related to the Supreme Lord.

Thus, first of all, since it is prescribed that "therefore, there is an *oṃ* at both ends of every syllable," when the meaning fails to be conveyed due to the intervention of the syllables of the root-mantra manifested as Sāman—which results in a conditional ignorance of the word-division (*pada*)—he states the extraction of the words (*padoddhāra*) in order to make known the measure of the words by means of a hidden condition: namely, the conveyance of the meaning without such intervention.

One should indeed know his first station as Ugra; he who knows it attains immortality. The second station is Vīra, the third Mahāviṣṇu, the fourth Jvalant, the fifth Sarvatomukha, the sixth Nṛsiṃha, the seventh Bhīṣaṇa, the eighth Bhadra, and the ninth Mṛtyumṛtyu—to him I bow.

"One should know that the tenth day is the eleventh station; he who knows this attains immortality. Or, the *anuṣṭubh* consists of eleven feet; by the *anuṣṭubh* all this was created, and by the *anuṣṭubh* all this is withdrawn. Therefore, one should know that all this is *ānuṣṭubha*; he who knows this attains immortality. || 3 ||

The passage beginning with "tasya ha vā" and ending with "sarvam upasaṃhṛtam" has a clear meaning. One should know the *sthāna*; one should know the *pada*. Since the concluding statement says, "The *anuṣṭubh* consists of eleven *padas*," all preceding occurrences of the word *sthāna* refer to the *pada*.

Since the manifold of designations and designated objects is not distinct from the designation itself—according to the Vedic scripture, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name"—and since the manifold of names, consisting of generalities and particulars, is not distinct from the name *anuṣṭubh*, and since *anuṣṭubh* is the transformation of the primordial *brahman*, it is established as *brahman* by virtue of its representing the *sākāra-brahman* (the Brahman with form); and since *brahman* is the material cause (*upādāna*) because it is the cause of both creation and reabsorption, therefore *anuṣṭubh* alone is the material cause. Consequently, the passage beginning with "therefore everything is *ānuṣṭubha*" and ending with "it goes" has a clear meaning and should be explained according to the sense already stated.

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati, "Now, why is he called Ugra? He, Prajāpati, replied: "Because by his own greatness he seizes up (*ud-gṛhṇāti*) all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings; he emits them unagingly, he emits them, he causes them to dwell; he utters the *udgītha*, he is seized up. "Praise the famous one, who sits on the chariot-seat, the youthful, the beast, the terrible, the fierce, the one who strikes down. O Lion, being praised, be gracious to the singer! Let your armies lay others low than us! Therefore, he is called Ugra.

Now, why is he called *Vīra*? Because by his own majesty he causes all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings to cease, causes them to rest, creates the undecaying, emits, and causes them to dwell. From whom the hero is born—skillful in action, very dexterous, with joined pressing-stones, desiring the gods—for that reason he is called *Vīra*. Now, why is he called *Mahāviṣṇu*?

He who pervades all worlds and causes them to be pervaded—just as oil permeates a ball of meat, reaching it through and through, interwoven and pervasive, being pervaded and causing pervasion. Because there is no other born from him who is higher, he who has entered into the worlds; Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny, attends to the three lights—he is the Sixteenfold One. Therefore, he is called Mahāviṣṇu. Now, why is he called Jvalanta (the Blazing One)?

He who by his own majesty blazes, causes to blaze, is caused to blaze, and causes to be caused to blaze all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings with his own splendor—he is the Impeller (*savitṛ*), the Procreator (*prasavitṛ*), the Radiant, the Illuminating, the Shining; the Blazing, the Blazed, the Heating, the Warming, the Intensely Heating, the Luminous, the Radiating, the Beautiful, the Beautifying, the Auspicious. Therefore he is called "the Blazing One. Now, why is he called "the One Whose Face Is on All Sides"?

Because, though devoid of sense organs, he sees on all sides, hears on all sides, goes on all sides, grasps on all sides, moves everywhere, and stands on all sides; because he alone was that which existed before this world, from whom the protector of the universe arose; and into whom the universe enters at the time of the final transition—I bow to him who faces in every direction. Therefore, he is called "Sarvatomukha" (the one facing in all directions). Now, why is he called "Nṛsiṃha"?

Because among all beings there is none more powerful or more excellent than the lion, and since the lion is the most powerful and most excellent, he became *Nṛsiṃha* (the Man-Lion) in the supreme state. Indeed, this imperishable form is for the welfare of the world. Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic power: "The formidable beast, roaming the mountains, who dwells in the three wide strides, within which the worlds abide. Therefore, it is called *Nṛsiṃha*.

Now, why is it called "the Terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇam*)? Because upon seeing His form by His own majesty, all the worlds, all the gods, and all beings flee in fear, while He Himself does not fear from any quarter whatsoever. "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run forth. Therefore, it is called "the Terrifying. Now, why is it called "the Auspicious" (*bhadram*)?

Because He Himself is auspicious (*bhadra*), and always bestows what is auspicious; because He is radiant (*rocana*), shining (*rocamāna*), beautiful (*śobhana*), resplendent (*śobhamāna*), and excellent (*kalyāṇa*). "O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Worshipful Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise [Him] and attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods. Therefore, it is called "Auspicious" (*bhadram*). Now, why is it called "Death-of-Death" (*mṛtyumṛtyu*)? Because when merely remembered by His own devotees, He slays both death and untimely death.

He who is the giver of self, the giver of strength, whose command even the gods revere; he whose shadow is immortality, who is death unto death—to what god shall we offer worship with oblation? Therefore it is said, "death unto death. And why is it said, "I bow"? Because all the gods, those seeking liberation, and the speakers of the Veda bow to him. Now Brāhmaṇaspati truly utters the hymn worthy of praise, in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the gods have made their dwelling.

Therefore it is said: "I bow. Now, why is it said: "I"? "I am the first-born of Truth (ṛta), born before the gods, the name of immortality. He who gives me away—he indeed does not possess me. I eat the eater of food. I have overcome the wide world. The light of heaven!"—this is the secret teaching (upaniṣad) for one who knows thus. 4.
Thus ends the second Upaniṣad.

By means of a question and answer, he elucidates that very hidden condition (*gūḍhopādhi*) through which the knowledge of the words arose as a medium for conveying the intended meaning; and this [condition] must be explained here at length after having set forth the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) together with its limbs (*sāṅga*) as manifested by the *Sāmā*. That root-mantra consists of eleven words: the first quarter consists of three words, the second consists of two words, the third consists of three words, and the fourth consists of exactly that same number of words.

Thus, in this mantra consisting of eleven words, which has been stated following the five-fold ritual placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*), among the nine words ending in the second case, the final two words of the mantra and the first word of the third quarter—this triad—is appended to all the words below and above, except for the first word of the third quarter; however, that pair is appended to the first word of the third quarter itself. In this way, there is purity in the relationship of the connection between action, agent, and so forth.

In this regard, since the extraction of words and the explanation of their meaning have been recited immediately after the placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*), the meaning must be explained for all the quarters (*pāda*) along with their constituent parts. Thus, in the first quarter—which consists of three words and includes its parts—the explanation of the limbs of the root mantra and the heart-mantra of Brahman is obtained through the *Sāmopaniṣad*, which is to be meditated upon by means of the fire of the worlds and so forth, as well as the *praṇava* that is a limb of the Sāman. In that context, each individual word is to be explained in its many meanings. Likewise, there are the subsequent verses consisting of eleven words, which exist within the Brāhmaṇa portion situated between questions and answers.

"Regarding this, the following has been declared"—thus, these [verses] should be described as being intended to explain each individual word of the root mantra within the Brāhmaṇa, which is manifested as a witness for the meaning stated in the Brāhmaṇa and consists of the Great Cakra (mahācakra) composed of the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha-manifestation. Likewise, the Brāhmaṇa should be explained as being intended to explain each individual word of the root mantra within the Brāhmaṇa pertaining to the primary Nṛsiṃha-manifestation associated with the Ocean of Milk at the hub of the Great Cakra, characterized by the previously mentioned qualities.

For this very reason, we shall clearly demonstrate the citation of the Ṛgveda and Brāhmaṇas as witnesses therein, along with the sequence of their division, at the occasion of explaining each respective term.

In that regard, how will Prajāpati express the vast multitude of meanings for each individual word through its connection with verbal roots, prefixes, and so forth; and how will he explain them to us who are already proficient? Thinking thus, the gods, filled with wonder and joy, spoke to Prajāpati. Having asked for an explanation common to all words, they then asked: "From which division of root and suffix is the first word, consisting of that which is not a verb, spoken and explained in both cases?"

"In the primary Nṛsiṃha array and in the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha array, [He is] 'Ugra' (the Fierce). The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the question. That Prajāpati, seeing those gods—who were devoted to the worship of the Supreme Lord and were inquiring about the intended meaning—became delighted and spoke the answer. This same logic should be applied to the subsequent questions and answers as well. Because, by His own majesty—that is, by His independent power, *māyā*—He is independent precisely because that power is under His own control.

The expression "by its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*) indicates that the word from the beginning of the third quarter, which possesses all powers, is to be supplied [to the preceding]. Thus, at the occasion of explaining each respective term: "all worlds," such as the earth and others, distinguished by sub-species of the class *pārthiva*; "all gods," such as Agni and others; in the view of the explanation of the *praṇava*, those ending with the *gārhapatya* fire, which are established by the first *mātrā* of the *praṇava*; "all selves," such as Viśva and others, which will be mentioned in the explanation of the *praṇava* as a limb of the Sāman; and "all beings."

"Udgr̥hṇāti": *ud* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) standing in place of the particle *u*; because of the similarity of phonemes, it carries the sense of the prefix *anu*. *Graha* is derived from the verbal root *grah* in the sense of "to take" (*gṛhṇāti*), specifically through a formation denoting state (*bhāvavyutpatti*). Thus, the meaning is "he favors" (*anugr̥hṇāti*). The term *ajaram* means "unceasingly. Furthermore, the verb *grah* preceded by the prefix *ud* occurs in the senses of emission, release, and abiding. From the middle voice endings (*ātmanepada*) in forms such as *udgrāhrate* and *udgṛhrate*, it is established that there is both the status of an instigating agent (*prayojakakartṛtva*) and the status of a direct agent (*sākṣātkartṛtva*); this confirms the very meaning already stated.

And thus the meaning is as follows: the state of being the cause of grace (*anugrāhakatva*) for the previously mentioned meanings; and since the root *sṛj* preceded by *vi* has the sense of withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), it possesses that same meaning or the sense of liberation (*vimocana*); and the state of being the cause of stability (*avasthitikārayitṛtva*) constitutes the instrumentality (*prayojakatva*) in grace—by virtue of existing within the two-fold manifestation (*vyūha*) of the Root Nṛsiṃha.

That which is to be worshipped. Having thus explained the word *ugra* as being intent upon the worship of the secret heart of the Root-Nṛsiṃha, he now speaks this verse to explain that same word as being intent upon the worship of the thirty-two-fold manifestation (*vyūha*). He addresses the worshiper directly with "Praise! (*stuhi*), while referring to the object of praise in the third person. "The heard" (*śrutam*) refers to the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha manifestation, which has been heard precisely through the scriptural verses beginning with "He who is indeed Nṛsiṃha."

"Gartasadam" means one who sits in the pit (gartasada); it is derived from the root *gṛ* meaning "to praise," thus [the word] *garta* signifies that which is praised or extolled. He "sits" (*sīdati*) there, hence he is called Gartasada. "Yuvānam" refers to the well-known [Lord]. "Mṛgam" means one in the form of a lion. "Nabhīmam" means not causing fear. "Upahatnum" means one whose nature is to approach everywhere for the sake of bestowing grace. "Ugram" refers to the form of the twenty-eight-fold Nṛsiṃha array. Here too, the term "Nṛsiṃha endowed with Śakti" is to be supplied. The syntactical connection is: "Praise [Him] in this manner."

Thus, when the twenty-two-fold manifestation of Nṛsiṃha has been praised indirectly, that manifestation became visible to the worshiper by its own power and because of his being endowed with the hearing of the syllables; having thus made it manifest, he speaks with the second half [of the verse]: "O Lion, O twenty-two-fold manifestation, you who are being praised—be gracious (mṛḍa), bring happiness to the singer (jaritre), the composer of the hymn. Or rather, the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative: let your armies (senāḥ) cast us down (nivapantu), that is, destroy others than us."

Alternatively, having received favor from you, he prays for the favor of others: "May those armies of yours, in the form of their battle arrays (*vyūha*), favor (*anugṛhṇantu*) someone other than us"—here the root *vap*, preceded by *ni*, functions in the sense of favoring. Since the term *ugra* is appropriate for both objects of worship in the manner previously stated, it is therefore called *ugram*. The word *iti* indicates the conclusion of the preceding [section]. Having thus understood that the first word is suitable for worship by both, now follows the second question of the gods in order to explain the second word as being applicable to both objects of worship; and that is:

This has been explained by the first question of the deity; now, as to why he is called "Vīra," Prajāpati spoke the answer, appending what was previously stated: "Because by his own majesty... and so on, up to "...all beings," the meaning of which has already been explained. He "viramati" (rests) or "virāmayati" (causes to rest); he delights in various ways those mentioned before. [The root] *ram* is used in the sense of sporting. In that very manner, he causes them to sport. When it is asked, "In what way does he cause them to sport? he says: "He makes them ageless... and so on, up to "...he causes them to dwell," the meaning of which has already been explained.

This is what is meant: the activities of Brahmā and the others—namely, the acts of creation, sustenance, dissolution, and liberation—are "sports" (*krīḍā*) whose meaning has been explained previously. Therefore, the pair consisting of the Root Nṛsiṃha and the Vyūha Nṛsiṃha, endowed with these sports, is to be worshipped. Having thus explained the second word as being devoted to the worship of the Root Nṛsiṃha, he speaks the half-verse beginning with "yato vīraḥ" in order to explain that same word in the context of the worship of the thirty-two-fold Vyūha Nṛsiṃha.

"Devakāmaḥ" means one who desires to cause those various deities, such as Brahmā and others, to descend in their own forms; or alternatively, it refers to one who, while maintaining the very manifestation (vyūha) of Nṛsiṃha, reveals the form of Brahmā and others—sometimes by means of weapons and sometimes according to the principle of assuming the appearance of the world—as seen in passages such as "He who is the divine Lord Nṛsiṃha and he who is Brahmā," and "He who is the divine Lord Nṛsiṃha and those who are the eight Vasus."

Thus, one who desires the gods is born as a hero (*vīra*). Alternatively, a hero is one whose nature is to delight in the manifold and beautiful cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through various incarnations; he is "active" (*karmaṇya*), meaning his nature is to perform the actions of those various incarnations for the sake of favoring his worshippers. He is "very skillful" (*sudakṣa*), meaning his strength is honored, or simply "honored. He is "one with the pressing-stones" (*yuktagrāvā*), joined with the stones, appearing in the form of the *adhvaryu* priest and others during the Soma sacrifice—as stated in such Vedic mantras as, "He who is indeed the Lord Nṛsiṃha, and who is everything. Since the word "hero" (*vīra*) is appropriate for both [the devotee and the Lord] when worshipped in the manner described, therefore it is said:

Regarding the word "Vīram": the particle *iti* indicates the conclusion of what follows. Now, in order to explain the third section, there is the question of the gods; its meaning has already been stated. In all interrogative sentences, the word *atha* signifies the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of each respective point. Regarding the question, "Why is he called Mahāviṣṇu?", the particle *iti* indicates the conclusion of the recurring question. The answer follows by connecting with the phrase, "He, Prajāpati, said."

In the phrase "He" (*saḥ*), by the principle of ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) from the preceding [phrase], the word "Nṛsiṃha," as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), is also to be supplied along with "by his own majesty. In the phrase "he pervades (*vyāpnoti*) and causes to pervade all worlds (*sarvalokān*)," the term "all worlds" includes those who have become the self of the gods, according to the maxim of "beginning with that" (*tadādinyāya*), since they were understood to follow the previously established order. The form "Viṣṇu" is derived from the root *viṣlṛ* (to pervade). Since that quality of pervasion attains the status of greatness through its lack of a qualifying prefix, it is further confirmed by the word "Great" (*mahat*).

Alternatively, *maha* is a name for brilliance (*tejas*), meaning that which is pervasive (*vyāpaka*). He provides an illustration for this pervasiveness: just as oil and the like (*sneha*)—such as sesame oil—is woven through (*ota*), interwoven (*anusyūta*), and thoroughly permeated (*protam*, i.e., extensively interwoven and adhered) within a lump of flesh (*palalapiṇḍa*, a mass of meat), such that it pervades (*vyāpyate*) and causes [the flesh] to be pervaded (*vyāpayate*) by being intermingled with its constituent parts; since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed in the illustration, while the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is employed in the case of the subject of the illustration, it follows that this verbal root is conjugated in both voices (*ubhayapadī*).

He demonstrates this: what is meant is that the direct pervasiveness and the causal pervasiveness toward all the worlds and so forth previously mentioned are to be meditated upon within the heart of the Root-Nṛsiṃha-Brahman.

Thus, having first explained the third station of Mahāviṣṇu as being devoted to the worship of the *sāṅga-mūla-nṛsiṃha-vyūha*, he now speaks this *ṛc* to explain that very same station as being devoted to the worship of the thirty-two-fold *nṛsiṃha-vyūha*: From which thirty-two-fold *nṛsiṃha-vyūha* no other has been born superior or more excellent—because there exists nothing else outside of it, since everything is included within it—that *vyūha* has entered (*āviveśa*) all (*viśvā*), that is, all (*sarvāṇi*) worlds (*bhuvanāni*) and beings.

In order to pervade [all things] by assuming various forms and manifesting as the Universal Form (viśvarūpa), Prajāpati also appears together with his progeny through such manifestation; being in full consciousness and understanding, he attends upon and serves the three lights—the Gārhapatya and the others—as objects of worship. While performing this worship, that Prajāpati became the sixteenth digit (kalā) through the state of formless Brahman.

And this is the sequence of worship for that first worshipper, Prajāpati, or for any other worshipper: in this context, the traditional convention handed down from the ancient teachers is that the object of worship is the Root-Nṛsiṃha-arrangement (mūlanṛsiṃhavyūha) associated with the Ocean of Milk situated at the hub of the Great Wheel.

And there, having first uttered the seed-syllable of Śakti preceded by the *praṇava*, and having placed [the syllables] upon the wheel manifested by the Sāman in its seventy-two syllables, one should worship each respective manifestation (*vyūha*) with its corresponding mantra—each syllable being encapsulated by the *praṇava*—and meditate upon it in that very same manner.

Thus, having worshipped one's own self as Mahāviṣṇu through the meditation on the twenty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha-arrangement (vyūha), and having performed the five-fold ritual placement (pañcāṅganyāsa) upon that Nṛsiṃha-arrangement—since it is heard in this section [of the scripture] by means of the root-mantra with its limbs manifested along with the Sāman-limbs—and likewise having performed the five-fold ritual placement upon that Mahāviṣṇu according to the tradition, one should then begin the worship together with its limbs.

In that regard, within the first chapter consisting of three parts, one should worship the primary Nṛsiṃha-arrangement (vyūha), characterized by the qualities set forth in the explanation of the first part and preceded by the word "Nṛsiṃha" [possessing power] and the word "salutation" (namaskriyā) as the final element; and having worshipped that, one should worship the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha-arrangement as propounded in the Ṛgveda. This [latter] is characterized by the qualities set forth in the Sāman-limb Praṇava-mantra and the Brahmadaiva-mantra.

Thus, following each step preceded by the worship of the Mūla-Nṛsiṃha-vyūha, there is the worship of the thirty-two Nṛsiṃha-vyūhas. For this very reason, while explaining the meaning of the heart-mantra and other limb-mantras, we have stated in the *Prapañcāgama-śāstra*: "Because it is accessible to the intellect, the heart is the object of salutation; therefore, the word 'namas' is employed for the heart. Hence, the act of salutation is performed toward that which is accessible to the intellect."

Thus, having performed the previously described meditations on each respective word in the second, third, and fourth quarters (*pādas*), the practitioner should abide either in the form indicated by the final word—which is the form of Mahāviṣṇu—or in the form of the object of meditation, or in the form of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*) through union (*sāyujya*); or else, according to the fitness of his internal organ’s purity, he should remain in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). In the first and second meditations, one should abide preceded by the optional recitation (*japa*) of the Sāman, the root-mantra, and the *praṇava*.

Likewise, wherever there is the recollection of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), there one should perform the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) with the seed-syllable of the power of *praṇava*. Even in that case, the recitation of *praṇava* preceded by a slight recitation of the root mantra is superior, because it is the most excellent and is ordained as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the recitation of all mantras, according to the Vedic revelation: "He who studies the *praṇava* studies everything."

In the case of the two final meditations, since they abide in a formless state within the *antya-sāman*, there is neither recitation nor contemplation of anything else; rather, there is abiding solely in *samādhi*. Thus it is established that this discernment of the supreme secret is not to be imparted to anyone. Because this is the station of Mahāviṣṇu, capable of manifesting both objects of meditation, it is therefore called "Mahāviṣṇum. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the answer to the question concerning the third section (*pada*). In this manner, the first quarter (*pāda*) has been explained.

Having thus prescribed the meditation on the first quarter along with its ancillaries, Prajāpati begins the inquiry in order to prescribe the meditation on the second quarter in the same manner and to explain that first [quarter], which is the fourth quarter in relation to the mantra. That [inquiry] has its meaning already stated. Now, why is it said, "the blazing one"? The word *iti* has been explained. [The answer] follows by connecting it with: "Prajāpati said..."

He who, by His own majesty and His self-dependent *māyā*, blazes with His own splendor—that is, illuminates by His own light—all the worlds previously mentioned and those yet to come, including all the worlds situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); all the gods contained therein, such as Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and others; all the persons consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva* Vedas; other sages who are commentators on the *Sāman* limbs and the *Sāvitra* mantras; and all beings—these aforementioned and those yet to be mentioned—He causes to shine by His own radiance. This is the splendor residing within the head.

This has been explained, because it is heard in scripture that the limbs are mutually connected by pervading all parts and the whole, according to the Vedic text: "Therefore, the limbs are interwoven. Thus, although the connection with the fire contained within the head-portion is established both as a direct motivator and through its relation to itself and others, he employs the verbal root in both voices—first in the *parasmaipada* and now in the *ātmanepada*—in order to make this very point known: "it is kindled" (*jvālyate*) and "it kindles itself" (*jvālayate*).

Having thus explained the fourth quarter in relation to the worship of the Mūlanṛsiṃhavyūha, he recites the Ṛgvedic verse to explain it in relation to the Dvātriṃśannṛsiṃhavyūha: "Savitṛ. Because it exists as a circle like the solar orb, this Dvātriṃśannṛsiṃhavyūha is Savitṛ; for that very reason, it is Prasavitṛ, the one who grants permission for the performance of all rites, since the worship of other [deities] is preceded by the worship of this Vyūha.

"Blazing" (*dīptaḥ*), "causing to blaze" (*dīpayan*), and "blazing forth" (*dīpyamānaḥ*): just as this Sun is "blazing"—shining and authorized for the performance of ritual action by destroying the night of darkness, so too this array of the twenty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha, when worshipped, is "blazing"—shining and authorized for the primary worship—by destroying the night of ignorance for the worshipper who has practiced the primary Nṛsiṃha array. The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* in the words "blazing" and "blazing forth" signify the present time and serve to reinforce the very meaning already stated.

"Blazing" means burning; "illuminating" means making manifest. Alternatively, although the word *jvalan* occurs in both cases in the sense of burning, it should be explained here as the burner of ignorance. In that context, it is the burner of the world's ignorance which is like darkness, while in the present case, it is the burner of the ignorance of the practitioner.

Blazing, he performs the burning away of ignorance; blazing, he is the agent of the burning away of ignorance. Heating, he produces heat; heating, he causes the scorching of ignorance. Cooling himself, he produces cooling; cooling, he causes the alleviation of ignorance. These present-tense participles (*śatṛ-pratyaya*) show that at the very time this worship of the array (*vyūha*) is taking place, the worshipper is Mahāviṣṇu himself, whose nature is light and who possesses the requisite qualification. Shining, he does not cause agitation; shining forth, he fulfills desires.

Therefore, it is "beautiful," "shining," and "auspicious. This is what is meant: the splendor situated upon the elevated head-limb of the Mūla-Nṛsiṃha array is the illuminator of all and the burner of all ignorance; thus, as explained by the Sāvitra mantra of the subsidiary limb, it is to be meditated upon. Since the word *jvalantam* ("blazing") is capable of conveying both objects of meditation, he concludes by referring to both objects of meditation: "Therefore it is said, 'the blazing one' (*jvalantam*). The word *iti* has been explained.

Now, the question of the deity (devapraśna) is introduced in order to explain the fifth word with respect to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*)—which is the second with respect to the quarters (*pāda*)—as it follows in due order. [The question is: "Why is it called 'Sarvatomukha' (Facing All Directions)? And that has already had its meaning explained. [The answer is given by] Prajāpati, which is to be supplied as the response. It is to be explained by supplying the phrase "by his own majesty" (*svamahimnā*). He is "without senses" (*anindriya*); this means that although he possesses a body whose nature has been explained as having senses, he is "without senses" because he is devoid of identification (*abhimāna*) with them.

This primary Nṛsiṃha-vyūha, though devoid of sense organs, "sees everywhere and hears everywhere," which indicates the existence of the cognitive (buddhi) organs; "it moves everywhere, grasps everything, goes everywhere, and stands everywhere," which indicates the existence of the organs of action (karma-indriya). Thus, it shows that this vyūha, although free from the egoistic identification with both sets of organs, possesses the power to perform the functions generated by both types of organs, and should therefore be worshipped as being present in the head.

Having thus explained this "all-facing" word (*sarvatomukhapada*) as being intent upon the worship of the Root-Nṛsiṃha, he now explains it through a *ṛc* verse as being intent upon the means of worshipping the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha: "In the beginning, the One existed in front, in the east, in the form of Nṛsiṃha; from whom all this has come into being, the Protector (*gopā*) of the world, Viṣṇu himself, became Nṛsiṃha."

"That into which the entire world goes—that is, enters into dissolution—at the time of the final end (saṃparāya), he indeed became Nṛsiṃha, the Great Lord (Maheśvara). By mentioning the first of the three established arrangements (vyūhas) at the very outset, this mantra includes the remaining nineteen arrangements according to the principle of "mentioning the first" (*tadādinyāya*). By stating the two words "I bow" (*namāmi*) and "I pay homage" (*namaskaromi*)—that is, "I bow to that arrangement"—the author demonstrates that these are connected throughout the explanation of all the terms.

Because of the inclusion of the phrase "by its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*) everywhere, the word *Nṛsiṃha*, which possesses power, is also connected to each of those instances. Regarding the term *sarvatomukham*: he whose faces are in the form of Nṛsiṃha on all sides is thus described; the meaning is, "I bow to that Nṛsiṃha who is *sarvatomukha*. Since this word is capable of conveying both objects of worship, it concludes by stating "therefore" (*tasmāt*) as the means of conveying both: "Therefore, it is called *sarvatomukha*."

This is what is meant: in the second foot (*pāda*), the primary manifestation (*mūlanṛsiṃhavyūha*) is to be meditated upon, characterized by the head as its limb, and distinguished by the qualities of being the illuminator of all things, the burner of all ignorance, being devoid of the conceit of both sets of sense organs, and possessing the power to perform the functions of both sets of sense organs; this is further qualified by the attributes explained in the *sāmāṅga-savitṛ-mantra*. From that [first manifestation], the other manifestations follow. Thus, because the head is situated at the elevated part of the body from the first limb, it is called the "head" (*śiras*); its nature is elevation.
