For this very reason, the head is the Sun—the most excellent light of all.

"To that Exalted One, who dwells on high, the Sun, the most supreme light, Svāhā!"—this is the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Having withdrawn the mind from that form of the phenomenal world back to its own [true] form, one should meditate solely upon the form of Nṛsiṃha; such is the meaning of the mantra of the Head limb, according to the Śruti: "He who is indeed the divine Lord Nṛsiṃha, he is all."

For this very reason, it has been stated by us while explaining the meaning of the *śiro'ṅga* mantra in the *Prapañcāgamaśāstra*: "Because the *śiro'ṅga* has the sense of 'exalted' (*tuṅga*), its splendor lies in the seizing of objects; and by means of the *śiromantra*, the cognition of exalted objects is proclaimed."

Thus, having described the worship with its ancillaries (*sāṅgopāsanā*) in the second quarter (*pāda*), in order to describe the worship of the third quarter in the same manner, the question of the gods is posed to explain the first word of that [quarter]—which is the sixth word with respect to the root mantra—as the object of the aforementioned worship: "Now, why is he called Nṛsiṃha? This has already been explained. The answer follows, supplied by the phrase "Prajāpati said. And here, because of the use of the word "yasmāt" (since), it shows that the phrase "by his own majesty" (*svamahimnā*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).

Since, among all beings, the man (nṛ) is the most heroic in form, and since the lion (siṃha) is more heroic and superior than even that—exceeding all others—the meaning already stated is that he is the most heroic and the most excellent. Furthermore, by demonstrating his dual nature as both man and lion, he shows that he is capable of assuming whatever form he desires merely through play (*līlayā*). Because it is so, the grammatical connection is: "Therefore, the Supreme Lord became Nṛsiṃha."

Nor can there be the syntactical connection (anvaya) "and [the one] in Nṛsiṃha, the Supreme Lord, existed," because that would result in a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya); for when a coreferential (sāmānādhikaraṇya) connection is possible, a non-coreferential one is untenable. Therefore, it is established that Nṛsiṃha is the Supreme Lord, three-eyed, blue-throated, and the wielder of the Pināka bow.

"Ṛta" and "satya" have been explained previously, and it is stated [in the Vedic hymns] that "jagaddhita" means the welfare of the world; it is well known (*vai*) that this very form—which was previously described as the Imperishable (*akṣara*) to be meditated upon—becomes possessed of form for the sake of favoring the meditators. The syntactical connection is that that which is the Imperishable, indestructible, of the nature of consciousness, and formless, becomes indeed possessed of form.

Having thus explained the sixth term, *nṛsiṃha*, in the context of the worship of the primary *nṛsiṃha*-manifestation (*mūlanṛsiṃhavyūha*), he now explains that very term through a verse in the context of the thirty-two-fold *nṛsiṃha*-manifestation (*dvātriṃśannṛsiṃhavyūha*): Viṣṇu is the "deer" (*mṛga*) and the "lion" (*siṃha*). He is "praised" (*prastavate*), meaning he receives praise through hymns for the sake of his prowess—that is, for the sake of his respective powers. He is "not terrible" (*na bhīmaḥ*), meaning not frightening. He is "wandering everywhere" (*kucaraḥ*); he does not wander anywhere [in a limited sense], but rather wanders by his own play (*līlayā*) within the forms of all the gods. The meaning is that he assumes the playful forms of all the deities.

*Giriṣṭhāḥ*: "Abiding on the mountain"; *giri* means mountain or *parvata*, and the meaning is that He who abides there has the nature of the Lord (*Īśvara*). Alternatively, *giriṣṭhāḥ* refers to Him who, in the praises consisting of speech (*vāk*), establishes within Himself whatever form the worshiper desires while longing for it. "In whose three strides"—*vikramaṇeṣu* means various strides or manifestations, namely those consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. *Adhi* denotes the sense of "above" or "beyond. [He dwells] "upon the high ones," that is, upon His many playful incarnations (*līlā-vigraha*).

All worlds dwell—that is, they reside—by their very nature; they dwell and abide [thinking], "We remain within these sport-forms (līlāvigraha). Thus, the root *kṣi* denotes the act of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), meaning they attain sovereignty. In this way, for the sake of valor (*vīrya*) and power (*sāmarthya*) in His various strides and descents, Viṣṇu—in the forms of the deer, the lion, and so on—is praised; the meaning is that He receives supreme hymns of praise.

Since this word *Nṛsiṃha* has been explained as referring to that which is to be worshipped in both [aspects], he concludes with "therefore": "Therefore it is called *Nṛsiṃha*. Having thus explained the first and sixth words, *Nṛsiṃha*, with reference to both aspects, there now follows a question to explain the second and seventh words with reference to both: "Now, why is it called *Bhīṣaṇa*? The answer follows, supplied by the phrase: "Prajāpati said."

Because of the inclusion of the word "since" (*yasmāt*), the phrase "by its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*) is to be supplied as a continuation. Since, by its own majesty, all the gods—the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—who dwell in the radiance of its limbs, as well as all these beings, became terrified upon seeing that form which is composed of invincible splendor; whose essential nature is the root-manifestation of Nṛsiṃha; which is complete with its limbs and possessed of the *śikhā* limb; which is endowed with a mass of lunar luster in the region of the crown; which is explained by the *Sāma*, *Yajus*, and *Lakṣmī* mantras; and which is joined with a mass of splendor condensed from the four worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Mahar—[all were struck with fear].

Out of fear they flee; they run away. The Lord himself does not fear anything whatsoever; He is the one to be worshipped, distinguished by the quality of unsurpassed fearlessness. Having thus explained the word *bhīṣaṇa* (the terrifying) with respect to the aforementioned worshipful form, he explains that same word by applying it to the second manifestation (*vyūha*), beginning with "bhīṣā" and so forth: "Out of fear (*bhīṣā*)—that is, out of dread—from this root manifestation (*mūlavyūha*), the wind (*vātaḥ*) blows (*pavate*). By the inclusion of the word "wind," the manifestation of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtavyūha*) is indicated.

"Out of fear of Him the sun rises"—by this, the arrays of Soma and Sūrya are indicated. "Out of fear of Him fire [blazes]"—this is the Āgneya array. "And Indra..."—this is the Sarvavyūha. "Death runs as the fifth"—this is the Mṛtyu array.

In this regard, although five manifestations (*vyūha*) are mentioned in this verse, nevertheless, according to the principle of "the first [representing] all" (*tadādinyāya*), because fear is seen as the synthesis of everything, there exists a twofold nature for all of them—whether they be Vāta, Āditya, and so forth. This twofold nature consists in either the inclusion of all [beings] such as Brahmā and others by way of perceiving fear in their own respective forms, or through the entry of Nṛsiṃha, whose nature is the absence of fear, or by assuming those various forms themselves. Thus, all possess this dual form.

In this regard, by assuming the respective forms of each individual deity, he displays both forms; and by showing that both [the elements] and the deities are included within himself, he demonstrates the dual nature. Thus, the meaning of the *ṛc* is that it subsumes the entire thirty-two-fold manifestation (*vyūha*) through this dual form. Since the term "terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇa*) has been explained in this way as referring to the object of worship for both [aspects], he concludes with "therefore": "Therefore, it is called 'terrifying'."

Having been addressed thus, after explaining the previously mentioned term regarding the object of worship (*upāsya*), the question of the gods is now posed in order to explain the third and eighth terms—which relate to both—as pertaining to the object of worship for both: "Now, why is it called 'Bhadra'? Prajāpati replied, supplying the answer by connecting it with the phrase "by his own majesty" (*svamahimnā*) which follows from the mention of that term.

Having himself become auspicious (*bhadra*) and worthy of worship, and having become a source of blessings (*māṅgalika*), he always bestows what is auspicious and blessed; thus it is shown that his very nature as a giver of blessings is to be meditated upon within the primary manifestation (*mūlavyūha*). He is "radiant" (*rocana*), meaning endowed with brilliance. He is "shining" (*rocamāna*), producing a brilliant luster through the member that is the crest (*śikhā*), because of the presence of the present participle suffix (*śānac*). That member possesses a form of brilliance even greater than the second member, which is of the nature of splendor.

Therefore, it should be meditated upon as follows: the splendor residing in the crown adorned with various ornaments overcomes the inherent splendor of the deities contained within it. For this very reason, we have stated while explaining the *śikhāṅga-mantra*.

In the *Prapañcāgama-śāstra*: "The syllable *ṭha* is designated as the *tejaḥ* (splendor); *vaṣaṭ* is said to be the limb (*aṅga*). Therefore, that splendor of this [mantra] is declared to be the *śikhā* (crest) of the practitioner by means of the mantra. The meaning is that the *śikhā* is a constituent part of unsurpassed splendor, according to the Vedic revelation: "He whose crest consists of knowledge. It is beautiful by its own nature, and it shines with the splendor of the crest-limb; for this very reason, it is *kalyāṇa*, the auspicious primary manifestation of Nṛsiṃha.

Having thus explained the eighth word (*pada*) regarding the object of worship (*upāsya*), he now explains the thirty-two-fold manifestation (*dvātriṃśad-vyūha*) by means of that very word through a Vedic verse: "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" (Auspiciousness with our ears...). This verse was already explained at the beginning during the recitation of the *Śānti*. The distinction here is: "by these very bodies," meaning by these firm limbs which are the *tanū-mantras*. Since the hymns of praise are included within the fifth limb, the explanation of both [the limbs] is given for the object of worship; therefore, he concludes: "Therefore it is said, 'Bhadram'."

The word *iti* has been explained. Thus, having described the worship with its limbs (*sāṅgopāsanā*) by means of the explanation of each respective term in the third quarter (*pāda*), [the text] proceeds to describe the worship of the fourth quarter in the same manner. Regarding the first term of that [quarter], which is the ninth term in relation to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), the question of the gods is posed in order to explain both objects of worship: "Now, why is it called 'Death of Death' (*mṛtyumṛtyu*)? The answer follows, connecting with the words "Prajāpati said": "Because, by his own majesty... (this phrase is to be supplied).

For His own devotees, when they worship Him with single-minded devotion, He—being remembered and meditated upon alone—destroys both death that has arrived at its appointed time (*mṛtyu*) and untimely death (*apamṛtyu*) that occurs prematurely; untimely death being that which occurs between the birth-rite and the full lifespan determined by the science of astrology. Such armor, which destroys these things even without being requested by those who worship Him with single-minded devotion, is the limb to be meditated upon.

The meaning is that, because it is explained through its constituent parts of the sāman-mantra, the Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī, and the form of Nṛsiṃha, it brings about for those who worship it their own true nature and destroys both death and untimely demise.

This is because of the mantra-text: "The Lord Nṛsiṃha is indeed threefold, as is the individual soul (jīva). Having previously explained this aforementioned term (*pada*) as referring to the object of worship in the primary Nṛsiṃha manifestation (*vyūha*), he now explains the thirty-two-fold manifestation by means of that same term through a verse. That which is the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha manifestation is *ātmadāḥ*—one who gives the self; that is, the giver of one's own true nature. The meaning is that, having bestowed the essential form upon all the gods, it sustains them.

*Baladāḥ* means the giver of power; the sense is that He grants the capacity to His own devotees to assume their respective forms. *Yasya praśiṣam*: the instruction (*praśiṣam*) of the four limbs of the primary *Nṛsiṃha-vyūha*; "instruction" (*praśiṣam*) is so called because it is taught preeminently (*prakarṣeṇa śiṣyate*). This refers to the remaining twenty-two *vyūhas*, which all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), meaning all the deities, worship (*upāsate*), that is, they practice and perform.

Its shadow is immortality; "shadow" (*chāyā*) is a name for the house (*gṛha*), and "shadow-immortality" (*chāyāmṛta*) refers to the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*), because this manifestation (*vyūha*) is contained within it. This manifestation is the death of death—the death even of death—according to the Vedic revelation: "Death is its condiment. It encompasses Prajāpati, the Brahma-manifestation, because, by the principle of the "beginning" (*tadādinyāya*), it includes everything due to its fixed sequential order. It is divine (*deva*), according to Yāska’s statement: "A god (*deva*) is so called from giving (*dāna*), or from shining (*dyotana*), or from illuminating (*dīpana*)."

By means of *havis*—that is, by the offering of oblations, by *homa*, or by the presentation of food (*naivedya*) and worship. For this very reason, he will state in the section on the Great Wheel (*mahācakra-prakaraṇa*): "One should perform the *homa* with the *anuṣṭubh* [verse], and perform worship with the *anuṣṭubh*. We shall serve (*vidhema*), that is, we shall attend upon. Alternatively, according to the statement of Yāska that "the root *dhā* (vidhati) signifies the act of giving," we give the oblation for the sake of the arrays (*vyūha*) beginning with the *brāhma-vyūha*; here there is an inversion of case endings in the words *ka* and *deva*.

In that context, the essential meaning is that the act of worship is the service [of the deity]. Thus, the term "death of death" (*mṛtyumṛtyu*) has been explained with respect to the previously mentioned object of worship; he concludes this by saying, "Therefore, it is called 'the death of death'. Having thus explained the previously mentioned term in relation to the previously mentioned object of worship, the question of the gods is now posed in order to explain the second and tenth terms in relation to both: "Now, why is it called 'I bow' (*namāmi*)? To this, Prajāpati replied, supplying the answer to follow.

The phrase "by its own majesty" (*svamahimnā*) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. Since the word "I bow" (*namāmi*) is a finite verb (*ākhyātapada*), [the author] explains its root-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), setting aside the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), which refers to the sense of "I" (*asmadartha*). Thus, this [phrase "by its own majesty"] is to be supplied everywhere, being connected to all the preceding words. Because of the employment of the word "since" (*yasmāt*), the phrase "by its own majesty" is supplied by way of the root-meaning.

Because all the gods—those residing in the earth, the intermediate space, and the world of Brahmā, as well as the worshippers of the Great Wheel—bow down and pay homage to Him, who possesses the previously mentioned attributes and is the primary manifestation of Nṛsiṃha; thus he shows that He is the object of worship, distinguished by qualities worthy of universal homage. Furthermore, he states the specific qualification for the two classes of worshippers among the gods: "those seeking liberation and those who proclaim [the word] *brāhṛ*," for otherwise, the twofold division would be impossible, as there are no others who do not proclaim *brāhṛ*.

Alternatively, the connection [of the verse] is that those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the proponents of the Brahman (*brāhmavādin*), and the liberated (*mukta*) assume a form through divine play (*līlā*) and bow down. This is what is meant: in the world of Brahmā (*brāhmaloka*), the manifestation (*vyūha*) of Nṛsiṃha—explained by the *Nṛsiṃha-Gāyatrī* which is the essence of the Vedic mantras such as "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Hari"—is to be worshipped as the locus of the fourth limb, the Armor (*kavaca*). And that Armor encompasses all these objects of worship, including the others contained within the four limbs.

Therefore, we have stated while explaining the meaning of the mantras for the limbs of the armor (*kavaca*) in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The origin of the armor (*kavaca*) is from the verbal root *ka-vac*, meaning 'to take up' (*graha*); because of that splendor, splendor is taken up by it, and thus it is called armor."

Having thus established the meaning of the word together with the meaning of its root, and having declared the common quality of being worthy of universal homage, he now explains the meaning of the root again through a verse, as it is common to the *sāman* and other mantras, beginning with "pra nūnam": "Brāhmaṇaspati—the Lord (*pati*) of *brāhman*, which is both with form and without form—is the protector (*pātā*), that is, the guardian, by means of instruction; [he is] the one to be praised (*ukthya*), that is, the most excellent."

"Surely," meaning certainly, the collection of mantras beginning with "Praise the King of Soma" (*sāmarājaṃ stuhi*) and ending with "those who give themselves" (*ya ātmadāḥ*) consists of thirty-two arrangements (*vyūha*). In the aforementioned mantra, Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and the gods have made their dwellings—that is, their homes—for the sake of worship; this means they have established them there. By this, he demonstrates that just as there is devotion toward the deity to be worshipped and toward the guru, so too there must be devotion toward the mantra.

As it has been said: "Equal devotion is required toward the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra. And because in that context, the Mantra is heard to be worthy of salutation. Thus, the verbal form *namāmi* (I bow) has been explained with respect to the aforementioned object of worship; he concludes with the word *tasmāt* (therefore): "Therefore, it is said..."

"I bow. Having thus explained the word "I bow" (*namāmi*) in connection with its basic meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), the question of the gods is now raised in order to explain the agent-word "I" (*aham*) in a general sense: "Now, why is it said 'I'? In this context, since the word "I" is already obtained by implication from the use of the first person singular in the verb, the reason for its explicit repetition is intended as a formal objection: "And for what reason is that used? To this, the answer follows, connecting with the phrase: "Prajāpati said: *Note: The term *prakṛtyartha* refers to the root meaning of the verb; *kartṛpada* refers to the word denoting the agent; and *ākhyātottamapuruṣaprayoga* refers to the use of the first person singular in a finite verb.*

The fruit for the practitioner of the five-limbed worship (*pañcāṅgopāsanā*) is now indicated as being characterized by identity (*tādātmya*). Nor should it be said that this is undesirable for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because when sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is attained, this fruit is acquired. For the one who desires to remain here [in this world], the Lord grants the sovereignty characterized by identity at the end of the body; for the scripture states: "The Supreme Brahman is the Savior. Thus, this is a term for the fruit and not a term for the practitioner. And that [fruit], manifested through the individual *sāman*, he explains by means of the mantra.

And this [term "Sāman"], being attached to all the words, demonstrates the rule that the entire collection of words is explained as being manifested by the Sāman; and thus, every meditation mentioned previously is preceded by the Sāman.

Then, the practitioner who has engaged in the previously mentioned meditation through the relationship of the object of worship and the worshipper, having purified his inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by means of that meditation, realizes the object of worship as being none other than the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and says this *sāman* in order to show the fruit of meditation for others: "I am"—I am that aforementioned object of worship; "the first-born"—born first from the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of meditation.

"May I be first among the gods, at the navel—the center—of the world of Ṛta, which is both manifest and unmanifest, of the nectar that is milk; he who gives me, accepts me, or sustains me, he indeed has thus protected me. Thus, by means of this mantra praising food, which is manifested through the Sāman, it indicates the declaration of the fruit and shows that this meditation concerns the ocean of milk. "I myself become the food, the milk, the very foundation of worship."

I eat—that is, I consume—that person who eats food while not eating [the true] food; that is, one who does not give food to the gods and Brahmins. Or rather, I eat—that is, I consume—the one who eats food, the agent of eating, who has attained the state of a living being (jīva); the meaning is that through the fivefold meditation, I destroy his transmigratory form. Since this is so, I have overcome, I surpass, the entire universe (viśvaṃ bhuvanam), like the light of the sun (suvar jyotiḥ).

Alternatively, this is an indication of the fruit: "I myself become the light—the radiance—of the one with form who is to be meditated upon. And this fruit is to be connected, by way of association, to every word and every quarter-verse. For through repeated instruction on the meaning of the sentence as having both form and being indivisible, there will be firmness—just as in the case of the ninefold instruction, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Thus, for one established in the qualified [Brahman], if the internal organ is purified, then this very fruit is explained.

For this very reason, there is no concluding summary here as there was previously with the words "therefore it is said," because through the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*), non-duality (*advaita*) is attained; as the Śruti states: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? All of this will be clarified during the exposition of the *hṛdaya-mantra* within the *praṇava*, which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Sāman. The practitioner who thus knows—that is, meditates upon—the aforementioned object of worship either through the meditation of identification (*ahaṃgraha-upāsanā*) according to the gradations of spiritual capacity, or through the relationship of worshiper and worshipped (*upāsyopāsaka-bhāva*).

The word *iti* indicates the conclusion of the previously described meditation along with its fruit. The term *upaniṣad* has been explained. This [text] which has been studied is employed as an offering (*naivedya*), and it should be understood as being in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; it is neither six-syllabled nor accompanied by [musical] limbs (*sāṅga*), because it was explained in that very manner during the third explanation of the word *yat* in the first *Upaniṣad*. Furthermore, that which is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter is to be chanted with the two *anuṣṭubh* accents.

And those two are the first and the last; for likewise, on the occasion of explaining the origin of beings, when the *ṛc* was cited as a witness, in the passage "of that [sāman], this is the verse," it says: "The *anuṣṭubh* is the first, the *anuṣṭubh* is the last," thus explaining the first and last tones by the word *anuṣṭubh*. Furthermore, since the word "speech" (*vāk*) is applied even to mere melody in the statement "Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*," and since it is said, "This speech speaks among the trees—that which speaks in the drum, that which... [and so forth].

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "In the debt [is] that which is in the lute. They proceed by speech alone; they proceed by song alone, meaning they sing with the first tone. They rise up by speech alone; they rise up by song alone, meaning they sing the syllables with the highest tone. Furthermore, "The Anuṣṭubh is indeed the supreme among meters"—thus it is called the Anuṣṭubh meter.

Consequently, in this context, three meanings are expressed by the word *anuṣṭubh*: in some cases the first and last tones, in some cases the song itself, and in some cases the meter. These should be understood according to their respective fitness; such is the secret regarding the extraction of the Sāman from the Anuṣṭubh.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
The commentary on the second Upaniṣad in the Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīyopaniṣadbhāṣya is complete.

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us the limb-mantras of the Nārasiṃha King of Mantras, which is in the Anuṣṭubh meter. He, Prajāpati, replied: "One should know the limbs to be the Praṇava, the Sāvitrī, the Yajurlakṣmī, and the Nṛsiṃha-Gāyatrī; he who knows them attains immortality."

"Om"—this syllable is all this. Its further explanation is as follows: whatever has been, is, or will be, all that is indeed the syllable Om; and whatever else is beyond the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Om. All this is Brahman; this Brahman is the Self (Ātman). This Self has four quarters. The first quarter is the waking state, whose sphere is the external world, who perceives outwardly, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences gross objects; he is called Vaiśvānara. The second quarter is the dreaming state, whose sphere is the internal world, who perceives inwardly, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences subtle objects; he is called Taijasa.

The second foot is that wherein one, being asleep, desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream; that is deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Being in the state of deep sleep, he has become unified, a mass of consciousness alone, consisting of bliss, enjoying bliss, having the mind as his gate—this is the third foot, the "wise one" (*prājña*). He is the all-bestowing, he is the all-knowing, he is the inner controller, he is the source of all, for he is the origin and the dissolution of all beings. He is neither conscious of the external, nor conscious of the internal, nor conscious of both; he is not conscious, nor is he unconscious.

They consider the Fourth to be a mass of consciousness, unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without marks, without signs, unthinkable, indescribable, whose essence is the realization of the one Self, the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, and non-dual; that is the Self, that is to be known. || 1 ||

The passage beginning with "The gods indeed... and ending with "Prajāpati said" is clear in its meaning. It is said that *māyā* is dependent upon the person who possesses *māyā*; for in the world, *māyā* is seen to be under the control of the one who spreads it. "Vai" indicates what is well-known. This [power] belongs to Nṛsiṃha and is dependent upon Nṛsiṃha; since this [power], being dependent upon the Brāhmaṇa-mantra in the form of Nṛsiṃha, creates all this and so forth, up to the point where it destroys it, the meaning is clear.

The causality of the world’s birth, maintenance, and dissolution is dependent upon this [Māyā], because the pure Brahman is not a cause. Since this is so, one should know this Māyā as Śakti; one should worship it as being subordinate to Nṛsiṃha. He who knows and worships this Māyā as Śakti—regarding the fruit of that worship, the text says "he consumes evil," and so on, ending with "attains," which is clear in meaning. Those who argue for the nature of *brāhṛ* deliberate and investigate: "Is it short, or long, or protracted?"

Since it follows that [the vowel] is indeed protracted (*pluta*) because it is included within the *sāman*, this inquiry is undertaken for the purpose of establishing a specific connection between the results and the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted vowels. He states this [inquiry]: the passage beginning with "If [it is] short" and ending with "goes" is of clear meaning. The doubt is as follows: does the connection with the short, long, and protracted vowels belong to the vowel together with its consonant (*savyañjana*), or does the connection belong to the vowel alone, setting aside the consonant known as the *ākāra*? Regarding this doubt, for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion, the seer (*ṛṣi*) stated the following illustration (*nidarśana*) or example: "That indeed... (*sa īm*).

The separation of the vowel together with its bindu from its form and consonant [is performed]. Therefore, in the case of a vowel with a bindu, there is a connection with the short vowels and so forth, as well as worship through the intellect of Māyā. The compound *sa-īṃ* consists of the letter *sa* and *riṃ*, making *sa-īṃ*. In its vocative address as *īṃ*, there is no fault because it is a particle (*nipāta*). O *sariṃ*—O vowel with a bindu—by taking you as one's support, protect and guard these powers (*śakti*) which are about to be described. Alternatively, *sa* is used separately; for there is an obligatory connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tad*.

He who is *ṛjīṣī*—desiring upright conduct (*ṛjubhāvecchuḥ*) and *tarutraḥ*, meaning one whose nature is to cross over—protected (*pāḥ*), that is, preserved, the *ṛm* with the bindu (*riṃ*), which is the vowel (*svara*) worshipped through the intellect as Śrī and the other [energies]. The root *pā* means "to protect. Because the power to be protected (*pālanīya-śakti*) is dependent upon the protector, it is certain (*hīti*) that they are to be worshipped by taking the vowel with the bindu as their support. In that regard, he states the energies associated with the *vyūha*: he protected (*pāḥ*), that is, preserved, *śriyam*, the energy of Viṣṇu; or alternatively, "protect" (*pāhi*). Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, there is a twofold connection.

I enter for refuge Lakṣmī, the power of Nṛsiṃha; Aupalā Ambikā Gaurī, the power of Maheśvara; Gā Sarasvatī, the power of Brahmā; and Ṣaṣṭhī, the power of Skanda—her whom they call Indrasenā, the power of Indra, Indrāṇī; Vidyā, the power of Īśvara; and Brāhmyonī, who is the cause for the attainment of Brahman, possessing form and appearance—I enter for refuge all those respective powers here into the vowel with the bindu, for the sake of long life, that is, for the increase of a lifespan conducive to spiritual practice.

Having thus explained the determination of the *śakti*-syllables, the sevenfold worship of the powers based upon them, and the worship of the long and other *mātrās* along with their fruits, [the author] now states the determination of the *bīja*-syllables and the worship based upon them along with its fruits; the passage beginning with "Of all" and ending with "entering into" is clear in meaning. The word "space" (*ākāśa*) denotes the letter *ha*, as is well known from all the scriptures of the *Āgamas* and from the *Upaniṣads* which take the form of the *Āgamas*.

Since this is so, one should know that the seed-syllable *ha*, which is denoted by the word "space" (*ākāśa*), is the seed. One should worship it as the seed—the source, the root cause—either through the cognition of that [reality] it represents, or as the very form of the particle that denotes it. Furthermore, since this relationship between the signified and the signifier is not well-known in the world, it is to be understood solely from the scriptures of the Mantras and Āgamas. Likewise, the syllable of power (*śaktyakṣara*) is also "power" (*śakti*) because it signifies power, or because it is to be worshipped with the cognition of that [power]. The secret is this: the worship of the seed of power with the cognition of that [power] occurs precisely because it signifies it.

Just as the syllable *praṇava* was to be meditated upon with the idea that it is Brahman because it denotes Brahman, so too is the seed-syllable (*śaktibīja*). This is the illustration spoken by the Seer (*ṛṣi*), and its meaning has already been explained. *Haṃsa* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). *Haṃ* is the primordial cause, the Great Reality (*sad-bṛhat*). Alternatively, it is that which is connected with the syllable *sa*, existing in the form of the *ajapā-gāyatrī*, issuing from both nostrils, accessible to all including Brāhmaṇas, women, and Śūdras, bestowing fruit through mere intention, and denoting the Supreme Self as "Sa. The sentence is completed thus: "The *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self, became everything that is to be described hereafter."

He sits in the pure intellect; thus he is *śuciṣat* (the sitter in purity). He is the *haṃsa*, the divine *vasu*. He sits in the intermediate space; thus he is *antarikṣasat* (the sitter in the intermediate space). Because of his expansive nature (*bṛṃhaṇatva*), the deity who rests in the intermediate space is himself the *hotṛ* priest. He sits on the sacrificial altar (*vedi*); thus he is *vediṣat* (the sitter on the altar). He is himself the guest (*atithi*). He sits in the dwelling (*duroṇa*); *duroṇa* is a name for the house, as it is difficult to enter (*durvā*) and difficult to cross (*dustarṇa*). He sits therein; thus he is *duroṇasat* (the sitter in the dwelling). He sits among men (*nṛ*) while they live; thus he is *nṛṣat* (the sitter among men), according to the Vedic revelation: "He who dwells within the self."

He is *varasat* because he sits (*sīdati*) in the most excellent (*vara*) and highest (*variṣṭha*) place. He is *ṛtasat* because he alone sits by means of *ṛta*, that is, truth. He is *vyomasat* because he alone is perceived and thus sits within the *vyoman*, the space of the heart. He is *abjāḥ* because he is born (*jātaḥ*) in the waters (*apsu*), that is, in the ocean of milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*), as the object of worship; or he is *gojāḥ* because he is born among the cows (*goṣu*) as the one to be realized through worship. He is *ṛtajāḥ* because, according to the Vedic verse "ṛtam is truth," he is born as the object of worship. He is *adrijāḥ* because he is born in the mountain (*adrau*), that is, in the cloud (*meghe*).

In Vedic usage (*chandasi*), this word *janiḥ* is seen ending in *s* when used with a nominal suffix; thus, when accompanied by an upapada, it ends in a visarga and is long, as in the example *sutejāḥ*. Likewise, the Supreme Self alone is "bṛhat," meaning great. "Ṛtam" means truth; the word "to be known" (*jñeyam*) is understood as the remainder of the sentence. The worshipper who thus knows—that is, understands—the reality of the Supreme Self, which is denoted by the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) and is to be meditated upon through the intellect—the word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the determination of the seed of power (*śakti*).

Alternatively, because the particles *yad vā* and *iti* have multiple meanings, the word *iti* connects this very seed-syllable of power (*śaktibīja*) with the words read in the *Mahopaniṣad*, as indicated by the term "thus" (*evam*) in the phrase "Thus [is] the Mahopaniṣad. Consequently, in the sixth word of the root mantra, which consists of three syllables, one should exclude the syllable *nṛ* and the syllable *sa*; the remaining two syllables should be understood as the seed-syllable of power exactly as they are recited, by virtue of the inherent capacity of the context.

The second *haṃsa-ṛc* from the *Atharvaṇa*, which denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is that which was recited first. Thus, in all the hymns of praise (*stuti-mantra*), excluding the letter *nṛ* (the syllable *nṛ*) and the letter *sa* from the fourth quarter, the two remaining syllables as they were recited constitute the *śakti-bīja*. This is the reality and the secret; such is the determination of the letters of the *śakti-bīja*.
Thus ends [the work] composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
The commentary on the third Upaniṣad of the Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīyopaniṣad is complete.

In the very same order in which the enumeration of the constituent parts was made, he provides their explanation, beginning with: "The syllable 'Om'. But how does the determination of the syllable *oṃ* become the means for attaining the realization of the principle of the Self with its forms?

It is said: "Om—this is the support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8.1); "O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2); "One should yoke the Self with Om" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1); "Om is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8.1); "All this is indeed the syllable Om" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3)—from such scriptural passages, just as the non-dual Self, being the ultimate reality, serves as the locus for the conceptualization of a snake and so forth upon a rope, so too the entire expansion of speech concerning the Self, including the vital breaths and so on, is nothing but the syllable Om.

And that *ānuṣṭubha-aṅga* is indeed the very nature of the self of pure being (*sattvātmasvarūpa*), because it denotes that [self]. Furthermore, everything beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is denoted by words that are modifications of the syllable *oṃ*—is a conceptual construction of the self (*ātmavikalpa*) and does not exist apart from its designation. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.1.4–6); "All this is bound together by speech as a thread, by names as cords" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.12); and "For all this is indeed within the name" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.1.5). Therefore, he says: "This entire world is this imperishable syllable *oṃ*."

This entire collection of objects, consisting of both the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*), is not distinct from its signifier; and since the distinctions among signifiers are not distinct from the syllable *oṃ*, this whole universe is indeed *oṃ*. Furthermore, the supreme Brahman is understood by means of the signifier and the signified; thus, it is *oṃ* alone. Regarding this very imperishable syllable, which consists of the higher and lower Brahman—namely, the syllable *oṃ*—one should understand that the "further explanation" (*upavyākhyāna*) is now commenced. This is because it is a clear exposition and a manifest declaration that serves as a means for attaining Brahman and stands in close proximity to Brahman. It is not, however, a mere grammatical ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).

According to the maxim, "Because of the intervention of a pause, there is no connection [between words]," that which is delimited by the three times—past, present, and future—is indeed the syllable *oṃ*, by virtue of the aforementioned reasoning. Furthermore, whatever else transcends the three times, is to be understood through its effects, and is not delimited by the three times—such as the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so forth—that too is indeed the syllable *oṃ*. Thus, since the designator and the designated are one, this instruction is made with emphasis on the designator, as in: "This entire [universe] is this syllable *oṃ*," and so forth.

The re-statement, by way of emphasizing the denoted meaning, of that which was previously indicated by way of emphasizing the denoting expression, is for the purpose of realizing the identity of the denoter and the denoted. Otherwise, since the comprehension of the denoted depends upon the denoter, there might arise the suspicion that the status of being the denoted is merely figurative for the denoted. Furthermore, the purpose of realizing this identity is that, by dissolving both the denoter and the denoted through a single effort, one realizes the Brahman which is distinct from them.

And so he will say later: "The feet are the measures, and the measures are the feet. Thus he says: "For all this is the Brahman; all that has been described as consisting of the syllable *oṃ* alone is this Brahman. And he specifically points out that Brahman, which was previously mentioned in an indirect manner, by means of direct perception—saying, "This Self is Brahman. By the word "this," he indicates the inner self (*pratyagātman*) being divided into four quarters, pointing it out directly through a physical gesture: "This is that Self."

This very Self, denoted by the syllable *oṃ*, is established as both supreme (*para*) and non-supreme (*apara*), and is four-footed like a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin, not like a cow which is four-footed [by birth]. The realization of the fourth (*turīya*) state occurs through the successive dissolution of the three states beginning with the waking (*viśva*); thus, in this case, the word "foot" (*pāda*) is derived instrumentally (*karaṇasādhana*). For the fourth state, however, the word "foot" is derived objectively (*karmasādhana*), meaning that it is that which is reached. Regarding how it is four-footed, he says: its place is the waking state; thus, it is "waking-state-located" (*jāgaritasthāna*).

"Bahisprajña" means one whose wisdom (*prajñā*) is directed toward an object external to his own self; the meaning is that his wisdom, produced by *vidyā*, appears as being directed toward external objects. Likewise, "saptāṅga" refers to one whose seven powers (*saptaśaktayaḥ*) reside in the "limb" known as the heart (*hṛdaya*); this is so because it is well-known that the powers of Viṣṇu have their locus in the chest of Viṣṇu.

This is because of the Smṛti passages: "She who rests upon the chest of Viṣṇu," "She who dwells on the chest of Viṣṇu," and "The All-pervading Lord, bearing Śrī upon his chest, while she holds blossoming lotuses in her two hands. Likewise, he is called "the one with nineteen mouths" because the nineteenth syllable—the seed-syllable (*bīja*)—relative to the root mantra, is the "mouth" of that root Nṛsiṃha-manifestation (*vyūha*); the limb called the heart (*hṛdaya*) is located above his navel and prior to his head.

Therefore, whether there is identity or difference between the object of worship and the worshipper, the assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the heart and other parts is not contradictory. Now, one might object: "In this way, there would be seven other limbs, such as 'the head itself is *sutejas*,' and so forth; he who possesses these is thus described."

Likewise, its nineteen "mouths"—namely, the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) beginning with *prāṇa*, along with mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*)—are like mouths because they serve as gateways for perception. Why is it that these two statements, which were explained in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* within the science of the *Praṇava* as referring respectively to Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Supreme (Paratattva), are not likewise explained here? It is said: because here [in this context], this [text] is dependent upon the section concerning the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*).

Because it is applied as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the science of the *praṇava*, one should understand that the *praṇava* is an ancillary of that *sāman*; likewise, because this [verse] is recited as an ancillary immediately after the determination of the *śakti-bīja*. Furthermore, in the *Māṇḍūkya*, since the science of the *praṇava* is studied without being introduced as a subordinate part, it possesses primacy; and because there is no application of it as an ancillary, and because the *śakti-bīja* is not under discussion there, and because the sciences are distinct, and because the meaning differs according to different commentaries, it is more appropriate to perceive them as having separate meanings.

[Objection: Since the identity of the two knowledges (*vidyā*) is established by the recognition of the text as being neither deficient nor redundant in both places, there must be either an extension (*utkarṣa*) of the subordinate knowledge (*aṅgavidyā*) or the inclusion of the subordinate knowledge within the principal knowledge (*pradhānavidyā*). To this it is replied: By the principle, "If it be argued that there is a difference because of the word, no, because there is no distinction," a difference between the two knowledges is indeed more appropriate, just as in the case of the sentences concerning optional sacrifices for prosperity (*ābhyudayika-kāmyeṣṭi*). [Objection: Even if they are different, let the application (*viniyoga*) be such that the subordinate knowledge belongs to the principal knowledge, and let there be identity of the knowledge due to recognition.

That is not so; for, according to the maxim "in a different context, there is a difference in purpose," a distinction [between the two] is more appropriate, just as in the case of the regular *agnihotra* and the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana-agnihotra*. Furthermore, even though there is a great deal of similarity in the recitations in both places, a difference in reading is observed in some instances. For example, at the point of defining the fourth *mātrā*, the reading in the *Māṇḍūkya* is: "This is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), this is the Ruler (*īśāna*), this is the Lord (*prabhu*)."

In the *Tāpanīya*, however, the reading is "ṭha eṣo'ntaryāmyeṣa yoniḥ," excluding the two terms *īśāna* and *prabhu*. Therefore, because they are distinct, that which is appropriate and relevant here should be explained accordingly. Thus, he is the "Eater of the Gross" (*sthūlabhuk*) because he eats—that is, experiences—the gross earth situated within the heart and limbs; and he is the "Universal Man" (*viśvānara*) because he brings all men (*viśveṣāṃ narāṇām*) into himself in manifold ways; and *viśvānara* itself is *vaiśvānara*.

Now, an objection may be raised: just as in the *Māṇḍūkya*, by the force of the term "Vaiśvānara," the two sets of seven limbs and nineteen mouths were explained respectively as referring to Virāj and Hiraṇyagarbha, so too here, by the force of the term "Vaiśvānara," let it be explained as referring to both; why then is it explained as referring to Śakti and Bīja? For the proximity of the context (*prakaraṇa-saṃnidhi*) is stronger than the proximity of the sentence (*vākya-saṃnidhi*). True.

If the word *vaiśvānara* here were to function solely with reference to the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, then it would be so; however, this cannot be the case, because it has been explained as referring to something else through its etymological derivation (*yaugikī vṛtti*). Furthermore, since there is a difference in the objects to be enjoined at various points, the sentences are distinct, and thus their proximity (*vākya-saṃnidhi*) is not established. Therefore, since the proximity of the context (*prakaraṇa-saṃnidhi*) is equal in both instances, the previously mentioned interpretation alone is superior.

The first quarter: therein, by virtue of being supported by the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, or by virtue of denoting them, there arises such a specific cognition; thus it is the first quarter. It is considered "first" because the comprehension of the subsequent quarters is preceded by this one. Now, an objection may be raised: since this inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the subject at hand as being four-footed according to the text "This Self is Brahman," how can there be a mention of the limbs of the *śakti* and the *bīja*? This is not a fault, because the intended meaning here is the non-difference between the object of meditation and the meditator.

This being the case, there is established the non-duality of Nṛsiṃha and Brahman; the Self would be seen as one abiding in all beings, and all beings would be seen in the Self. Furthermore, the meaning of such scriptural passages as "He who [sees] all beings [in the Self]" would thus be properly summarized. Otherwise, the inner Self (pratyagātman) would be perceived as merely limited, as by the Sāṃkhyas and others. Moreover, it is accepted that all the Upaniṣads aim to establish the oneness of the universal Self.

Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that for this worshipper, with the intention of asserting the identity of his own self with the self that is the object of worship, there is the statement regarding the seven limbs and the statement regarding the mouth. Dream is the state of this Taijasa; thus he is "one whose state is dream. Waking cognition, which possesses many means and appears as if directed toward external objects, while vibrating within the mind, deposits a corresponding latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the mind. That [is] the mind.

Likewise, the conditioned [body], like a variegated cloth, being impelled by ignorance and karma without depending on external instruments, appears as if in the waking state. And so it has been said in the *Atharva-veda*: "Having taken a portion from this entire world," and so forth; and having introduced the passage, "In the supreme divine mind he becomes one," it continues, "In this state, this god experiences his majesty in dream."

Because the mind (*manas*) resides within in relation to the sense faculties (*indriya*), the wisdom (*prajñā*) obtained internally in the form of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) during dream is that by which one is "internally wise" (*antaḥprajña*). It is called "radiant" (*taijasa*) because it exists as the subject (*viṣayin*) in a wisdom devoid of external objects, consisting solely of light. In the case of the "universal" (*viśva*), wisdom possesses objects and is gross, thus being an object of enjoyment; here, however, the wisdom consists only of latent impressions and is not fully manifest, yet it is an object of enjoyment—thus it is said to be a "distinctive enjoyment. This is the intermingling of the letter *u* with the seed-syllables of power (*śakti*).

The rest is the same. Since the second state, consisting of fire (*taijasa*), is indistinguishable from deep sleep (*suṣupta*) in all three places by its characteristic of being unawakened to reality, he distinguishes deep sleep from the previous two with the words: "where, sleeping, he knows nothing whatsoever," and so forth. For in deep sleep, unlike in the previous two states, there exists neither the dreaming vision characterized by the perception of things otherwise, nor any desire whatsoever. Thus, this is his "deep-sleep place" (*suṣupta-sthāna*); it is that in which the vibration of the mind—which constitutes the entire manifold of duality—is distinguished from the other two states.

For example, due to the lack of full comprehension of form (*rūpa*), it has fallen into non-discrimination; like a day seized by dense nocturnal darkness, its manifold conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) becomes unified. For this very reason, the cognitions that are the movements of the mind in the states of dream and waking have become, as it were, solidified. Because this state consists of discrimination (*viveka*), it is called "the mass of cognition" (*prajñānaghana*). Just as at night everything undifferentiated by nocturnal darkness appears as a single solid mass, so too is this "mass of cognition. By the word "only" (*eva*), the meaning is that there is no other distinct category of existence.

Because it is free from the suffering of the mental exertion involved in the vibration of the mind into the forms of objects and subjects, it consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), meaning it abounds in bliss; it is not bliss itself, because that would not be ultimate—as in common worldly experience, one who remains without effort is said to be an enjoyer of primary bliss, according to the Śruti: "This is supreme bliss. Furthermore, because it serves as the gateway for the mind during the awakening from dreams and so forth, it is "mind-faced" (*cetomukha*); or, its "face," which is the door characterized by cognition, is the means for the arrival of dreams and the like, and thus it is called "mind-faced."

Because he knows both the past and the future, it is he alone who possesses knowledge of all objects; thus he is the "Prājña" (the Intelligent One). For even when asleep, he is called "Prājña" by way of his previous state. Alternatively, he is called "Prājña" because pure consciousness (*prajñapti*) alone is his unique characteristic. While the other two states also possess specific forms of cognition, this one is distinguished by its nature as pure intelligence; this is the third foot.

For he, abiding in his own essential nature, is the ruler of the entire range of differentiated entities including the divine; he is not of a different genus from them, as is the case with others, according to the Vedic revelation: "For the mind, my dear, is bound by breath. For this very reason, he is the Lord of all. For this very reason, he is the knower of all states of differentiation; thus he is the omniscient one. He is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī); having entered within the bodies of all beings, he is indeed the regulator of all.

Therefore, as it has been stated, this source (yoni) gives birth to the waking state along with its divisions; for this very reason, it is both the origin (*prabhava*) and the dissolution (*apyaya*) of beings, since "this alone is the origin and dissolution of all beings"—the reading is identical in both cases. Hereafter, in the *Māṇḍūkya*, having recited verses regarding the very same meaning, the fourth quarter (*turīya-pāda*) is presented; however, in this *Tāpanīya*, the fourth quarter is presented without those verses.

Even regarding that [text], some variation in the reading has already been shown during the occasion of its commentary; the verse relevant to that context is recited as follows: "The Viśva is in the mouth of the right eye, the Taijasa is within the mind, and the Prājña is in the space of the heart; thus he is established threefold in the body. This verse is intended to demonstrate the experience of the triad beginning with Viśva even within the waking state.

He whose face is like the right eye is so described; for although there is no distinction among all the sense organs, since proficiency in perception is observed in the right eye, when a specific reference is made to it, one who has seen a form with the right eye and then closes his eyes perceives that very same thing within the mind—as if in a dream—in a manifested form of latent impression (*vāsanā*). Just as it is here, so it is in a dream.

Therefore, when the mind is internalized, it is indeed the Taijasa, who is Viśva himself; upon the cessation of the mental activities of seeing and remembering external objects such as space, it becomes Prājña, unified and consisting of dense consciousness alone, due to the absence of mental activity. For the vibration of the mind consists precisely of seeing and remembering; in their absence, because it abides without distinction within the heart as the self of Prāṇa, it is Prāṇa, according to the Śruti: "Prāṇa indeed withdraws all these. The Taijasa is Hiraṇyagarbha, because he resides within the mind.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the mind (*manas*), according to such scriptural passages as, "This person consists of mind" (*manomaya*). Now, an objection may be raised: since the differentiated vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists in deep sleep, its causal conditions must be of that same nature; how then can there be an undifferentiated state (*avyākṛtatā*)? This is not a fault, because the undifferentiated lacks distinctions of space and time.

Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed in a state of manifestation (*vyākṛta*) when there is the conceit of being a village-dweller, nevertheless, the cessation of the conceit of specific limitations belonging to the physical body occurs within the vital breath; thus, for those who possess the conceit limited by the vital breath, it is indeed unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). Just as there is a state of unmanifestness in the vital breath for those who possess the conceit of limitation at the time of the dissolution of the vital breath, so too is there a commonality of unmanifestness for those who possess the conceit of the vital breath, because they have attained a state of non-distinction.

Furthermore, its nature as consisting of the seed-syllable *praṇava* and its presiding over that [unmanifest], as well as the oneness of the one who exists in the state of manifestation with those presiding over limited notions—this previously mentioned qualification, "become one, a mass of consciousness" (*ekībhūtaḥ prajñānaghanaḥ*), and so forth, is thus established. Because of the reasons stated therein, the term "breath" (*prāṇa*) applies to the unmanifest, according to the Vedic scripture: "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to breath" (*prāṇabandhanaṃ hi somya manaḥ*). In this way, by the statement "for the origin and dissolution of beings," the knowledge of all through the knowledge of the One has been demonstrated.

Likewise, in the *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā*, the three states are described as being within the waking state itself; therein, in order to turn back the mental activity directed toward that threefold nature and to direct the mental activity instead toward the previously mentioned object of worship, he describes the essential nature of that object of worship: "Not one whose cognition is external," and so forth.

Because the outward activity toward objects has ceased and the waking state is negated, it follows that the mind would engage in its own internal activity, whereby the inner Self would possess internal cognition (*antaḥprajña*) and thus be of the nature of *taijasa*. To negate this, he says: "not having internal cognition. Since activity in both [external and internal] directions is negated, it might follow that there is activity in the interval between them; to negate that, he says: "not having cognition on both sides. The meaning is that in the interval between waking and dreaming, the mind should not be engaged for the sake of cognition.

By negating activity in the intermediate state, when activity in both states simultaneously would otherwise follow for the sake of cognition (*prajñā*), he negates that with the words "not cognizing" (*na prajñam*). Thus, because all mental activity is negated, the mind would remain unmanifest, as if non-existent or absent; he negates even that with the words "not non-cognizing" (*nāprajñam*).

Since the persistence of that [dream-state] has been negated, and the dream—of which ignorance is the witness—has thus arrived, he negates it by saying, "not a mass of consciousness" (*na prajñānaghana*). Now, having negated what is contrary to the object of meditation through the six negations—which constitute the limbs of the science of the *praṇava*—and having turned [the mind] away from that, he points out the actual object of meditation upon which the mind must be fixed without turning away, by saying, "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). For such an object of meditation is not seen anywhere as having either a human form or an animal form, such as a cowherd or a tortoise.

That [reality], however, possesses both forms, consisting of Nṛsiṃha, with three eyes and the Pināka bow in hand; for this very reason, it is beyond conventional usage. For this very reason, it is "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇa*); that which has no characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) or sign (*liṅga*) is "without characteristics. For this very reason, it is "inconceivable" (*acintya*), whether by inference or by reasoning. For this very reason, it is "indescribable" (*avyapadeśya*), by means of words that convey a fixed form or an object of meditation.

For this very reason, it is said to have "the realization of the single Self as its essence" (*ekātmapratyayasāram*): the realization of all selves in one is the "realization of the single Self" (*ekātmapratyaya*), and that which has this as its essence is so described. For this very reason, it is "the cessation of phenomenal expansion" (*prapañcopaśama*).
