The word *atha* (now/then) signifies immediate succession as established by the order of the text. Even though the word "Savitṛ" does not appear in the mantra, he calls it the *sāvitrī*; this shows that, like the light of the sun at its time and like the light of deep sleep, this illumination of the head-portion (*śiro'ṅga*) dispels both external and internal darkness, thereby removing dense ignorance (*nibiḍāvidyā*). Because it consists of eight syllables, it is the *gāyatrī*. He explains that *gāyatrī* by means of the *yajus*: "That which is declared by the *yajus*, by that all this is pervaded. Thus, the head-portion has been explained, as well as how it is to be meditated upon.

He counts the syllables: *ghṛṇi* has two syllables; *sūrya* has three, counting the *repha* (the letter *r*) separately; *āditya* has three. "This indeed is the eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra mantra, consecrated with glory (*śrī*). The meaning is that its head is consecrated by the seven personified powers, beginning with Śrī, according to the principle of the primary [syllable], using golden jars filled with nectar and inlaid with clusters of jewels. He now points out the fruit for the practitioner who meditates in this manner.

He is indeed consecrated with glory; the meaning is that he too is consecrated by the previously mentioned powers (*śakti*) in the manner previously described. This very point is expressed by the *ṛc* (verse), which conveys the aforementioned sense. "The *ṛcs* sat down" means they performed constant service. The mention of *ṛc* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, *ṛcaḥ* is in the genitive case: the powers propounded in this [verse] beginning with "the *ṛc*s together," or the Vedas.

Not only the powers (*śaktayaḥ*), but also all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*)—upon (*adhi*), that is, above—the head, which is the imperishable (*akṣara*) because it does not perish nor dissolve, and which is the supreme void (*paramaṃ vyoman*) because it is the gateway to all consecrations and the gateway to liberation—in that head, what will the worshipper accomplish with the *Ṛk* (the *Ṛgveda*, etc. if he does not know that head as being consecrated by the Vedas and the gods and goddesses in the manner previously described? He shall achieve nothing.

Or rather, what will one do with this verse, "O Sarasvatī, protect [us]"? Those who know and worship that head thus consecrated—they, these worshippers, sit together; that is to say, they sit properly and are happy. He explains the word from the *ṛk*: "Indeed, there is no purpose or need for him through the *ṛk*, nor through the *yajus*, nor through the *sāman*, who knows the Sāvitrī as the head and the tuft (*śikhā*) which serves as the means. And therefore, this is the meaning:

Having recited the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī, all the aforementioned Vedic deities and others consecrate [the practitioner]; thus, the meaning of the reality is that the eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitrī is the basis, and that very foot is the "eight-syllabled head" upon which those eight syllables are for the purpose of consecration.

Thus, having first described the Nṛsiṃha-brāhmaṇa-vidyā—which is beneficial to the head and the ancillaries (aṅgas) and is to be consecrated with the Sāvitrī—[the author] now describes the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā of the Sāma-veda, which is beneficial to that [preceding vidyā] by way of the Śikhā-aṅga: "Oṃ Bhūrlakṣmīḥ. These powers, preceded by the Praṇava-vidyā, are the Vyāhṛtis beginning with Bhūḥ. Regarding "Bhūḥ": from the root *bhū* in the sense of "to exist," it exists here in the sense of being (*sattā*).

For this very reason, we have stated while explaining the seven *vyāhṛtis* in the *Prapañcasāra*: "From the word *bhūḥ*, the *vyāhṛti* arises; the word *bhūḥ* exists in the sense of 'being' (*sat*). That state is declared to be 'Being' (*sat*) because it is pure existence (*sanmātra*). Because of its reality (*bhūtatva*) and its causality, the word *bhuvaḥ* is appropriately applied. Because it appropriates everything as its own self, it is called *svar*. Because of its greatness (*mahattva*) and its vastness (*maha*), the word *mahas* is uttered. Consequently, according to their respective order: *bhūḥ* is *lakṣmī*.

The pervasive power of Brahman as pure Being (*sanmātra*) is called Bhū-lakṣmī; the power of Brahman in the form of pure Cause (*kāraṇamātra*) is called Bhuvar-lakṣmī; the power of Brahman abiding everywhere as one's own self (*svātmatayā*) is called Suvaḥ-kālakarṇī; and the power of the Bhuvaḥ-Brahman, which consists of the manifestation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), is called Mahālakṣmī. Each of these powers is that limb known as the *śikhā*, consisting of radiant energy (*tejomaya*).

Because that foot is to be meditated upon in the form of Soma as consisting of the nectar of Suṣumnā, the Śruti declares: "One should know the third foot of that Sāman as Soma, the Lord of Stars, who prevails over the herbs. Soma is the Moon, for the Śruti says: "Suṣumnā is the ray of the Sun, the Moon. [The phrase] "may it impel us" (*naḥ pracodayāt*)—the root *cuda* meaning to impel—means: may it impel us; may each of its limbs, as an embodied power, impel us toward the flow of nectar.

This verse in the Gāyatrī meter is a prayer addressed by the empowering energies (śaktis) who perform the consecration to the energies presiding over the crests [of the head]; it is the speech of Yajur-Mahālakṣmī. Consequently, her limb [the crest] is to be meditated upon as having the form of nectar (*amṛta*). Alternatively, each individual energy [prays]: "May she impel our limb"—that is, may she inspire us so that we may make the limb free from dispute.

This indeed is Mahālakṣmī, the Great Gāyatrī of the Yajus, so called because she is the expounder of the "Great Ones" (mahatīnām), such as Mahālakṣmī and others. By stating that there is no Yajus in this Sāvitra mantra, he shows that even though it is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the Sāman, it consists of two auxiliaries devoid of chanting (gīti). He counts the syllables for their inclusion within the Praṇava, saying, "It consists of twenty-four syllables. The form "caturviṃśat" is a Vedic archaism. Indeed, this Gāyatrī is the third auxiliary, which is everything, the whole of whatever exists here.

Since this is so, he points out the fruit for one who knows—that is, who worships—this crest-lock (*śikhā*) of the Supreme Lord, which is Mahālakṣmī, belonging to the Yajurveda, and which is to be worshipped as the power (*śakti*) whose form was previously described: "he attains great fortune" (*mahatīṃ śriyam aśnute*); the meaning is that he obtains great prosperity. The essential point is this: one worships the crest-lock, which consists of nectar, for the sake of the flow of nectar or for its binding, so that the powers mentioned in connection with the Gāyatrī may become embodied and serve to assist the powers of consecration (*abhiṣecana*).

Thus, having first described the third ancillary mantra of the Sāman, which is beneficial to the Nṛsiṃha-Brāhmaṇa-vidyā, he now states the fourth ancillary mantra of the Sāman, the Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī: *Oṃ*. The *praṇava* has been explained. Its ancillary part, known as the armor (*kavaca*), belongs to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*). "Dhīmahi" means "let us meditate. For what purpose? "For Vajranakha Nṛsiṃha"—the dative case here denotes purpose. To that end, "we know" (*vidmahe*) means we understand; for that very reason, "may the Lion impel us" (*siṃhaḥ pracodayāt*)—the meaning of this has already been stated.

By discarding the word "man" (*nara*) and speaking of "Lion" (*siṃha*), this [text] demonstrates the predominance of the lion-form within this Vidyā. The word *iti* indicates the completion of the mantra. This is indeed the Nṛsiṃha-Gāyatrī; because it establishes the armor (*kavaca*) that has the meaning of Nṛsiṃha, it is called Gāyatrī, and it demonstrates its inclusion within the Praṇava. It becomes the source and the fundamental cause for the Vedas and the deities residing within the heart-lotus of Brahmā, who are themselves enveloped by that armor. It now points out the fruit for the practitioner.

"He who knows thus becomes possessed of a foundation. From this, the meaning is as follows: the limb of the Supreme Lord known as the Armor (Kavaca), which is connected to the *Ṛgveda*, is to be meditated upon as the foundation of all the Vedas; and because it establishes that [Armor], Gāyatrī—connected to the *Ṛgveda*—is called the foundation of all the Vedic deities. This is the essential truth (*tattvārtha*).

Thus, in order to describe the Great Wheel (Mahācakra) called the "Nṛsiṃha-brāhmaṇa-vidyā-aṅga," which pervades the four ancillaries and is beneficial to that knowledge, [the author] begins with a narrative in the form of questions and answers to present those mantras. This wheel has thirty-two petals, upon each of which the syllables of the Root Mantra are placed, encapsulated by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and on each individual petal, he demonstrates the respective deity and the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha, which is obtainable through the power of the words of the hymnic mantras.

The passage beginning with "The gods indeed said to Prajāpati" and ending with "He, Prajāpati, said" has a clear meaning. For here, all the mantras begin with the *praṇava* (Om); according to the principle of "beginning with that," he shows the *praṇava* at the start of the root mantra and again the *praṇava* within all the mantras. Indeed, in these mantras, by means of two *yat*-clauses, having referred back to what is established elsewhere, in some cases through the force of the words and in others through the force of the singular form "to him" (*tasmai*), only one single manifestation (*vyūha*) is understood.

And that [form] is of two kinds: in some cases it is perceived as accessible to various deities through their respective uncommon weapons, and in other cases it is the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*). By that same logic, in both instances, the form is that of Nṛsiṃha, established in yoga (*yogārūḍha*), with the two lower hands in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), holding the weapons of the respective deities with the two upper hands, and in some cases also holding the conch, discus, and mace—all of which we shall clarify.

Just as in this very context, the manifestations (*vyūha*) in the form of Nṛsiṃha—consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are understood through their weapons, namely the discus (*cakra*), conch (*śaṅkha*), and trident (*triśūla*); so too is the manifestation of the Person (*puruṣavyūha*) in the form of Nṛsiṃha, who has two arms, ten fingers on his hands, and ten toes on his feet, according to the Vedic revelation: "As vast as the Person is."

From this point upward, all the Nṛsiṃha arrays (vyūhas) are four-armed and have Nṛsiṃha as their essence. The Īśvara array is accessible through the weapons of Īśvara. Corresponding to the five preceding ones, there is the fivefold Śakti array, consisting of women who are the embodiments of Sarasvatī, Śrī, Gaurī, Prakṛti, and Vidyā; they are accessible through their respective weapons. Thus, within the ten syllables of the root mantra, beginning from the northeastern direction and enclosed by the Praṇava (Oṃ), they are to be meditated upon as white in form and adorned with all ornaments.

In this manner, all the arrays (vyūhas) to be described hereafter are to be meditated upon within the syllables of the root mantra according to their respective numbers. Within each individual Nṛsiṃha array, the following are to be meditated upon as being included therein in due order: the Praṇava array [meditated upon] by means of a single syllable of the Praṇava; the form of Vāsudeva marked on the chest; the form consisting of the fourfold Praṇava; the form of the Vedas with their branches; the form of the five fires; the form of the seven Vyāhṛtis; the forms of the eight world-protectors (lokapālas); and the forms of the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, the eight planets, and the five great elements. Thus they are to be meditated upon.

The ten manifestations (*vyūhas*), which possess universal forms (*viśvarūpa*), are to be worshipped. These manifestations—consisting of Kāla, Anumṛtyu, Yama, Antaka, Prāṇa, Sūrya, Soma, Virāṭpuruṣa, Jīva, and the form of the conscious and unconscious that is the self of all (*sarvātmaka*)—are non-universal forms (*aviśvarūpa*), being accessible through their respective unique characteristics. Thus, each individual manifestation is to be worshipped and praised with its corresponding mantra. Thereafter, the Lord reveals his own self and his own form, both as the universal form and as the non-universal form, as is appropriate.

Since this is so, therefore the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) who constantly and regularly praises [the Lord] with these mantras beholds—that is, realizes through direct perception—the God who is both of universal form (*viśvarūpa*) and non-universal form (*aviśvarūpa*). The passage from "He attains immortality" (*so 'mṛtatvam*) up to the end of "the Great Upaniṣad" (*mahopaniṣad*) is clear in its meaning. In that context, the repetition of the result—"he attains immortality"—demonstrates that the supreme fruit is obtained merely through praise and reveals the power of the mantras. The term "Great Upaniṣad" refers to the abundance of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om); thus, everything is pure.

Thus ends [the work] composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Śrī Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
The commentary on the fourth Upaniṣad of the Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīyopaniṣad is complete.

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us of the wheel called Mahācakra, which fulfills all desires and is the door to liberation, as it is taught by the yogins. Prajāpati replied: "This Sudarśana Mahācakra has six spokes; therefore it has six spokes. It is a wheel with six petals, for there are six seasons; it is commensurate with the seasons. In the center is the hub, for these spokes are established upon the hub."

All this is indeed enveloped by *māyā*, yet *māyā* does not touch the Self; therefore, it is enveloped on the outside by *māyā*. Now, there is an eight-spoked wheel with eight petals. The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables; thus, it is commensurate with the *gāyatrī*. It is enveloped on the outside by *māyā*; for this *māyā* becomes the field (*kṣetra*) for each and every field.

Then there is a wheel with twelve spokes and twelve petals; for the Jagatī meter consists of twelve syllables, so it is commensurate with the Jagatī. It is encircled on the outside by Māyā. Then there is a wheel with sixteen spokes and sixteen petals; for the Puruṣa consists of sixteen parts, and this entire universe is indeed the Puruṣa, so it is commensurate with the Puruṣa. It is encircled on the outside by Māyā.

Now, there is a wheel with thirty-two spokes and thirty-two petals; for the *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables, and it is commensurate with the *anuṣṭubh*. It is encircled by an outer *māyā*; it is firmly bound by its spokes, for these spokes are indeed the Vedas. It moves all around by means of its petals, for the meters are indeed the petals. || 1 ||

The gods, exceedingly delighted by hearing that previous praise, said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, please tell us about this wheel named the *Mahācakra*—that is, the wheel endowed with this name; or rather, the circular wheel endowed with this very name, which stands in an upper-and-lower arrangement and pervades the four limbs, being the limb called the *astra*. It is 'all-yielding' (*sārvakāmika*) because it is the means for accomplishing all desires. "Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) is used as a form of address. It is "all-yielding" because it is the instrument for achieving every wish.

Alternatively, it is called *sārvakāmika* because in that wheel all the emanations (*vyūha*) of all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, are desired as one's own self and as one's very nature through the emanation of the nave and so forth. For this very reason, it is the "door to liberation" (*mokṣadvāra*). Due to the abundance of the *praṇava*, when [the mantra] is encapsulated by the *praṇava*, the number of *praṇava* syllables becomes double the number of syllables in the root mantra; thus, there are sixty-four.

And in this science, liberation occurs solely through the gateway of the *praṇava*, according to the scriptural statement: "At the end of the body, the Lord explains the supreme Brahman, the *tāraka*. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: that [wheel] is so called because it has the gateway known as the *praṇava* for liberation; it is the wheel which the Yogins teach to their disciples. "Prajāpati said" refers to the meaning already explained.

This Sudarśana Great Wheel (mahācakra) is indeed six-spoked; "Sudarśana" is another name for the Great Wheel itself, derived from its connection with the Sudarśana mantra. Alternatively, it is so called because "excellent vision" (*sudarśana*) is found within it. Below the petals of this [wheel], there is a stalk-like form denoted by the word "spoke" (*ara*). That in which six spokes exist is "six-spoked" (*ṣaḍara*); because it is thus, it becomes six-spoked.

The wheel has six petals; a petal is that which is shaped like a leaf, possessing three corners in the upper portion above the spokes. That in which six petals exist is thus described as "six-petaled. He praises this very [wheel]: "Or there are six seasons; it is commensurate with the seasons. From this explanatory passage (arthavāda), the spokes and the petals are to be meditated upon with the cognition of the seasons. He states the location for the support of the spokes: in the center of the wheel, in the middle, is the hub (nābhi), which is circular in shape.

These spokes previously mentioned are indeed established at the navel, and by the same principle, the petals previously mentioned are also established there. By means of *māyā*—that is, by the syllable of the power of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) previously mentioned—all of this, consisting of six spokes and six petals, becomes completely enveloped. Since *māyā* does not touch the self, which is the essential nature of the wheel consisting of spokes and petals, it is therefore externally enveloped by *māyā*.

Alternatively, it is the inward-facing consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*) alone, pure and absolute, that is to be worshipped through the intellect of the wheel (*cakra-buddhi*). Therefore, Māyā does not touch the Self, which is inward-facing consciousness, just as she does not touch a master of illusion (*māyāvin*). Consequently, [the Self] appears as if externally enveloped by Māyā. The fourfold set consisting of the eight-spoked/eight-petalled wheel, the twelve-spoked/twelve-petalled wheel, the sixteen-spoked/sixteen-petalled wheel, and the thirty-two-spoked/thirty-two-petalled wheel is explained by means of the six-spoked/six-petalled wheel.

In this regard, there is this distinction: on the first circle, the spokes and petals are to be meditated upon with the thought that they are the seasons (*ṛtu*). On the second, third, and fifth [circles], the spokes are to be meditated upon with the thought that they are the Vedas, while the petals are to be meditated upon respectively with the thought that they are the *gāyatrī*, *jagatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters; for there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The Vedas themselves are the spokes, and the meters are indeed the petals. On the fourth circle, the sixteen spokes and sixteen petals are to be meditated upon with the thought that they are the sixteen digits (*kalā*); or rather, each field (*kṣetra*) becomes this very *māyā*.

"Man alone is all this; it is measured by man"—thus [the scripture] speaks of the inner consciousness as pure, untouched by *māyā*, as indicated by the word "outside. Having projected such a wheel within that [consciousness], it is to be worshipped; this is the meaning.

And likewise, the encircling by the syllable of Śakti (ŚRĪM), accompanied by the bindu, around the word *arapatra* and the word *bahiḥ*, is—respectively according to their number—the form of the hub (*nābhi*) as the support for each successive wheel, being untouched by the outer petals of each preceding wheel. Thus, the encircling by *māyā* (HRĪM), which is untouched by the petals of the Sudarśana wheel, is the form of the hub as the support for the Nārāyaṇa wheel consisting of the subsequent syllables. In this way, the encircling of the eight-syllable [mantra] is the form of the hub for the twelve-syllable [mantra], and the encircling of the twelve-syllable [mantra]...

The sixteen-syllable *mātṛkā* with the nasal bindu (*sabinduka*) constitutes the hub (*nābhi*) for the sixteen-spoked wheel; the sixteen-syllable *mātṛkā* with the initial bindu encircles it to form the thirty-two-spoked wheel, which is its hub; then the thirty-two syllables encircle that, forming the twenty-eight-spoked wheel, which is not a hub in itself but lacks a central core. Thus, there are five hubs corresponding respectively to the Sudarśana, Nārāyaṇa, and Vāsudeva wheels of sixteen, thirty-two, and twenty-eight spokes. The essential meaning is this: the first hub is devoid of the *māyā*-syllable, while the subsequent hubs and the final enclosure are formed by the *māyā*-syllable. The nature of being an enclosure is defined only in relation to the hubs. The first hub is without the *māyā*-syllable; the upper hubs and the final enclosure are formed by the *māyā*-syllable. This is the true significance.

Now, if that is so, then since the word *atha* is used in various places and because of its connection with the previous cycle (*cakra*), why are the five wheels with five hubs not accepted as being employed separately?

And likewise, even though there is only one wheel, why would there not be the conceptualization of five wheels—including the surrounding enclosure—rather than the conceptualization of a single true hub? To this it is replied: from the beginning, "Tell us the wheel called the Great Wheel," up to the conclusion, "That indeed is the Great Wheel," and because of the understanding that the Great Wheel is a single unity, it is understood that the four wheels are contained within it alone.

The employment of the word *atha* in each respective instance is intended to demonstrate auspiciousness (*māṅgalikatva*) at the commencement of each particular *cakra*. Likewise, since there is no prohibition against conceiving a navel for the enclosures (*veṣṭana*), and because it is both appropriate and results in parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*), these two are not conceived separately.

In some places the word *māyā* is read preceded by the word *bahiḥ*, while in others it is read in the reverse order; the intention here is as follows: where the word *bahiḥ* precedes the word *māyā*, there *bahir-māyayā* means "by means of a *māyā* that has become external," with *bahiḥ* serving as a qualifier of *māyā*. Where, however, the word *bahiḥ* follows the word *māyā* and precedes the word *veṣṭana*, there the word *bahiḥ* is not a qualifier of *māyā*, but rather a qualifier of *veṣṭana*, [meaning] "by means of an unqualified *māyā*" in that context.

Indeed, *māyā* is of two kinds: that which resides in the root mantra of Nṛsiṃha, consisting of the letter *e* with the *bindu*, is understood from the word *māyā* when it is used without an adjunct (*nirupapada*); the other, however, consisting of the letter *e* with the *bindu* joined by the letters *ra* and *ha*, is understood from the word *māyā* when it is accompanied by an adjunct (*sopapada*). Therefore, the essential meaning is that [the deity] becomes enveloped by the *māyā* external to the root mantra, which takes the form *hyīm*.

Then, in the Sudarśana-cakra, there is an encircling by the Māyā residing in the root-mantra; in the sixteen-spoked cakra as well, it is exactly the same. Because the word "external" (*bahiḥ*) is employed prior to the act of encircling, the term "encircling" is qualified by the word "external" for the purpose of excluding an internal encircling. In the Nārāyaṇa-, Vāsudeva-, and Nārasiṃha-cakras, the encircling is performed by the external Māyā, as has already been explained. This is the discernment regarding the extraction of the encircling cakras.

Having thus explained the winding and the extraction of the Great Wheel (mahācakra), he now states the placement of syllables in its hub (nābhi) in order to install the prescribed mantras upon the extracted wheel:

That very Sudarśana is the Great Wheel (Mahācakra). In its center, at the hub, is the Savior (Tāraka), which is the single-syllabled Nārasiṃha. On the six petals, there is the six-syllabled Sudarśana; on the eight petals, the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa; on the twelve petals, the twelve-syllabled Vāsudeva; and on the sixteen petals, the sixteen digits (kalās) beginning with Mātṛkā, accompanied by the bindu. On the thirty-two petals—

The thirty-two-syllable king of mantras is the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter. This indeed is the Sudarśana Great Discus, which fulfills all desires, is the door to liberation, and consists of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, and the nectar of immortality. The Vasus sit to its east, the Rudras to the south, the Ādityas to the west, and the Viśvedevas to the north. Brahmā and Viṣṇu are in the nave, and the sun and moon are on the two sides. This is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "In the imperishable, supreme syllable of the Ṛks..."

"In this sky, the gods have settled upon it. He who does not know it, what will he do with the Ṛg-verses? But those who know it—they sit together here. This is the Great Wheel; whether a child or a youth knows it, he becomes great, he becomes a guru, he becomes a teacher of all mantras. One should perform the fire-oblation with the Anuṣṭubh and the worship with the Anuṣṭubh. This is the slayer of demons and the deliverer from death; having received it from a guru, one should bind it around the neck, the arm, or the topknot. [It is] possessed of the seven continents.
Land is not suitable for the purpose of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); therefore, whatever one may give with faith, that becomes the sacrificial fee. || 2 ||

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us the fruit of this King of Mantras, the Ānuṣṭubha. He, Prajāpati, replied: "He who constantly studies this Nārasiṃha King of Mantras, the Ānuṣṭubha—he becomes purified by Agni; he becomes purified by Vāyu; he becomes purified by Āditya; he becomes purified by Soma; he becomes purified by Satya; he becomes purified by Brahmā; he becomes purified by Viṣṇu; he becomes purified by Rudra; he becomes purified by the Vedas; he becomes purified by all; he becomes purified by all. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first chapter.
The Second Chapter.

Whoever constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter—he crosses over death; he crosses over evil; he crosses over the murder of a Brahmin; he crosses over the murder of an embryo; he crosses over the murder of a hero; he crosses over everything; he crosses over everything. 2.
Thus ends the second chapter.
The Third Chapter.

Whoever constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, he paralyzes fire; he paralyzes wind; he paralyzes the sun; he paralyzes the moon; he paralyzes water; he paralyzes all the gods; he paralyzes all the planetary spirits (grahas); he paralyzes poison—he paralyzes poison.
Thus ends the third chapter.
The Fourth Chapter.

He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, conquers the Bhūrloka; he conquers the Bhuvarloka; he conquers the Svarloka; he conquers the Maharloka; he conquers the Janoloka; he conquers the Tapoloka; he conquers the Satyaloka; he conquers all the worlds; he conquers all the worlds.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
The Fifth Chapter.

Whoever constantly recites this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, he attracts human beings; he attracts gods; he attracts nāgas; he attracts yakṣas; he attracts planetary spirits (grahas); he attracts everyone; he attracts everyone. 5.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
The Sixth Chapter.

He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, he performs the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; he performs the Ukthya sacrifice; he performs the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice; he performs the Atirātra sacrifice; he performs the Aptoryāma sacrifice; he performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice; he performs all sacrifices; he performs all sacrifices. || 6 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
The Seventh Chapter.

He who constantly studies this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter—he studies the Ṛgveda; he studies the Yajurveda; he studies the Sāmaveda; he studies the Atharvaveda; he studies the Aṅgiras; he studies the Vedic branches (śākhās); he studies the Purāṇas; he studies the Kalpas; he studies the Gāthās; he studies the Nārāśaṃsīs; he studies the Praṇava. He who studies the Praṇava studies everything; he studies everything. 7.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
The Eighth Chapter.

One hundred uninitiated persons are equal to one who has been initiated; one hundred initiated persons are equal to one householder; one hundred householders are equal to one forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); one hundred forest-dwellers are equal to one ascetic (*yati*); a full hundred ascetics are equal to one reciter of the *Rudra*; one hundred reciters of the *Rudra* are equal to one reciter of the *Atharvaśiras-śikhā*; and one hundred reciters of the *Atharvaśiras-śikhā* are equal to one reciter of the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*). It is the same as that.

This is the supreme abode of one who meditates upon the King of Mantras, where the sun does not scorch, where the wind does not blow, where the moon does not shine, where the stars do not gleam, where fire does not burn, and where death does not enter; it is eternal bliss, supreme bliss, auspicious, peaceful, ever-auspicious (Sadāśiva), saluted by Brahmā and the other gods, the object of meditation for yogis, having gone to which yogis do not return. This has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse: "That is the supreme [abode] of Viṣṇu..."

"The wise ever behold that station, like an eye extended in the sky. The inspired poets, praising and ever-watchful, kindle it—that which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu. This indeed belongs to one who is free from desire; this indeed belongs to one who is free from desire.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth chapter.

By the word *tat* (that), it is the wheel (*cakra*) with thirty-two spokes and thirty-two petals that is indicated; by the word *eva* (only/itself), having restricted the reference to that very wheel, he shows—by the principle of "that being the beginning" (*tad-ādinyāya*)—that the four wheels above, such as the Sudarśana and others, are also of the nature of the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*), because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "Great Wheel. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in its center," since "navels" (*nābhi*) are the central hubs that serve as the enclosures for the Great Wheel, the expression "in the center, in the two navels" (*madhye nābhyām*) is stated in order to distinguish those [central hubs] from the [other] centers located at the middle of the earth.

It is called *tāraka* because it delivers one across *saṃsāra*; thus the syllable *praṇava* is the *tāraka*. That which is the single syllable of Nṛsiṃha is the *akṣara*. Furthermore, this form is explained as the *akṣara* for the welfare of the world; this was explained during the commentary on the word "Nṛsiṃha," and it is recognized from that very word *akṣara*. Likewise, from the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) "Nārasiṃha," everything beginning with the Sāman is understood as the object of worship.

Then, in order to state that when all objects of worship have been realized, there is only one object of worship called the primary manifestation of Nṛsiṃha, he qualifies [the subject] by saying, "That becomes the single syllable. Having restated that which is the imperishable (akṣara) Nārasiṃha as the object of worship, the meaning is that the meditation is enjoined—both as being "that one" and as being "imperishable"—by virtue of its residing in the center of the hub of the Great Wheel and its connection with the Ocean of Milk.

In this regard, some maintain that because of the inclusion of the qualification "the single-syllabled Nārasiṃha," the *praṇava* mixed with the single-syllabled Nṛsiṃha mantra should be placed on the navel; this too is not contradictory, as it is based on tradition. Even under that view, from the secondary derivative (taddhita) "Nārasiṃha," the single-syllabled Nṛsiṃha mantra mixed with the *praṇava* is understood to be the object of worship pertaining to the fundamental Nṛsiṃha-arrangement (*mūlanṛsiṃhavyūha*) within the context, excluding the thirty-two-fold Nṛsiṃha-arrangement.

And therefore, this single-syllable Nṛsiṃha mantra, being a constituent part of this vidyā, because it denotes the aforementioned object of worship, stands as an alternative to the *praṇava* alone; however, for the single-syllable Nṛsiṃha mantra, the *praṇava* is indeed mandatory.

This is the true meaning. From this point forward, regarding the placement of the respective mantras upon the various wheels (*cakras*), the mention of "petals" (*patra*) should be understood as intended to exclude the spaces between the petals and the intervals between them. On six petals, there is the *Sudarśana*; the meaning is that the six-syllabled *Sudarśana* mantra is to be placed starting from the petal in the northeast (*aiśāna*). This should be applied similarly to the subsequent petals. On eight petals, there is the eight-syllabled *Nārāyaṇa*; some maintain that it consists of eight syllables by including the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) within it.

In the same way, on the twelve petals, there is the twelve-syllabled Vāsudeva mantra; here too, the state of having twelve syllables is as before. On the sixteen petals, there are the sixteen vowels—the first letters of the Mātṛkā-mantra—accompanied by the nasal bindu (bindusahita). On the thirty-two petals, there is the thirty-two-syllabled Ānuṣṭubh king of mantras manifested from the Sāman, which consists of each individual syllable of the root mantra itself.

As for the fact that each individual syllable on each leaf must be encased by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), this is because of the Vedic scripture which states: "The syllable Oṃ occurs on both sides of every single syllable. That limb called the *astra*, when worshipped as the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*), causes terror when directed toward an undesirable object; therefore, it is the fifth limb, the *astra*. For this very reason, while explaining the *astra* limb-mantra, we stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The two verbal roots *su* and *tras* exist [in the word *asutra*], having the meanings of casting away and trembling."

"Having cast away what is undesirable by means of those two, it is struck down by the fire of the *phaṭ*-sword"—this is the meaning of the phrase "the door to liberation that fulfills all desires," as already explained. Regarding the statement "it becomes consisting of *Ṛk*, consisting of *Yajus*, consisting of *Sāman*, consisting of *Brāhmaṇa*, and consisting of *Amṛta*," the five suffixes *mayaṭ* should be understood in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). Thus, it is abundant in *Ṛk*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan*. As for "consisting of *Brāhmaṇa*," by the word *brāhmaṇa* the *Atharvaveda* is meant; this is the *Brāhmaṇaveda*.

This is because they are designated as "Brāhmaṇas. They are called "Vedas" because they are to be meditated upon with the understanding that they are the Vedas due to their abundance of Vedic content. Alternatively, the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*); thus, the meaning is that they consist of modifications of the Vedas. [The term] "consisting of nectar" (*amṛtamaya*) means having a navel abounding in milk, or having a navel that is a modification of milk. By the word "of that" (*tasya*), Viṣṇu residing in the navel—the primary manifestation (*mūla-vyūha*) of Nṛsiṃha—is referred to.

He speaks of the attendant deities: "The Vasus sit as attendants in the east, the Rudras in the south, the Ādityas in the west, the Viśvedevas in the north, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara at the navel. Having thus described the directional and central attendants, he now describes the lateral attendants: "The Sun and the Moon [are] on the two sides," that is to say, in the regions of the flanks. This very Great Wheel is celebrated by means of a Ṛgvedic verse.

In that great wheel (*mahācakra*), which is imperishable (*akṣara*); [the word] *aśu* is a form of the root *aś* in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and *sara* is used in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvarthe*), thus meaning "that which possesses pervasion. It is supreme (*parama*), excellent, and situated as all-pervading like space (*vyoma*). The prefix *adhi* denotes the sense of being above. The mention of *ṛcaḥ* (of the *ṛks*) is for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtha*); the *ṛks* are the Vedas. In that wheel, all (*viśve*) the gods (*devāḥ*) sat down (*niṣeduḥ*), remaining there in the form of Nṛsiṃha. Alternatively, *ṛcaḥ* may be taken as a genitive.

In the wheel characterized by pervasiveness, which is connected to the *anuṣṭubh* [meter], all the Vedas reside; this means it is the wheel associated with the *Sudarśana-mantra* and others. As for the practitioner who does not know—that is, does not worship—that great wheel: what is the use of the *ṛc*, whether that is the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, or specifically the *ṛc* consisting of the *anuṣṭubh* meter? By this, he demonstrates that one should perform the worship of the *anuṣṭubh* only as being imbued with the worship of the Great Wheel, and never devoid of it.

"Those who know this thus—in brief"—this has been explained according to its meaning. The word *iti* indicates the completion of the *Ṛk*. He who knows or worships this Great Wheel (*mahācakra*)—whether he be a child or a youth—attains this fruit: he becomes great; he attains a great standing among people; or alternatively, he becomes "Great Viṣṇu. He is a teacher to be worshipped like a god by all. He becomes the instructor and the one who imparts instruction for all mantras.

"One should perform the oblation with an Anuṣṭubh verse manifested by the Sāman"—this oblation is an ancillary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*). Since no specific substance is prescribed therein, one should daily offer as the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) boiled rice accompanied by clarified butter (*ājya*). Likewise, since no specific number is prescribed, it may be performed once or twelve times. Alternatively, because the ten words contained in the Sūtra have been explained in both the *Mūlanṛsiṃhavyūha* and the *Dvātriṃśadvyūha*, one should perform the oblation with reference to both.

Then, having offered with the words "to the fierce Nṛsiṃha, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, who has three eyes, and who holds the Pināka bow in his hand," one should offer to the fierce Nṛsiṃha who consists of the thirty-two manifestations beginning with Brahmā; in this manner, the root mantra is repeated at every step. Alternatively, because of the singular number in the word "anuṣṭubhā," one should recite the root mantra once, ending with the word *svāhā*, and perform the renunciation (*tyāga*) for each individual step.

Likewise, there is an ellipsis to be supplied: "one should perform worship with the *anuṣṭubh* verse manifested by the *sāman*, including the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and so forth. Here too, as with the *mantra* for the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should choose whether there is a repetition of the *mantra* or not. This very *Mahācakra*, which destroys demons and delivers one from death, should be bound upon the neck, the arm, or the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) by one who has obtained it through the grace of the Guru. For that Guru, even the earth consisting of the seven continents, though doubled over, would not suffice as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Therefore, with faith and devotion, whatever land one can give according to one's capacity—that shall be the sacrificial fee.

Thus, the previously mentioned meditation based on scripture was understood as being subsumed within the *pañcāṅganyāsa* according to one school of thought. Now, upon examining other schools, it is found to be subsumed within the *mahācakra* itself; therefore, because the *praṇava* is subsumed within the syllables of the root mantra in the passage, "therefore there is an *oṃkāra* on both sides of every syllable," this *mahācakra* is primarily centered on the *praṇava*. Since an abundance of *śaktis* is heard of in that [wheel], it becomes externally enveloped by *māyā*.

Because it is heard repeatedly that [the Self] "is enveloped by external *māyā*," and because, in the course of explaining the extracted words, it is heard at every step—specifically in the passage beginning "by its own majesty (*mahiman*) all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings"—that *māyā*, denoted by the word "majesty" (*mahiman*), serves as the instrument for all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings; therefore, [the Self] is, respectively, enveloped by *māyā* as the substratum for the worlds such as the earth, the Vedas such as the *Ṛgveda*, the gods such as Agni, and the selves.

Because it is heard that this is a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this worship consists precisely of the encircled *māyā* support situated within the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*). It does not, however, pertain to the root *Nṛsiṃha* for the purpose of the five-limbed ritual placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*). Because it is more internal, this worship pertains to the Great Wheel alone. Furthermore, since even that [Great Wheel] has come down through tradition (*sampradāya*), it should be adopted; such is the alternative regarding the worship. In that regard as well, some maintain that the latter worship alone should be adopted, because it has come down in greater accordance with tradition.

In that view, the fourfold mantra consisting of the Praṇava, Sāvitrī, Yajurlakṣmī, and Nṛsiṃha-Gāyatrī is a limb manifested as Sāman; it should be applied according to its suitability as the illuminator of the Great Wheel (mahācakra), and likewise worshipped as the Great Wheel—this is the secret and the essential truth.

Having thus fully expounded the Nṛsiṃha-hṛdaya-vidyā in accordance with all the schools of thought, [the author] now introduces a narrative in the form of a dialogue to state the fruit for its practitioner by means of the maxim of *kaimutya* (a fortiori):
the first chapter.

In this context, there are eight chapters beginning with "The gods, indeed... and ending with "...that belongs to one who is free from desire. At the conclusion of each chapter, there is a double repetition. The gods said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us the fruit of this mantra, which is distinguished by the aforementioned meditation. Prajāpati replied as previously explained. He [the practitioner], being a twofold meditator, [should recite] this King of Mantras, the King of Samans, which is referred to by the word "this" (*etam*) and which contains the previously mentioned knowledge.

The *Nārasiṃha* [Sāman] contains within it the meditation (*upāsanā*) on the Brahman in the form of Nṛsiṃha; it is composed in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter (*anuṣṭupchandaska*). It is called "eternal" (*nitya*) because, by means of the realization of the Brahman with form, it brings about the realization of the eternal, formless Brahman. He studies—that is, recites—it constantly. Since the attainment of the fruits to be described occurs merely from the recitation of such a Sāman, what need is there to mention the performance of the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*)? With this intention, he says "he studies, he studies" in various places. Alternatively, "he studies constantly" means he studies it as a rule (*niyamena*).

Alternatively, *nityam adhi* means "constantly above," that is, he knows [it]. All roots meaning "to go" (*gaty-artha*) also mean "to know" (*jñānārtha*). The meaning is: he who, having completed his daily duties such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), practices this knowledge at the prescribed time. Alternatively, because of the construction *nityam ānuṣṭubham*, it shows the constancy of the *ānuṣṭubha* Sāman, and not of the other forms of the Sāman. Alternatively, *nityam* refers to the ritual acts such as the twilight worship; he knows [them] "above" (*adhi*). This is what is being said:

Therefore, one worships the deities to be propitiated through the daily twilight rites (*nitya-saṃdhyopāsana*), the *agnihotra*, and so forth, as having the playful form (*līlā-vigraha*) of Nṛsiṃha; that is to say, they are permeated by this very knowledge (*vidyā*). Alternatively, that practitioner who is incapable of knowing the method for practicing the aforementioned knowledge, yet daily studies, recites, or mutters the text that expounds this knowledge according to the rule of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), he too attains the fruit to be described hereafter.

By the power of his recitation (japa), the Supreme Lord, out of compassion, explains right here the method for practicing that vidyā, from the stage with form (sākāra) up to the stage without form (nirākāra). And so it is heard at the end: "This indeed is the supreme abode for one who meditates upon, recites, or chants the King of Mantras (mantrarāja) which contains this vidyā," and so forth.

That lay follower (upāsaka) becomes purified and sanctified by means of the forms of Nṛsiṃha to be worshipped as Fire, Wind, Sun, Moon, Truth, Brahman, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Vedas; he becomes purified by all other forms of Nṛsiṃha to be worshipped as well. The repetition [of the final phrase] indicates the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the commentary on the first chapter.
The Second Chapter.

From this point forward, he speaks in order to describe the incidental results—whether they be those desired for specific goals (*kāmya*) or devoid of such desires—which arise from the constant practice of this *vidyā*, the study of the texts that expound it, or its recitation (*japa*). A practitioner (*upāsaka*) who, by means of the constant practice of this *vidyā* or its recitation, desires the destruction of sin, constantly studies this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha, in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter; the meaning of this has already been stated.

Likewise, from this point until the final chapter, wherever the word *ya* (masculine) occurs, it refers—by virtue of its established status as the previously mentioned Nṛsiṃha-vidyā—to either the reciter or the student who has mastered that vidyā through its recitation; similarly, by the masculine pronoun *tat*, that very same person is referred to. Furthermore, because of the repeated use of the masculine pronoun *tat* in various places, the fruit is understood to accrue—either individually or collectively, according to suitability—to that very same constant practice or recitation.

He crosses over death, evil, the killing of a learned Brahmin—where "bhrūṇa" means a fetus—or else where "bhrūṇa" refers to one who has been initiated and is an expounder of the meaning of the Veda along with its limbs; he crosses over the killing of a hero—a hero being a son or a Kṣatriya engaged in a Soma sacrifice—as well as every other sin. The repetition of the final phrase indicates the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the commentary on the second chapter.
The Third Chapter.

Whoever constantly studies this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, he paralyzes fire, wind, the sun, the moon, water, all the gods, the planets, and poison; this is the indication of the fruit of paralyzing. The repetition at the end indicates the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the commentary on the third chapter.
The Fourth Chapter.

The declaration of the fruit is as follows: he who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, conquers Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, Satya, and all else, including the world of Pātāla. The repetition at the end indicates the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth chapter.
The Fifth Chapter.

The declaration of the fruit is as follows: "He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, attracts humans, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, grahas, and others besides them. The repetition [of the final word] indicates the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth chapter.
The Sixth Chapter.

The declaration of the fruit is as follows: "He who constantly studies this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, performs the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, the Aptoryāma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, and indeed all other sacrifices. The repetition at the end indicates the conclusion of the chapter. Nor should it be argued how this can be a declaration of fruit according to the maxim "the others are purposeless" (*anyānarthakyāt*).

Since the practice of this knowledge is to be accomplished solely through mental activity, and since such activity is extremely difficult to achieve compared to the performance of ritual action, there is no futility of other [means] due to the difference in qualification; thus, everything is faultless.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth chapter.
The Seventh Chapter.

He who constantly studies this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter—he [studies] the Ṛks, the Yajus, the Sāmans, as well as the Atharva and the Aṅgiras; for this is the encapsulation of the Triple Veda (trayī), since the three Vedas exist within its interval.

And likewise, in that very Brāhmaṇa, it is stated repeatedly that Prajāpati first saw the Atharvan, then the Trayī (the three Vedas), and then the Aṅgiras; therefore, the statement "he studies the branches, the Purāṇas, the Kalpas, the Gāthās, the Nārāśaṃsīs, and the Praṇava" is a declaration of the fruit [of study]. And here, by saying "he who studies the Praṇava studies everything," the author shows the equality of both [the root-mantra and the Praṇava] through the equality of their fruits. Consequently, there is an option between the two for both recitation (japa) and meditative concentration (samādhi).

And likewise, regarding the performance of obligatory rites when there is a desire for a specific fruit, there is a particular mode of practice: some say that at the end of the recitation of the root mantra, the utterance of the word denoting that specific fruit must be performed; others, however, maintain that this should be done by desire alone, even without that [utterance]. One should investigate which of these is the traditional practice (*sāṃpradāyika*). The repetition [of the concluding phrase] indicates the completion of the chapter. Thus ends the commentary on the seventh chapter.
The Eighth Chapter.

Having thus described all the incidental fruits of constant practice, he now declares the supreme excellence and the most excellent fruit for the one who practices that knowledge—the reciter and the student—by way of their relative degrees of superiority: "One hundred uninitiated [students] are equal to a single initiated one; one hundred initiated students are [equal to one lifelong celibate], but not with reference to the perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika), because the latter is the most excellent of all."

One hundred householders are equal to one [of another] householder; one hundred forest-dwellers are equal to one forest-dweller; and one hundred ascetics are equal to one ascetic. This gradation pertains merely to the formal adoption of the stages of life (āśrama), and not with regard to the performance of duties prescribed for those stages.

Furthermore, a full hundred ascetics who have merely accepted the stage of life (*āśrama*) and reside in any [such] hermitage performing the *rudrajāpya* is equal to one hundred *rudrajāpyas* performed by someone residing in any hermitage who recites the *Atharvaśiras* and *Śikhā*; and a hundred such reciters of the *Atharvaśiras* and *Śikhā* is equal to one reciter of the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*). Since this gradation of excellence culminates in the reciter of the King of Mantras who possesses this Vidyā, one who possesses this Vidyā is the most excellent of all.

It is understood. Just as the state of increasing degrees of bliss culminates in its rest within the *brahman*, therefore the bliss of the *brahman* alone is the most excellent. For this reason, it is well known that this is the supreme abode, the station for the practitioner, the reciter, or the performer who meditates upon the King of Mantras containing this Vidyā.

There, in the place of the Ocean of Milk, the sun does not scorch; where the wind does not blow; where the moon does not shine; where the stars do not gleam; where fire does not burn; where death does not enter; where [neither]...

[It is] suffering, eternal bliss, supreme bliss, everlasting, peaceful, ever-auspicious, saluted by Brahmā and others, the object of meditation for yogis, that place having gone to which yogis do not return; this very station is celebrated in a Ṛgvedic verse as "that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. By the word "which" (yat), the station situated in the Ocean of Milk is referred to, because of its recognition as the "supreme abode" (paramapada).

The wise ones (*sūrayaḥ*) are the worshippers (*upāsakāḥ*). If, through the distinction of their worship, there is identity (*tādātmya*) within that worship, then the fruit is union (*sāyujya*); and consequently, Viṣṇu alone is the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*). In both cases, the genitive case in "of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇoḥ*) should be understood as being like [the expression] "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*).

Alternatively, if it is by way of the relationship between the object of worship and the worshipper, then the *Anuṣṭubh*-knowledge belongs to that Nṛsiṃha-Viṣṇu; his supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*) is his supreme abode, such as the center of the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*) or the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīrodārṇava*), and the worshippers—those who practice, recite, or study it—always, at all times, behold him there.

When it is asked what that [state] is like, he says: "Like the eye in heaven"—that is, like the solar orb in the celestial world (*dyuloka*), which is spread out (*ātatam*) on all sides, extensive, circular, consisting of light, and the cause of the eclipsing of all other lights; therefore, the entry of the sun, moon, stars, and so forth into it is prohibited, as is their power to burn, by such passages as "where the sun does not shine," and so on.

Thus, when suffering pertaining to the divine (ādhidaivika) has been negated, he negates the attainment of internal suffering (ādhyātmika) with the words "where there is no suffering. When the mere absence of suffering is attained, there would be a state of insentience like deep sleep; to exclude that, he says "ever-blissful" (sadānanda). "Worshipped by Brahmā and others" means that place called the Great Wheel (mahācakra), which is to be worshipped by its attendants—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—who reside in the navel according to the principle of being at the beginning [of the sequence]. "Having gone where... [refers to that place].

He states that this is the place to be reached: "tadviprāsaḥ" (to that, the wise). That such a place [is reached by] "viprāsaḥ"—the wise ones, the Brāhmaṇas, the practitioners who are "vipanyavaḥ," meaning intelligent and endowed with the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) in *samādhi*. Being "jāgṛvāṃsaḥ," even while in the waking state, having transcended the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], they "samindhate," meaning they kindle it thoroughly. However, in the view of identity (*tādātmya*), the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa passage should be explained according to their own literal forms. The word "iti" indicates the completion of the mantra.
The practice of these four quarters illuminates the conclusion of all the Upaniṣads; thus, everything is established as stainless.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth chapter.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācāryas.
The commentary on the Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīyopaniṣad is complete.
